Quest for the most beautiful of women.
Quest for the most beautiful bride.
Quest for bride as handsome as the hero.
Hero visits all islands to see if he can find woman to rival wife’s beauty.
Quest for the most beautiful bouquet.
Quest for the finest of chains.
Quest for the best of bread.
Quest for the best of meat.
Quest for the worst of meat.
Quest for the finest of linen.
Quest for the smallest of dogs.
Quest for the finest of horses.
King seeks one richer (more magnificent) than himself.
Quest for bride richest and poorest.
Quest for the greatest of fools.
Quest for three persons as stupid as his wife.
Quest for person who can withdraw sword.
Quest for the spring of the biggest of three rivers east of Gardariki.
Quest for ornament (jewel, etc.) to match one already at hand.
Liar escapes from devil: quest for greater liar.
Quest for only person who can cure certain sickness.
Quest for the most beautiful rug.
Quest for the most beautiful ring.
Quest for marvelous objects or animals.
Quest for things seen in dream.
Quest for Water of Life (water which will resuscitate).
Quest for the water of youth.
Quest for silver pillar covered with golden flowers.
Quest for three feathers of marvelous bird.
Makes all other birds sing with him.
Quest for fat of water blackbirds.
Quest for pigs killed by night and revived by day.
Quest for cow with liver of tallow.
Quest for horse with peacock tail.
Quest for creature with a single horn mounting to heaven with single red hair on its head.
Quest for sheep that is a hound by night and a sheep by day.
Quest for marvelous parts or possessions of animals.
Quest for vulture’s egg figured with golden letters.
Quest for animal with golden chain.
Quest for oil of magic pig.
Quest for liver of thunder and heart of dragon.
Quest for honey from the royal bee-hive.
Quest for marvelous fruit with princess inside.
Quest for apples that are under the sea.
Quest for berries from tree guarded by giants.
Quest for flower that sends forth its fragrance for hundred miles around.
Quest for flower of a tree inside the seventh of a series of forts.
Quest for wonderful but man-killing flower.
Quest for branches of tree guarded by dragon.
Quest for axe which sticks in beam outside a tower.
Quest for ferule to fit staff.
Quest for covering that is kept in an emerald box by the well.
Quest for garment of spider web.
Quest for beautiful saree for the queen.
Quest for silken turban on tree sixteen rivers and seven seas away.
Task: achieving kingship by bringing silk from bazaar.
Quest for roll of cotton driven by the wind.
Quest for marvelous objects or animals—miscellaneous.
Quest for marvelous golden wood for knife handle.
Quest for great tank of Indra (god).
Cubs furnish lion’s (tiger’s, etc.) milk to hero.
Quest for cheese made from milk of wild white buffaloes.
Quest for wonderful but vicious horse.
Quest for place where sun comes up.
Quest for the bottom of the sea.
Quest for tears shed into the sea.
Quest for ornaments bride has worn in former birth.
Quest: learning what fear of Death is.
Quest for the anger of God.
Man is so fortunate that people say that he has everything but the anger of God. He seeks it and finds it with much misfortune.
Quest for glass of all waters.
Quest for bouquet of all flowers.
Quest for the hazelnuts of ay, ay, ay.
Quest for wood neither crooked nor straight.
Quest for king’s joy and woe.
(King tells of adventures in which his brothers are all killed.
Woman seeks unknown father of her child.
Boy twitted with illegitimacy seeks unknown father.
Boy twitted with illegitimacy seeks unknown mother.
Quest for bride for king like picture he has seen.
Quest for unknown woman whose picture has aroused man’s love.
Quest for girl hero has seen in dream.
Quest for dangerous maiden as bride.
Quest for princess transformed into skein of silk.
Quest for woman exactly like another.
Quest for princess hidden by father.
Quest for son of sinless couple.
Quest for unknown bridegroom who has certain name and is only son among seven children of father.
Quest for unknown objects or places.
Hero seeks them on the heads of swallows, the necks of swans, the backs of geese, and the tongues of reindeer.
Quest for unknown lines of poem.
Unspelling quest: journey to disenchant (free) captives.
Quest for vanished wife and son.
Husband seeks wife and son in many countries.
Quest for husband who has been reincarnated as cat.
King in quest of his prime minister who has left him in anger.
Question: What is it women most desire.
Quest for armor from a grave mound.
Quest for gold from a grave mound.
Quest to distant sage for advice.
Quest for person who has not known sorrow.
Heroes seek judgment as to which is greatest.
A person is put to various tests in the attempt to make him show fear.
Deity assumes frightful guises to frighten child.
Chief of dead assumes frightful guises to frighten visitors.
Ogress assumes frightful guises to frighten messengers.
Fear test: behaving as if enemy is coming in order to see who will flee and who will stay and fight.
Suitor tested by apparent threats to his person.
Fear test: serpent put in flour so that fearless youth kneads it into the dough.
Test: going without fear through a wilderness filled with all manner of beasts.
Fear test: staying in frightful place.
Fear test: staying in haunted house.
Fear test: staying in haunted house where corpse drops piecemeal down chimney.
Fear test: staying in haunted house where horse carcass drops down chimney.
Fear test: staying in haunted house infested by cats.
Fear test: night watch with magic cats.
Fear test: staying in enchanted castle at night where the devil gives a moral speech and prophesies.
Fear test: spending night in house (hall) haunted by demon (monster).
Fear test: spending night in church.
Fear test: going into the church at night and ringing the bell.
Fear test: staying under gallows at night.
Fear test: spending night by grave.
Fear test: taking boy to frightful enemy’s tent.
Fear test: playing cards with devil in church.
Fear test: passing through door guarded by savage hound and armed soldier.
Fear test: undergoing terrifying experience out of doors on Hallowe’en.
Fear test: bringing from a hill, seized by a demon, the fattest of goats.
Fear test: stealing clothes from ghosts.
Fear test: playing game with reassembled dead man.
Fear test: eating and drinking from skulls.
Fear test: fetching skulls from a charnel house.
Fear test: keeping goal in hurling-match for corpses.
Fearless hero frightened by being awakened with cold water.
Fearless hero frightened by being awakened by eels put down his back.
Vigil for dead father: youngest son alone endures frightful experiences.
Ceiling, floors, and walls knock together.
Three-night watch over grave to guard man from devil.
Watch for thieves in the king’s garden.
Test: sleeping by princess three nights without looking at her or disturbing her.
Thumb cut and salt put on it in order to remain awake.
Dirk stuck into thigh in order to keep from sleeping.
Grains slowly munched in order to keep from sleeping.
Continual pricking with pin in order to remain awake.
Large fire and water for washing eyes as device of expectant lover.
Tested by making girl serve woman who has leprosy, etc.
Endurance test: scalding mush scattered on heroine’s naked body; rasp-tongued dogs lick wounds.
Test: sleeping naked on floor in cold.
Test: sewing clothes into boy’s hands and tearing them off together with the skin.
Endurance test: hero maintains silence in the snake pit.
Hero pursues and kills fugitive in spite of bleeding wounds.
Test: repeating incantation continuously for months.
Attempt to kill hero by burning him in fire.
Test: swallowing heated brass and iron ornaments.
Attempt to kill hero by feeding him burning food.
Attempt to kill hero by smoke.
Attempt to kill hero by having him smoke fatal pipe.
Attempt to freeze hero to death.
Attempt to kill hero by feeding him poisoned food.
Attempt to kill saint by giving him poisoned drink.
Hero given food in which thorns are hidden.
Attempt to kill hero by poisoning clothing.
Hero is sent to capture a giant clam, so that he can be killed.
Bent tree is released so as to tear hero to pieces.
Clashing rocks test: hero to pass between them.
Attempt to kill hero by throwing him on sharp spine or spike.
Vain attempt to kill hero on stairway set with razors.
Hero is caught in cleft of tree.
Unavailing attempt to kill hero by hanging.
Attempt to kill hero by letting plank fall on him.
Hero is pushed over a precipice.
Attempt to kill hero on dangerous toboggan.
Test: playing game with ferocious beast.
Bear demands that heroine play Blindman’s Buff.
Contest in enduring cold: frost and the hare.
Contest in enduring cold: wind overcomes frost.
Contest in crossing river of fire.
Bad character shown by the eyes.
Which was the most generous—husband, robber, or lover?

Woman has promised her lover to go to him on her wedding night. Husband lets her go. On way she meets robbers and tells her story. Robbers take her to her lover. She tells what has happened. Lover returns her immediately to her husband.
Which was most generous—husband, lover, or magician (similar)?
Ruler vies with minister in generosity. Minister declared loser and condemned to die. Pardoned on acknowledging defeat.
Philosopher teaches son to beg before stone statues.
In this way he will acquire patience.
Test of patience: king accepts strong reproof and criticism.
Test of patience: those who wish to enter city gate must endure insults of old men there who mock them.
Man shows his patience by accepting blow in face with stool thrown by his superior in monastery.
Monk fails in test of patience.
He tries to live alone to test it. One day he loses his temper at a cup which overturns and he breaks it.
Test of patience by asking irrelevant riddles.
Test of curiosity: mouse in jug.
A man is promised a beautiful clock if he can mind his own business for a whole year.
Plowman is promised a horse if he can say a paternoster without thinking of anything else. In the midst of the recitation, he asks if he will get the saddle and bridle too. He loses bargain.
Test of honesty: man entrusted with treasure.
Test of fidelity by feigning death.
Cock feigns death to see what hens will say about him.
Test of fidelity through submitting hero to temptations.
Test of fidelity through offering suspected assassin opportunity to commit the murder.
Lover’s fidelity tested by going to bed with mistress and only kissing.
Lover’s fidelity tested by making love to maid.
Wife tests her husband’s fidelity by tempting him in the guise of another woman.
Lover’s fidelity tested by substituting maid in mistress’s bed at assignation.
Old uncle tests nephew’s fidelity by sleeping with his beloved.
Husband’s (wife’s) willingness to die for mate disappears when Death seems to arrive.
Old woman’s willingness to die for daughter disappears when Death seems to arrive.
Rose given by supernatural wife to husband when he leaves for home will shed as many petals as times he thinks of her.
Test of fidelity by feigning sleep in same bed as calumniated hero or alone in the forest with him.
Obedience of sons tested by offering them apple.
They are each offered a slice of apple. The king says, “Open your mouth and receive what I give you”. Eldest son insulted; youngest obeys and receives kingdom as reward.
Adam’s (Eve’s) disobedience blamed: blamer immediately disobeys orders.
Old man contented till forbidden to leave city.
Pope tests women’s disobedience: not to look into box.
Obedience of king’s subjects tested by willingness to allow spear to be carried crosswise into houses.
King tests gardener’s obedience by playing thief.
Apple test of worthiness for friendship.
Father gives son three apples to offer to those he meets. If the man eats all, avoid him; if he divides, make friends with him.

A man kills a hog and tells his friends that he has killed a man and asks where he can hide the body. All of them drive him away and only his father’s half-friend remains true to him in his feigned trouble.
Of three friends the least loved proves true in emergency.
Test of friendship: substitute as murderer.

A man in misery gives himself up as a murderer rather than endure further misery. His friend tries to take on himself the guilt and be substituted. The real murderer, touched by the generosity, confesses.
Test of friendship: to go with one to death.
In the final test none help and only her legs save her.
Test of friendship: death feigned to test debtor friends.
Test of friendship: the imagined refusal.

Man wonders if his friend would lend him his palfrey. Decides he would refuse. Imagines that he has actually asked for the palfrey and has been refused. Cools toward his friend. The owner of the horse asks for an explanation. He agrees to lend him the horse and they are reconciled.
Test of friendship: the power of money.
Spendthrift loses his friends in poverty.
Sultan takes disguise of beggar to test friends.
Friends desert when man reports loss of his money.
Friends refuse to fight against each other.
Sword too heavy to lift against a friend.
Pregnant wife left in charge of friend.
Friendship kept up even during sons’ jealousy and enmity.
Test of friendship: to take a slap publicly from friend.
Test of friendship: mourner says dead husband can be touched only by sinless person; volunteers for cremating body immediately disperse.
Test of friendship: loyalty to condemned friend.
Fight with father’s old friend, though only to mention who he is would assure the youth a friendly reception.
Test of valor: not flinching under a blow.
Test of valor: rousing servant’s anger.

Nobleman, when examining servants for hire, bids each stand before him and comb his long beard. Occasionally he snaps at them as if to bite them. Those who dodge he lets go; those who offer fight he employs.
Test of valor worthy for kingship: taking possession of royal insignia placed between two ferocious lions.
Test of valor: fight with giant.
Test of valor: attack by warrior and hound.
Warriors battle against leader as test of valor.
Prince chooses shorter but more dangerous road.
Master tests disciple by asking him if he will be willing to plunge with him into the Indus.
Test of strength: pulling up tree by roots.
Test of strength: cutting tree with one stroke.
Test of strength: lifting stone (fireplace, etc.
Before undertaking rescue, bat tests strength by lifting stone.
Test of strength: breaking heavy glass bottle over loaf of rye bread.
Test of strength: heavy stone flung at boaster; he throws it back.
Test of strength: breaking spirited horse.
Strength contest: contestants stand with back to rock on opposite side, an iron ring around neck of each connected by chain.
They tug until ring severs neck of one.
Test of strength: breaking witch’s back.
Test of strength: pushing out heavy ferry.
Test of strength: pulling in two iron bars passing through hole.
Test of strength: shooting through seven iron plates with arrow.
Mighty-of-His-Mouth and Mighty-of-His-Hands decide to live together to test strength.
Test of gratitude: magician makes pupil believe himself superior.
Though he has promised magician great rewards he forgets his promise.
Test for admission to warrior band.
Frightful meal as test of leadership.
Test of leadership (obedience): swallowing mouse without vomiting.
Test of championship: sitting on pillow covering egg without breaking egg.
Man tests industry of prospective servant girl.
Stone under fertile woman produces milk; under barren woman produces blood.
Loathly deed performed as evidence of Christian virtue.
Druid attempts to shake king’s faith by magic manifestation.
Man commanded by saint to leap into fiery furnace: unharmed.
Magic manifestation required as proof in test of saintliness.
Saint tested by visit of deity in disguise.
Test of worthiness for bishop: plowing without plowshare.
Saint drinks poison without injury as proof of power of Christianity.
Saint’s horse miraculously preserved as proof of power of Christianity before fairy.
Transformation by saint as proof of Christianity before druid.
Wizard (druid) burned, saint saved in test of power of Christianity.
Test of steadfastness of love for God: though warned in dream man refuses to part with sacred stone.
Ability to cross bridge as test of righteousness.
Test of repentance: culprit exposed to situation identical to that in which he sinned.
Social rank determined according to portion taken from cauldron of food.
Fruitfulness of nature as proof of kingly right.
Test imposed on young princes as candidates for throne.
Two deities test virtues of a king.
The burning forge (smithy): he who salvages anvil will be king.
He who wins maiden queen is king.
Captives re-blinded if they cross stepping-stones without stumbling.
Tests of possession of magic powers.
Test of magic powers: telling sex of unborn goat.
Test of skill for a fakir: heating iron and passing it through hands without burning them.
Test of goddess’ favor: man throws away his wife’s jewel-box to see if she can regain it with the aid of goddess.
Test of goddess’s favor: husband drowns his son to see if his wife’s tutelary goddess can bring him back to life.
Test of sex: to discover person masking as of other sex.
Test of sex of girl masking as man.
Test of sex of girl masking as man: peas spread on floor.
Test of girl masking as man: nuts and corn spread on floor.
Test of sex of girl masking as man: spinning wheel brought.
Men take no notice; women interested.
Test of sex of girl masking as man: choosing flowers.
Girl will choose a carnation; man a rose.
Test of sex of girl masking as man: ball thrown into lap.
Girls spread legs to catch it; men not.
Woman throws apple to man in woman’s dress.
He puts his legs together to catch it.
Test of sex of man masking as girl: jumping over pit (only man succeeds).
Test of sex of girl masking as man: nuts and apples offered.
Men put them in their shirts, girls into their handkerchiefs.
Test of sex of girl masking as man: warned by a parrot, she picks only one flower.
Test of sex of man masking as girl: arms placed among baskets and war-trumpet sounded.
Recognition of good health by hearing voice.
Recognition of good health by smoke rising from chimney.
Time measured by worn iron shoes.
Time measured by fit of ring.
Land measured according to amount within person’s view.
Land measured according to amount encompassed during certain hours.
Test of cleanliness by being shaken to see if lice fall off.
Two opponents test their powers by having their dogs fight.
Litter of puppies tested by throwing them one by one at hanging hide of wild beast, and keeping the one that grips hide.
Puppy grows up to be great hunting dog.
Man and king compete by letting their domestic animals fight.
Goaling match between fairies and mortals as test of supremacy.
Death as penalty for losing foot-race.

Test of memory: Solomon asks Marchus question, receives answer; fourteen months later he asks second question based on first, again receives correct answer; four months later asks third question based on first two, again receives correct answer.
Golden apple as prize in beauty contest.
Women to appear naked in beauty contest.
Contest between man and other being.
Man bitten by snake fears snake-like rope.
Young ass avoids food eaten by animals before being slaughtered.
Runs to his mother and asks to have all remains of the hog’s food taken out.
Young sparrows have learned to avoid men.
Sparrow quizzes his four young as to how to avoid danger from men. Their year of experience has taught them enough.
Old racehorse in mill laments vanity of youth.
Serpent (bird) having injured man refuses reconciliation.
He knows that neither can forget their injuries.
Dove disregards experience and loses brood.
Rebuilds her nest in the place where she has lost former brood.
Animal learns through experience to fear men.
In spite of the warning of another animal he approaches man and is shot.
Tiger, jackal, and bear each learn to fear man.
They report him as head-thumper (he has beaten the tiger), turn-twister (he has swung jackal by tail), and top-tumbler (he has fallen out of tree on bear).
Incognito prince, beaten for his courtesy, realizes his folly and returns home.
“Consider the end”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Barber hired to cut king’s throat sees on the bottom of the basin the words “Whatever you do, do wisely and think of the consequences.” He drops the razor and confesses.
“Do not act when angry”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man returns home and sees someone sleeping with his wife. Though he thinks it is a paramour, he restrains himself and finds that it is a newborn son.
“Never attack anyone before unsheathing and returning sword three times”: counsel proved wise by experience.
After sleeping you will feel differently about suicide.
“Do not draw your sword against the innocent”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not uncover weapon in an assembly”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not shed the blood of women”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Control your anger at the beginning”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not go where an old man has a young wife”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Discovers a murder in an inn.
“Do not marry a girl from abroad”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not leave the highway”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not prefer a new road to an old one.”
Those who take the new one are killed by robbers.
“Take side road rather than main one where three roads meet”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“A way short yet long”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not ask questions about extraordinary things”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not cross a bridge without dismounting from your horse”; counsel proved wise by experience.
“Never wager more than a groat”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not bet”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not visit your friends often”: counsel proved wise by experience.
At last the man is treated shamefully.
Guest stays so long that host gives him black bread instead of white.
“Do not lend out your horse”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not walk half a mile with a man without asking his name”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man runs race unwittingly with his wife’s paramour and loses his wife on the wager.
“Rue not a thing that is past”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man lets bird go and then, having listened to bird’s false declaration that she had a precious gem in her body, he tries to climb a tree after her and falls.
“Never believe what is beyond belief”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man believes when bird tells him that she has a precious gem in her body.
“Never try to reach the unattainable”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“If you wish to hang yourself, do so by the stone which I point out”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Go to Goosebridge”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man with disobedient wife finds mules beaten there and made to cross bridge.
“Stay at church till mass is finished”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not trust the over-holy”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Wife so modest she will not travel with husband (adulteress); priest so pious he will not tread on worm (thief).
“Start your journey early in the day”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Prepare for night camp while it is still day”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not cross a swollen stream until it has run down”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not tell a secret to a woman”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Rise earlier”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man seeking explanation for being in debt arises earlier and catches his servants stealing.
“Do not make a horse run down hill”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not keep bad company”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Breaking of father’s first counsel causes the breaking of all the others.
“Don’t be too greedy in making a trade”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man refuses fifty ducats for horse. Horse suddenly dies.
“Do not adopt a child”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not trust a ruler who rules by reason alone”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Keep head dry, feet warm, and eat meat”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Never have to do with a woman unless wed to her”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not marry a woman before seeing her and finding her to be your equal”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not marry more than one woman”.
Man who wanted three, marries one and is weakened greatly.
“Bathe by yourself and not in the common bathing place”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man forgets purse in bath house.
“Move stool before sitting on it”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man thus saves self from falling into well.
“When in a strange place look about you”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not sit on a bed without touching it first”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Ruler should follow advice of majority” (not his own fancy): counsel proved wise by experience.
Thus finds money on body of dead traveler.
“Neglect not what four or five people say”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not go alone on journey”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Helpful crab saves from attack by crocodile.
“Do not take a woman’s advice”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“May God spare you from an evil man or evil woman.”
To teach a friend the wisdom of this greeting a man borrows money and then his creditor’s coat from him. In court the lender is discredited.
“Do not travel without money”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Don’t require honor from a strange country”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Be cautious before allowing yourself to fall asleep in a strange place”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Sleep not in an inn”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“A stranger does not close his eyes in sleep lest he close them in death”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“He who lies awake gains; he who sleeps loses”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Before eating food at a strange place throw some at an animal and watch”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“A country not examined in disguise will always be ruined”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Lean upon no relation in the hour of distress”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not undertake to be an arbitrator without being asked”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not make friends with a policeman (soldier)”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“You can only call your wife your own so long as she is with you”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not send your wife for a long visit to her parents”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Don’t do anything without investigation”: counsel proved wise by experience.
A purse full of money was found in dead man’s pocket by gravedigger.
“Never give a cup made of a single ruby as a present to the king”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Idleness begets woe; work brings happiness”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Do not stand and watch two people fighting”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Man does so and is called by both parties to depose in favor of both or he will be beheaded.
Disciple who stays in a city where everything is sold at one price finds justice is not even there.
“Never be rude to a self-made man of low birth”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Hardened clay is hard to mold”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Never publish a man’s sin if you can help it”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“Never dismiss and old servant for his first fault”: counsel proved wise by experience.
“When a man attacks you, kill him whether he be king or prince”: counsel proved wise by experience.
Boy who says “I know” gets into all sort of difficulties; now says “I don’t know.”
“Nothing happens that does not work for one’s good”: counsel proved wise is experience.
“He who throws himself against a wave is overthrown by it”: proved true.
Precepts of the lion to his sons.
Only the younger keeps them and is successful.
Precept of the lion to his sons: beware of man.
Precept of the lion to his sons: honor the woods.
Precept of the lion to his sons: keep peace with the neighbors.
Merchants try honesty for a year and find that it pays.
So advised by priest when they said that they could not do business without dishonesty.
Two fools in the habit of striking people are brought together when they strike each other until they appreciate the value of peace.
Why great man plays with children.
This is to be learned only when one has children himself.
Enemies can be won more by kindness than cruelty.
Man learns the fear of Death by meeting Life.
Life (old woman) beheads him and replaces his head backwards. Simpleton left in fear for hours before head is readjusted.
Encounter with clever children (woman) dissuades man from visit.
On way to a city meets children and they are so clever that he turns back home, fearing how clever their parents must be.
Cleverness of men disguised as peasants dissuades rivals from dispute.

Wise men of two rival cities engage in dispute. One delegation disguises as peasants and debates with their adversaries. Latter withdraw fearing how clever the educated must be if their peasants are so learned.
Arrow as man’s message shows lion how terrible man himself must be.
Blind man who feels young wolf recognises his savage nature.
How fine wine must been been to leave so good an odor.
Sight of deformed witches causes man to release wife from spinning duty.
They tell him that their deformity has come from too much spinning.
King observes retaliation among animals: becomes just.
Dog breaks fox’s foot; man breaks dog’s; horse breaks man’s leg; horse steps in hole and breaks his.
Understanding of universality of death from watching animals prey on one another.
King descends to bottom of sea in glass barrel to learn wisdom from observing fish.
Army saved from ambush by observation of birds’ movements.
Birds fly from part of woods in which ambushed men lie.
Ruler learns lesson from the example of an exiled king.
Rewards the exile rather than a successful merchant.
Unscrupulous conduct of business learned from observation of usurer’s own practices and used against him.
Ruler learns lesson from seeing city governed by king as uncharitable as he.
Hare instructs his sons to use their eyes to advantage.
Observation of dying people for a year takes man’s thoughts from lust.
Ducklings take to water from instinct.
Bridegroom thus brought to understand bride’s expertness in lovemaking.
Birds having learned their possible dangers are forced from nest by mother.
Drops of water make hollow in stone: thus repeated impressions penetrate mind.
Lazy pupil determines to be more diligent by watching man building home one wattle at a time, and seeing how water fills hole one drop at a time.
Solomon proves to his mother the inferiority of woman’s wisdom.
Minister taught by parable to make obeisance to the new king.
The dishes of the same flavor.
Man thus shown that one woman is like another and dissuaded from his amorous purpose.
Monotony of restriction to one’s favorite food.
Counselor refuses to arrange extramarital pleasures for his lord. Ruler feeds him only his favorite food until the counselor protests the monotony. Ruler drives home his point.
Society is like a dish: must be properly mixed.
Plates having salt, pepper, fish, etc. not edible without mixing.
Woman gives morsel of various foods to each guest, with explanation.
Parable comparing canons to a stew made of their individual meals.
Congregation follows evil ways of priest. He walks in mud but they will not follow him. He thus shows them the folly of following his evil ways.
The gray and the black hairs: enemies reconciled.
Duke summons two inveterate enemies. Has them tear out one of his hairs, one a gray, the other a black. Both pain him equally. He shows how their quarrels hurt him.
Picking up water thrown on ground no harder than the undoing of slander.
Chair over fiery pit as figure of precariousness of life.
Rocks falling together and thread entering needle’s eye suggest sexual intercourse: hence its beginning.
Men shamed for their cowardice by woman standing naked before them.
Wisdom taught by parable: cloud which gives rain to thirsting crops or drops it in ocean.
Monk shames accuser by telling parable.
Boy saves life by showing father foolishness of plowing up his crop.
Father has been persuaded to kill child.
Difficulty of thinking of God when occupied with worldly affairs.
Fool digs holes in edge of road.
Only those departing from straight path will fall in. Truth of principle later seen.
Man kills nest of ants: so God punishes man.
Lotus flower flourishes as long as it is in water: king should not leave castle.
Stones shaken in jar: difficulty in learning many dialects.
Relative pleasures of sexes in love taught by parable.
Father bequeathes four pots to sons: eldest finds earth in his; second, bones; third, rice husks; youngest, rupees (eldest to get land; second, cattle; third, grain; youngest to keep money).
Crow drops pebbles into water jug so as to be able to drink.
Bear learns how to catch crabs with his hairy claws.
Ungrateful son reproved by naïve action of his own son: preparing for old age.
Man gives his old father half a carpet to keep him warm. Child keeps the other half and tells his father that he is keeping it for him when he grows old.
Ungrateful son reproved by naïve action of his own son: preparing for old age (wooden drinking cup or bowl).
Father tells son not to drag him past the threshold, because he had dragged his own father only up to that point when he had thought of putting him out of his house.
Naïve remark of child: “You forgot to strike mother.”
A father in habit of beating his wife remarks that he has forgot something. The child says, “I know.
Seducer about to seduce mother of child refrains when child wisely remarks that he is sad because his father has left his mother exposed to such dangers.
King in disguise sees child’s game which represents the case.
Clever prince overrules seemingly just decisions of king.
Learning the virtue of patience from children.
When their meals are stolen, they quietly search for them.
Parents’s misdeeds innocently betrayed by children.
The wine needs no further water.
Guests asks small daughter of innkeeper for water to put into his wine.
Adulteress betrayed by little child’s remark.
Child unwittingly betrays his mother’s adultery.
Tells father not to step across chalk line drawn around secretary; if he does secretary may do to him what he did to Mother the other day.
Mouse teaches her child to fear quiet cats but not noisy cocks.
Animal gives wise example to man.
One wild goat steps over another.
They thus pass each other uninjured on a cliff. This shows advantage of peaceableness.
Ass refuses to drink after it has had enough.
Trained deer drinks wine till he breaks his leg but thereafter abstains.
Woman will not follow donkey on safe path: attacked by robbers.
Squirrel tries to dip out lake with his tail: difficulty of reforming the world.
Big fish eat little: robber will plunder weak neighbors.
Animal behavior teaches man what to avoid.
Cock’s second mate lets her stepchildren starve: woman warns husband accordingly.
Crow inspects the three worlds in search of happiness.
Wisdom learned from example of insects.
House dog blames master for teaching him lazy habits.
Man blames master for not correcting him in youth.
Untrained colt result of master’s neglect.
Well-trained kid does not open to wolf.
Hostile dogs made friendly by having them fight common enemy, the wolf.
King prefers educated men as company.
Child confined to keep him in ignorance of life.
Wisdom of hidden old man saves kingdom.
In famine all old men are ordered killed. One man hides his father. When all goes wrong in the hands of the young rulers, the old man comes forth, performs assigned tasks, and aids with his wisdom.
Wisdom from god as old (one-eyed) man.
Wisdom from old man: always say, “if it pleases God.”
Philosopher consoles woman for loss of son.
Wisdom from philosopher: give separate greetings to infants, youths, and old people.
Wisdom from philosopher: worldly honor like shadow.
If one goes toward it, it flees; if one turns his back on it, it follows and at times catches up with one.
Holy man’s prayer reforms rich man.
Holy man prays, “May God bless everything here that is good but cause to disappear all that is bad.” Everything disappears.
Hermit explains why anger is sin.
Dying saint leaves wise message to followers.
Message is cryptic, but is finally made clear.
Hero directed on journey by princess.
Serpent directed on journey by his beautiful wife.
King has amours with great men’s wives so as to learn secrets from them.
Caesar’s scorn of his wife’s advice leads to disaster.
Wife of usurer saves husband through her prayers.
Knowledge from mysterious women met in the forest.
Wisdom from harlot to a king.
Wisdom from fool: make peace before rather than after the war.
Wisdom from fool: absurdity of tight-rope walker’s performance.
Wisdom from fool: the present returned.

Nobleman gives fool a present; he is to give it to no one who is not a greater fool. Master is dying; doctor tells fool that master is going to take long journey. Since master is making no preparation, fool gives him the present. Master thus brought to repentance.
Fool says he does not want to go to heaven for he wants to stay with his master, who everyone says is going to hell.
Deity appears in dream and gives instructions or advice.
Wisdom from dream: the leper with the cup of water.
Man in dream willing to receive sacrament from unworthy priest.
Fate of parents revealed in dream.
Mother shown in Hell; father in Heaven.
Dream advises against the popularizing of science.
Solomon pays heed to angel’s warning.
Trial rehearsed before stick in the ground as judge.
Wisdom acquired by hanging in a tree.
Man buys a pennyworth of wit.
Man to bring wife a purseful of sense.
Fool is told to get a pottle of brains.
He tries to buy them. He finally learns that advice was to marry a clever girl.
Wisdom from books bought at great price.
Wisdom from books of the antediluvians.
Wisdom from continual reminder of foolishness in the past.
Unjust judge skinned and his skin stretched over a footstool kept in the presence of judges, so as to remind them to be just.
Inscription on walls for condensed education.
Counsel: if you take it you will be sorry; if you don’t you will also be sorry.
This advice given hero by helpful horse.
King questions six doctors: what do you like best of all on earth? That man has not what he wishes to have.
King questions six doctors: what do you like best of all on earth? That all joys are mixed with sorrow.
King questions six doctors: what do you like best of all on earth? That all evil and hypocrisy will have an end.
King questions six doctors: what must you most marvel at on earth? That those who are most respected are the biggest fools.
King questions six doctors: what must you most marvel at on earth? That those who speak of spiritual matters are usually the most depraved.
King questions six doctors: what must you most marvel at on earth? That man lives in a state in which he cannot die.
Crow flying away says, “A wise man remains not in the place of calamity; but a fool stays there, and sups fear and sorrow.”
Proverbial wisdom: “Seek to win over the accuser, so that he causes you no annoyance.”
Account of punishments prepared in hell brings about repentance.
Man is ordered by Senate to make tyrant stop bloodshed. He kills himself and family to satiate tyrant of blood.
Good and bad in all books.
Author says that a prudent man notes only the good in a vain book; a malicious person, only the bad in a good book.
Wisdom from robbers (thugs) who disguise selves and show cruel princess how she should treat her husband.
Humble Brahmin teaches king the difference between “mine” and “thine.
Wisdom learned in underground kingdom: the passions of a human being could not be satisfied on earth.
Man says that he is the youngest present, for he does not count the years before he became monk (or the like).
“Forty-nine gates of wisdom” open to Moses (and Solomon).
Wisdom wins contest of wisdom and wealth.
Minister’s clever daughter-in-law uses wisdom to defeat Brahmin’s wealth.
Wisdom lost by accepting bribes and gifts.
Other biblical heroes as wise men.
Hobson’s choice: choose what is put before you or nothing.
Choice between eggs: one egg or none.
Four choices, all of which are evil; man to make one choice only.
Choice: free poverty or enslaved wealth.
Man gives all his wealth away, for it is better to die than to give up virtue.
Fly jeers at king’s elephant for his lack of freedom.
Choice: plainness with safety or grandeur with danger.
Ass envies horse in fine trappings.
Horse killed in battle; ass content.
Choice: loss of beauty or speech.
Choice: suffering in youth or old age.
Present evil preferred to change for worse.
Wounded animal (man) refuses to have the flies driven away since they are now sated and their places will be taken by fierce and hungry flies.
Don’t set a hungry guard over food.
Parrot set to guard figs eats his fill. When replaced he calls attention to the fact that he is now full and therefore safer than another hungry parrot.
They would defame him among strangers. At home they serve to test the king’s patience and to reform his life.
Do not pluck off the well-fed leeches.
Wolf told not to do so lest hungrier ones take their places as he swims.
Old man chooses to be annoyed by occasional and loud chirp of swallows than by never-ending but soft chirp of sandpipers.
Oxen decide not to kill butchers, since inexpert killers might replace them.
Old woman prays for safety of cruel tyrant for fear a worse one will succeed him.
Heathcock prefers home with hardships to travel in foreign lands.
Monk goes to wilderness to escape work on material things.
Finds that he must work to live and returns to monastery.
Army faces enemy rather than the anger of their king who would kill them if they returned in flight.
Lamb prefers to be sacrificed in temple rather than to be eaten by a wolf.
Crab would rather be killed outright than imprisoned and starved.
Soldier asks to be stabbed in chest.
Prostrate soldier asks enemy to stab him in chest instead of back in order to save his honor. Captor frees him and the two become friends.
Saint chooses to die “after pride of youth” and before “misery of old age.”
Trickster overhears man praying for death to take him; the trickster appears at man’s house, usually in disguise, says he is God (or the devil).
The man tells him to take his wife (or he runs away).
Escaped lamb delivers himself to shepherd rather than to slaughter.
Discontented ass longs for death but changes mind when he sees skins of dead asses at a fair.
Enemies make peace rather than slay each other.
Lion and wild boar make peace rather than slay each other for benefit of vulture.
Choice: small injustice permitted rather than to cause troubles of state.
King overlooks wife’s unfaithfulness rather than to cause troubles of state.
Senator overlooks wife’s adultery rather than impair his reputation.
Man rebukes servants for telling him of his wife’s unfaithfulness.
King chooses small inconvenience of personal troubles to great troubles for his kingdom.
Man would rather pay 500 florins he did not owe than have it said he did not pay debts.
Rescue alone from shipwreck chosen over drowning with goods.
Choice between evils: pay tribute or lose both money and life.
Choice: apparent injustice over greater wrong.
Angel takes hermit with him and does many seemingly unjust things. Later shows why each of these was just.
Angel explains to hermit why God lets a sinner die in peace and have big funeral while holy hermit is slain by a wild beast.
God punishes many men because of one sinner, like a man who kills hive of bees for stinging of one.
Angel in form of young man shows skeptical hermit that ways of providence are inscrutable.
Youth made lame: had kicked his mother.
Lion sent to kill a man: frees him from possibility of sinning and sojourn in purgatory.
Angel takes cup from old man.
Done lest he love the cup too much.
Done because man is plotting a murder.
Angel kills man because he loves his child too much.
Saint gives liberally to gambler, little to beggar.
Forestman who longs to do evil is sent to hell: writer, who repents, is sent to heaven.
God justifies this to his sage.
Evil mother has fine funeral, good father poor.
Choice of freeing one son: adopted son or long-missing son.
Choice: blind son with long life or healthy son with short.
Choice: foolish son always with him or four wise daughters who will leave him.
Choice: staying at home with loving wife or going to tavern and having unfaithful wife.
Had rather die than suffer longer from him.
Choice: a big piece of cake with my curse or a small piece with my blessing.
Better send an ugly woman to the devil than a pretty one.
Choice between bad master, bad official, or bad neighbor.

Bad master can do evil if he desires to do so; bad official can harm a poor person and complain against him to his master; bad neighbor can betray secret things about his neighbors. Bad neighbor worst.
Bad choice between poor and miserly man.
Rower prefers to be stoned by his master rather than remain out in the storm.
Contentment with evil master for fear of worse successor.
Weaver prefers master with one hedgehog.
Insists on his master putting hedgehog out of house. When master refuses, weaver leaves. Next master has two hedgehogs, and next has three. Weaver returns to first master.
Man retains questionable bride for fear of getting one who is worse.
The smaller the evil the better.
Therefore choose the smallest woman possible for a bride.
Fool advises uncle, in letter which he did not send, to take money from wife’s paramour instead of revenge.
Prisoners given choice between emasculation and blinding.
God’s punishment: the sinner may have twelve years of famine or twelve hours of heavy rainfall.
Solomon, permitted by God to make any request, asks wisdom.
Health chosen as the most precious thing.
Athena chooses olive tree because of fruitfulness.
Sparrows and crickets ask peasant to leave tree standing. He refuses, but when he finds honey in the tree he consents.
Contest between rose and amaranth: worth lies not in beauty.
Pine and thornbush dispute as to their usefulness.
Beauty of form does not give worth; pine grows slowly but it will withstand storms.
Fox and panther contest in beauty.
Fox’s spirit worth more than panther’s skin.
Peacock proved to be bad king.
Chosen because of beauty; too weak to defend his flock.
Peacock and crane in beauty contest.
Better be able to soar like crane than to strut about like peacock.
Contest in beauty between swallows and crows (ants and flies): worth lies not in beauty.
Choice of a learned crow: a dead cat better than a golden crown.
In dividing property clever younger brother takes hind part of buffalo, upper part of tree, and use of curtain during night.
Dog and hog dispute over their children: worth lies not in speed.
Father with handsome son and hideous daughter.
Advises both to look in mirror daily lest son exchange handsome face for bad character; daughter to triumph over face by good manners.
Useful and ugly preferred to expensive and beautiful.
Man shown jewels that cost much money; he replies that he has better stones (millstones) that earn that much.
King who experiences the cultural civilization of an empire in dream would rather be poor and primitive.
Man criticizes the devil because his deeds are not fair.
Devil says that they are strong nevertheless. Hence strong speakers rather than clever are to be preferred.
Hero, despising weapons, fights with fists alone.
Man advised to choose good poor man for his daughter’s husband rather than rich man.
Practical knowledge more vital than theoretical.
The bookman and the boatman: each ignorant of other’s work.
Fox and noisy but empty drum.
Little coin in empty bottle noisy.
Among many vain words may be found some of wisdom.
Apparent beauty may be of the least importance.
Ruler admires jewels’s beauty but neglects to inquire about their marvelous virtues.
Choice between short and dangerous or long and sure way.
Choice between flattering lies and unflattering truths.
Raven drowns his young who promise to aid him when he becomes old.
He saves one who admits he will not help, because he will have to carry his own young.
Quality of offspring preferred to quantity.
Lioness thus answers fox (hog) who twits her that she has only one cub.
The present preferred to the past.
Count only the waves before you.
Fox sees man trying to count the waves. Advises him to count only those immediately before him and to pay no attention to those which have already passed.
Do not ask: “Why were the former days better than the present ones?”
Not what you were but what you are counts.
Wasp twits butterfly with coming from ugly chrysalis: unimportant where you come from.
Present possessions preferred to future possibilities.
A bird in the hand foolishly given away in hope of greater gain.
Today’s catch of fish traded for prospective larger catch tomorrow.
Little fish in the net kept rather than wait for uncertainty of greater catch.
Lion leaves sleeping hare to follow the shepherd.
Don’t injure yourself to insure your family’s future.
Man wagers he can run with his head off.
Asked what it will profit him, he says that it will profit his family.
Man to be reforged chooses present unhappiness.
He is in heaven and God is to reforge him, but he chooses not to change.
Children choose father they know rather than real father they do not yet know.
Woman confesses that child is not by her husband. Child, however, chooses to keep the father he knows.
Man prefers servant girl who is present to her absent mistress.
Soldier prefers to live rather than die and be avenged on enemy.
Weight of bodily member chosen rather than its loss.
Fox prefers to bear weight of his tail rather than give part of it to ape.
Barber leaves inexpensive village for high wages in city.
Finds cost of living more than enough to take all his profit.
In spite of master’s advice disciple stays in country where everything has cheap price.
Wise man refuses income of half a kingdom since expenses will outweigh gain.
Man refuses cure which brings greater inconvenience.
Drunkard refuses cure of fever if it is to take away his thirst.
What one has is neglected in search for other things.
The monkey and the lost lentil.
Lets all others he has in his hand fall in order to search for it.
Host wants to learn Hebrew even at risk of forgetting his own language.
The valuable neglected for the interesting.
Herdsman neglects his she-goats in favor of wild-goats.
When water dries up he goes hungry.
Better be content with what you have, than try to get more and lose everything.
Wealth and glory sacrificed for freedom and virtue.
Man refuses vast wealth because with it will come covetousness.
King lays aside crown since it brings too many cares.
Prince chooses exile and honor to foul life at his father’s court.
Rich merchant is poorer in happiness than poor man.
Man refuses rich marriage with house filled with dangerous wild animals.
Bodily member(s) sacrificed to save life.
Beaver sacrifices scrotum to save life.
Cuts it off and leaves it for pursuers.
Inconvenience disregarded when booty is in sight.
Wolf does not mind the dust.
Told that dust from flock of sheep will annoy him; he finds it useful.
Snake is willing to suffer the indignity of serving frog king as mount because frog king gives him frogs to eat.
Slight inconvenience in weather, large gain.
King upbraids wind for blowing away a poor widow’s last cup of meal. Finds that the wind has saved a ship full of people by that very act. The king is humbled.
Less inconvenience in fighting though tired than in losing all for a little rest.
Priest sells his donkey because worry for its safety distracts him from prayer.
Solomon refuses water of immortality for himself when he cannot have it for his possessions also.
Ape throws away nut because of its bitter rind.
No time for minor fights when life is in danger.
Bull being pursued by lion tries to go into cave. Goat refuses to let him in. Bull must go on, for with lion pursuing he has no time to fight goat.
King ridiculed for inventing trifle of musical instrument but praised for constructing a great mosque.
Kind foster-parents chosen rather than cruel parents.
Lamb chooses her foster-mother, the she-goat.
Owes more to her than to her own mother, who has deserted her.
Socrates builds himself a little house.
Great refuse to associate with lowly.
Boar refuses to fight with lowly ass.
Zeus refuses wedding present from snake.
Presents to be received only from equals.
Prince refuses to play with common children.
Noble poets refuse to associate with truly good poet because of his lowly birth.
Peasant ashamed of being thrown off by ass.
Shameful to be thrown by such a creature.
Wolf tries to make friends with lion: killed.
Dolphin and whale scorn crab as peacemaker.
Laurel and olive tree scorn thornbush as umpire in their dispute as to who is most useful.
Lion angry at impudence of mouse.
King refuses to quarrel with bird.
Leopard ashamed of having been bitten by lizard.
Rich man refuses to associate with poor sister.
Profitable association of great and lowly.
King asks three sons what kind of bird they would prefer to be.
Lion licks sick man, who is thereby disgusted.
Marriage with equal or with unequal.
Wife chosen instead of fairy mistress.
They let man choose between them.
Prince prefers first love to princess he later marries.
Unsuccessful marriage of jackals and turtles (different habits).
One’s own kind preferred to strangers.
Bird refuses to maintain friendship with bird of different habits.
Man prefers to live with ordinary rather than with pious man.
He will be virtuous by comparison.
Lion as king makes ass his lieutenant.
Lion makes lame goat his lieutenant.
Jackal realizes that the partridge was too clever for him and leaves.
Earthen and brazen pots in river.
Brazen pot thinks that they should stay together for company. Earthen pot, however, fears approach of brazen pot.
Buffalo refuses tiger’s invitation to dinner.
He sees fire prepared to cook him.
Association of rat with cat ceases as soon as mutual danger has passed.
The rat threatened by the weasel and the owl allies himself with a cat caught in a net. Saved by the cat, he rescues the cat with precaution and then prudently renounces further relations with her.
Association of mouse with cat ceases as soon as mutual danger has passed.
Friendship of snake and frog ceases when snake wants to eat frog.
Association of cow and tiger: tiger eats cow as soon as she is hungry.
Association of swan and swallow: swan unable to fly away from danger.
Associating with a bad friend is fatal: swan and crow.
Swan is blamed when crow drops filth.
Profitable association of young and old.
Old ox yoked with young ox.
Foolish association of young and old.
Foolish youth in love with ugly old mistress.
Foolish marriage of old man and young girl.
Association of the good and the evil.
Ass buyer returns ass which has associated with lazy companions.
God of wealth in bad company.
Bad associates bring death to bishop.
Doctor loses his life for him and lawyer his soul.
Senseless debate of the mutually useful.
Debate as to their usefulness. All mutually useful.
Tail and head of serpent quarrel as to usefulness.
Fortune, Intellect, Knowledge, and Health dispute as to which is the greatest.
Debate of tongue and other bodily members.
Common wives of man debate as to which has helped him most.
Tobacco, pipe, and match debate usefulness to smoker.
Deer, opossum, and snake each render indispensable aid to man.
Rice, wheat, and dal dispute as to which is the best.
Wealth and wisdom dispute as to who is greater.
Elephant and ape debate about superiority.
Owl gives them task neither can perform and ends futile debate.
Aristotle drinks both red and white wine to show that all philosophies are good.
Father leaves sons three jewels—Christianity, Judaism, Mohammedanism.
Only one is good although they all look the same. Same with religions.
Unnecessary choice: to go uphill or downhill.
Pomegranate and apple tree dispute as to which is worth most.
Blackberry reproves them for useless jangling.
Senseless debate: which is the greater, St. John the Baptist or St. John the Evangelist?
Inflicters rather than receivers of wounds chosen.
Men with many wounds recommended as soldiers. King had rather have those who gave the wounds.
King advised to marry maid rather than widow.
Widow would have things her own way.
If husband is good she will fear to lose him; if bad she will repent.
Her husband abides in her heart.
Widow refuses second marriage so her brother cannot kill a second husband.
Better to marry ugly than fair wife.
Better to marry a man lacking money than money lacking a man.
Young man advised to choose as wife a girl whose mother was chaste.
Choice: to do that which one knows or to learn something.
Death preferred above God and Justice.
Tame dog prefers food basin to fleeing hare.
Fox had rather meet one hen than fifty women.
Old sweetheart chosen in preference to new.
Little men preferred to big men.
Preacher prefers small men because the intellect has difficulty in reaching to one’s heels.
Choice: death and revenge preferred to life.
Monk chooses solitude and loneliness to company and temptation.
By living alone he escapes sin.
Given the choice of his friend or his mistress, man chooses his friend.
Eagle prefers own offspring to changeling.
One should not attempt to change his color.
Negro tries in vain to be washed white.
Animal should not try to change his nature.
Crab comes ashore: killed by fox.
Kite tries to neigh like a horse.
Loses his voice and gains nothing.
Camel tries in vain to dance.
Ass tries in vain to play lyre.
Wolf tries in vain to be doctor.
Crow tries to imitate partridge’s walk.
Mouse, bird, and sausage keep house together.
When they exchange duties all goes wrong.
Elephant, giraffe, snake, and ant try keeping house together: requirements different.
Ass tries to get a cricket’s voice.
Asks crickets what they eat to get such a voice. They answer, “dew.” He tries it and starves.
Lizard tries to make himself as long as snake.
Fox tries to mask as dove, but loses all thoughts of murder.
Camel and jackal exchange food: camel is led by his good friend to thorny fruit and thorn sticks in his throat.
Frog wants to be shod like a horse.
Jackal accidentally made king but joins other jackals in howling at night.
Snake wants to act as pet like parrot: killed.
Frogs want to collect honey like bees.
One should let well enough alone.
Birds seeking richer lands are nearly all killed.
Survivors advise their friends to let well enough alone.
Barber tries unsuccessfully to become a trader.
One should not be too greedy.
Kite tries to carry off so many partridges that he drops them all.
Finds hunter, gazelle, and wild boar dead. Tries first to eat the bowstring, and is mortally wounded.
Greedy man keeps demanding one more thing from complacent man; at last is magically blinded.
Greedy pig looks up into tree for figs.
Greedy man dissatisfied with gold looks for jewels; finds only iron and eventually nothing.
Fowler wants two rubies as ransom for a caught goose; loses goose and both rubies.
Peacock spends so much time preening for coronation that birds become impatient and make the owl king instead.
Good shepherd shears his sheep; does not skin them.
Emperor thus replies to suggestion of a new tax to be laid on the people.
Cocks who crow about mistress’s adultery killed.
Bird warns mistress against committing adultery: gets neck wrung.
Fool given the truth on his back.

He tells his master what the servants have done during his absence. The servants whip him on his bare back, saying at each blow, “That is the truth.” When the master returns and tells the fool to tell the truth, the latter replies, “There is nothing worse on earth than the truth.” Pauli (ed.
Doctor loses a horse for the sake of the truth.
Overlord asks two doctors whether he is entitled to all the possessions of his retainers. One doctor unrighteously answers yes and receives a horse. The other who tells the truth receives nothing.
Man asked to tell truth says that his host, his hostess, and the cat have but three eyes between them.
He is driven off for his truth telling.
Magpie tells a man that his wife has eaten an eel, which she said was eaten by the otter.
The woman plucks his feathers out.
Only youngest son tells king truth when asked where they got their food: banished.
Honest servant tells people that shop does not have many customers: dismissed.
Noblemen who quarreled over a device.
Wiser of the two shows foolishness of such a fight.
Noblemen being ruined by long lawsuit decide wisely to join their families in marriage and save their fortunes.
Bishop fond of lawsuits is ordered by king to settle them: bishop pleads for a few to be left so that he will have something to live for.
Serpent (weasel) tries to bite a file.
Helmet left for woman to quarrel with.
Woman insists upon quarreling with a nobleman. He says, “If you wish to quarrel, I shall leave my helmet here. You can talk to it.” Pauli (ed.
Brothers compose quarrel and save umpire’s fee.
In Castile a Spaniard maintains to a Portuguese that the Spanish king is best of all. In Portugal, that the Portuguese king is best.
Upbraided when found playing with children, he unstrings a bow and shows how good relaxation is.
Ruler interrupts meeting of Senate to amuse his small son.
Emperor rebukes overzealous servant as being a nuisance.
Instructions of mother followed literally by one daughter when she marries. All goes wrong. Second daughter follows them in conformity with her father’s explanations and all is well.
St. George teaches the poor man, “Who steals somewhat and lies somewhat will be rich.”
Forget God for five years and you will become wealthy.
Monk discouraged by large amount of work to be done persuaded to undertake but a small amount each day.
The small task will be done; the large one will merely discourage.
True penance for even a day is effective.
Man tracking gorilla sees animal’s strength.
Cow-herd looking for cattle thief recognizes him in the lion.
A waste of time to make a bed for a dog who lies down wherever he happens to be tired. Likewise a waste of time to help unappreciative people.
Man resuscitates a lion which devours him.
Fool fasts on roof till he becomes so weak he falls off.
When in anger say the alphabet.
Man thus restrained from hasty judgment.
King given three wheels to control his anger.
King in anger punishes misdeed on Easter day.
Is almost killed himself in retaliation. He submits and says that he deserves this punishment for hasty action.
Man has disinterested party punish servant for him lest he himself be unfair in his anger.
Master when angry will not punish servant who has ruined him.
King restrained from hasty judgment by being told story.
Judge not that you be not judged: thus judge upbraided when he is later accused in court and claims mercy.
Answer questions of a fool the next day.
Unpaid servant refuses to blame master: later rewarded.
Three men are pursued in battle. First throws himself on enemies; second waits a little; third does not fight until the enemy begins.
Foolishness of noise-making when enemies overhear.
He has drunk too much and sings in spite of the dog’s warning.
Paramour who insists on quarreling with mistress about escape caught by her husband.
He finds the escape different from that which had been described to him.
Monk’s enemies quarrel and thus save him.
Robber who wants to steal monk’s cow and devil who wants to steal his soul quarrel as to which shall begin first; they thus awaken him and the neighbors.
Kites and crows quarrel over division of wounded fox.
Foolishness of premature coming out of hiding.
Hidden goat discovered by his horn protruding above ground.
Hidden stag discovered when he begins to eat grapevine too soon after hunters have passed.
Clever girl refrains from eating figs which would bring on magic sleep.
Wise man before entering a quarrel considers how it will end.
Wise man considers whom he is attacking.
Flea had attacked abbess and been chased all night; fever, a washerwoman who nearly froze it to death by going to the river and washing clothes. They exchange and succeed.
Wise fear of the weak for the strong.
Frogs fear increase of sun’s power which will dry up all their puddles.
See two bulls fighting; know that the loser will take refuge in their marsh.
Forethought in prevention of others’s plans.
Swallow in vain urges other birds to eat seed as fast as it is sowed. Ridiculed, he builds his nest among the dwellings of men. Later, birds are caught in nets made from the hemp.
Snake gives away magic pills later used to kill him.
Swallow advises hen against hatching out serpent’s eggs.
She is hatching her own destruction.
Prevention of hostility by inspiring fear in enemy.
Snake complains to Zeus that people step on him.
Two sheep kill a fox who has licked up the blood they have spilled in a fight.
Sheep-dogs stop quarreling to hunt wolf who has raided the flock.
Enemy brothers unite to fight a common enemy.
Prevention of hostilities by agreeing to demands while in danger.
Barber makes heavy demands of customer while the razor is at his throat. Customer agrees but after the shave throws the barber out.
Prevention of hostilities by disarming the suspect.
Later learned that he is a fugitive murderer.
Man dissuades simpleton from hanging himself by telling him that hell is a place of pain and torments.
Crab takes hold of heron’s neck and fearing attack cuts neck and kills him.
King to avoid possible assassination singes his beard rather than have barber shave him.
King to avoid possible assassination has queen’s quarters searched before he enters.
One bird escapes as hunter bends his bow; other remains and is shot.
Lion suitor allows his teeth to be pulled and his claws to be cut.
Robbers persuaded to give hero sword with which they are afterwards killed.
Lion as king of animals reinstated after elephant is tired.
Avoiding places which have been fatal to others.
Fox sees all tracks going into lion’s den but none coming out.
Birds flee from cuckoo who, they believe, will later become a hawk.
Palamides, having injured Ulysses, seeks advice from him.
Bird hears voices from within unhatched eggs and flies away: voices plot to dine on their bird-mother when they are born.
Avoid enemies’ revenge either by making peace and friendship or by killing them all.
So says old man to conqueror.
Advice not to rob women while they are alone, for fear of returning husbands’ revenge.
Monkeys planning to found a city desist lest with walls up it will be easier to catch them than before.
Throstle giving all attention to sweet fruits is caught by bird catcher.
Man inattentive to the danger of drowning enters water to save treasure and is drowned.
Frog persists in living in puddle on road.
Disregards advice of another frog and is run over.
Swallows warn other birds against roosting in tree with glue.
Man disregards priest’s warning that he will seduce his wife.
Hector warns Trojans against attacking the stronger Greeks.
One of them is caught in it.
Avoiding things which are harmful by nature.
Thornbush blamed by fox for wounding him.
He should have known better than to lay hold of something whose nature is to lay hold of others.
Care in selecting the creature to carry one.
Youth trusts self to horse over which he has no control.
Tortoise lets self be carried by eagle.
Crane persuades fish to let him change him from one lake into another: he eats fish.
Mice decide that a bell should be put on the cat but can find no one to tie it on her.
Defences by strengthening one’s own weakest spots.
Ears stopped with wax to avoid enchanting song.
Cotton put in ears so as not to hear abusive words.
Defence when one needs it most.
Armor ordered thin in front and thick in back, since it would be most needed in flight.
Defences in and out of season.
Wild-boar sharpens tusks when no enemy is in sight.
Tells fox that when enemy comes there are other things to do.
Man decides to make himself strong in peaceful times rather than wait until attacked.
Man slays another in order not to be slain himself.
Son slays father in order not to be slain himself.
Youthful fencer yields to infuriated opponent who has picked up a pestle.
Foolishness of king’s taking a washerman for chief minister; washerman makes no preparation for war and kingdom is conquered.
Alliances which make both parties more vulnerable.
Rat and frog tie paws together to cross marsh.
Jackal and leopard tie tails together for mutual protection.
Frightened, they run apart and injure each other.
Foolishness of alliances with the weak.
Foxes desert their allies, the hares, when they foresee defeat by the eagle.
Ass turns on his driver who would save him from falling over the precipice.
Tame doves close wild ones in trap and thus help common enemies.
Tame fox helps dogs against wild foxes.
Is no longer trusted by latter.
Fox with lion protector goes hunting alone and is killed.
Foolishness of taking on too strong a partner: crow crowds sparrow out of its nest.
Cannot escape hunter; peacock flies off.
Man, lion, and bear in pit.
Bear tells lion not to eat the man, since he would grow hungry again. Rather they should have the man use his intelligence to get them out.
Man who is planting tree told that it will never mature in his day. He is planting for the next generation.
King improves kingdom before leaving it to his sons.
He leaves it smaller but much stronger and richer.
Sees bird feed its young and decides that God takes care of everyone without work. He is shown his mistake.
King (queen) teaches children to work at all tasks to prepare them for life’s possible hazards.
Looking for the keys of the abbey.
Monk goes about with downcast eyes until he is made abbot; then lives in luxury. He explains that he was looking for the keys of the abbey.
“Eat small fish now if you wish larger ones later.”
Bishop refuses to eat small fish as he used to when an abbot.
Safe provision for life not to be lightly surrendered.
Priest must give up his charge or his mistress.
Gives up his parish and immediately loses his fickle mistress.
Be diligent and spend little: how to become wealthy.
In time of plenty provide for want.
Lazy bird is put to shame by thrift of industrious bird. In winter he is in distress.
Improvident mouse eats grain stored for famine.
Loss is discovered and grain placed elsewhere. Mouse, who has saved nothing, starves.
King for a year provides for future.
Knowing that the custom is that he is to be deposed in a year, he sends provisions to a safe place out of the kingdom.
Wise man stores grain against coming famine.
Industrious ant works always at his harvest to keep it dry.
Ant brings stored grain out into sun to keep it safe.
City without provisions but with much money starves.
Make use of proper seasons for crops.
Lazy boy vainly asks God of the Seasons to delay the plowing season.
Kindness unwise when it imperils one’s food supply.
Eagle warns shepherds that wolf is eating sheep.
Crow rebukes eagle for thus imperiling his own food supply.
Do not discard clothing till cold weather is over.
More than one swallow to make a summer.
Spendthrift youth seeing swallow concludes that summer has come and sells his clothes. There is frost the next day and he is cold.
Build shelter for the whole year.
Bear builds house of wood; fox of ice.
Fox’s house fails him in summer.
Consider difficulties of course you are about to undertake.
Servant about to be caught for theft rehearses the lie he is to tell his master. He finds lies so transparent that he decides to tell the truth.
Lady answers queen so straightforwardly she gets light punishment.
In planning future, profit by the past.
Frogs decide not to jump into the well.
Their spring having dried up, they consider jumping into a well. They decide that the well may also dry up.
The only person in the bath.

Servant reports to master that there is but one person in the public bath Master finds three hundred. Only one person had removed stone from his path; rest had stubbed toes. He was only one worthy of the name of man.
All aspects of a plan must be foreseen.
Man allowed to manage the weather forgets to ask help of the wind. All goes wrong and he must give up management.
Doctor gives advice after patient dies.
Beware of following an interested adviser.
Tailless fox tries in vain to induce foxes to cut off tails.
Noseless man persuades fools to cut off noses.
Tailless jackal persuades other jackals to cut off tails.
Crane advises fool to empty reservoir so he can reap all grain.
Crane eats fish left at bottom.
Fish refuse fox’s invitation to live on dry land and thus escape danger of fishermen.
Old age must be planned for.
Child finds gray hair in wicked father’s head.
Father sees that it is time for him to reform.

Miller has four horses to carry grain. He uses only one, so that it soon dies. Four horses are childhood, youth, manhood, and old age. Don’t heap all burden of securing salvation on the fourth horse, old age.
Charges a pair of shoes to consort with men. When old she pays with shoes the men who will consort with her.
Priest keeps in container relic which when kissed renders people immune from pestilence.
They only kiss container, so that if they die he will not be held responsible.
Mark the way one is going in an unfamiliar country.
Do not work yourself out of employment.
Cat only drives rats away; if she killed them she would no longer have employment.
Policy in dealing with the great.
Ass divides booty equally between himself, fox, and lion. Lion eats ass.
Best part goes to himself as king of beasts; second, as strongest; third, as most valiant; fourth
Fox refuses to mediate between lion and lioness.
Lion decides to abandon lioness because of her bad odor.
King honors poet and critic: the first so that he will honor the king; the second, so that he will not dishonor him.
Ruler angered by evil spoken of him is placated by soft words of speakers.
Prime minister bribes priest to persuade king that ocean of milk he wishes sought for had curdled.
Fox with three hundred fables ready to tell against lion conveniently forgets them.

Has been imprisoned because the king did not like the way the musician looked at him. After a year the king returns as a conqueror and sees musician. The latter says that he saw the king’s conquests in a vision and was blessing him when he looked at him. The musician is honored.
Flatterer always agrees with king even in opposite opinions; defense: he is king’s servant.
“High-born alone recognizes one of equal rank with himself.”
Jackal sees man with instrument he is unfamiliar with, comes up to him and salutes him “Lord of Delhi.” Man calls him Lord of Jungle and tells above.
Flattery of the wicked to escape death at his hands: “This is an offering to my lord Esau from his slave Jacob”.
Dissenting minister to king: “Let the king do as seems good in his eyes”.
Unpleasant truths must be withheld from the great.
King of apes asks visitors how they like his children (courtiers). Truthful visitor tells that they are very ugly, and is punished. Liar praises their beauty and receives reward.
Brother who conforms to naked people’s customs honored.
Two brothers go to the land of Naked People. One of the brothers wears clothes and is punished.
Muddy bath prepared for blemished king.
King brought to sense of duty by feigned conversation of birds.
Philosopher pretends to know bird’s language and to be translating what they tell him.
King living apart from wife brought to sense of duty by philosopher.
King called baker’s son: he has given the poet only loaves of bread.
King sees jest and rewards poet.
King brought to sense of duty by woman’s words.
Drunken king sentences unjustly. Woman asks to appear before the king before he has dined. Her case is retried.
A soft answer turneth away wrath.
Man called a rogue by a nobleman makes a joke of the insult.
Physician willing to believe in four persons.
Angers a theologian by disputing doctrine of the Trinity.
King makes absurd statement about flowers.
With a silent person one is alone.
Angered bishop will not answer when addressed.
Yogi advises yogi blood for making king’s leaky tank hold water: king cuts off yogi’s head.
Keeping on good terms with hostile gods.
Dog asks raven why he sacrifices to Athene, since she hates raven because of his powers of augury.
Man plays fool to protect himself in dealing with king.
Man pretends idiocy so as to avoid compromising himself when summoned to testify by two rival queens before the king.
Man recounts unpleasant happening to king when in good humor and draws laugh; rest draw punishment.
The king and the cheap slippers.

Steward buys the king a pair of slippers. King thinks not enough has been paid for them and refuses them. Steward buys another like the first and charges a good price. Learns that this is the way to deal with kings.
Devil decides to leave of own accord.
It is decided to drive the devil out of a man who is possessed. Devil sees the inevitable and flees so that they cannot say that he has been driven off.
Vanquished ruler in disguise gets audience with victor.
“What would you do if your enemy were to kneel before you and beg forgiveness?” “I would forgive him.” Reveals identity and is pardoned.
Mohammed goes to the mountain (tree) when the mountain will not come to him.
Save themselves while oak is uprooted.
Ass foolish to kick against the pricks.
Fire burns man who doesn’t understand it.
Useful when one knows how to use it.
Wit interprets unfavorable decision of court as doing him great honor.
Consolation for misfortune found in food.
Consoled by a drop of honey.
Man in pit surrounded by perils thus comforts himself.
Man on sinking ship eats salt.
Otherwise he will not enjoy the large amount of water that he must drink.
Mouse (fly) dying in meat tub is happy that he has eaten to satisfaction.
Comfort in the contemplation of impossible pleasure.
Chased from chicken coop by dogs.
Fox about to be hanged asks to be allowed to see geese.
Consolation by thinking of some good aspect of a situation.
Dying toad thus comforts his paramour, the frog, whom he is leaving neither married nor widow nor maiden and pregnant.
Consolation by thinking of the past.
Unsuccessful fishermen console themselves that their earlier high hopes balance up their disappointment.
Mutual and undeserved compliments: donkey to camel, “What a beauty you are”; latter answers, “What a sweet voice you have.”
Doves in net console themselves because they think trapper’s tears are from pity for them.
Consolation by pretending that one does not want the thing he cannot have.
The fox and the sour grapes.
Pretends that the grapes he cannot reach are sour.
Fox asking for favor set on by dogs.
Fox in swollen river claims to be swimming to distant town.
Jackal covers up his inability to cross stream by saying he is looking for shallowest part.
Clever jackal covers up his clumsiness in catching cows by saying he was running to and fro because he was looking for the fattest calf.
Dog driven out of dining room claims to be drunk.
Says that he has drunk so much that he does not know how he got out of the house.
