Warrior having lost a city claims that he did not wish to sell it for a higher price.
Headless king and tailless tiger, each afraid of other, agree to be friends.
Scorned suitor consoles himself by realization that a wife who did not love him would be constant source of trouble.
Consolation by thought of others worse placed.
Timid animal consoled when he sees others more timid.
Lion comforted for his fear of the cock.
Finds that elephant is afraid of the gnat.
Man with unfaithful wife comforted when he sees the queen’s unfaithfulness.
Man with unfaithful wife comforted when he sees jealous husband who carefully guards wife cuckolded.
Man whose wife gives him bath only once a week comforted by one who does so once a year.
Poor man consoles self by thinking of misfortunes of rich.
Man compelled to live on peas takes comfort when he sees a man once rich eating the hulls.
Man in cold consoles himself thinking of rich men in hell or prison.
Hare upbraided by sparrow for letting self be carried off by eagle rejoices when sparrow is carried off by hawk.
Enemy horses captured by lion join forces and become friends.
Consolation: spiritual recompense for temporal misfortune.
Consolation: priest tells blind man that even flies have eyes but only man has the inner eyes of the soul.
Humility one of the qualifications of a prophet.
Judge should possess humility and modesty.
Humility of the wise “Sons of the East”.
Men not chosen for their ignorance; else he should have reached heaven.
Upbraided for not knowing answer to question, man answers that he was chosen for his position because of what he knew, not of what he did not know.
King orders piece of cloth shown after his death.
The measure of all that he has taken with him to the grave.
King refuses to have fine tomb erected for him since his stay on earth is so unimportant.
Rich man humbled by realization that he cannot take his wealth with him.
King has earthen vessels placed on table among the golden ones.
He had formerly been a potter and prefers the vessels which he had made to the ones now molding him.
King shows humility by mingling with common people.
King David dances with common youths before the Ark of the Covenant.
He humbles self to please God.
King of humble lineage cannot be flattered.
Abbot to avoid vainglory receives judge in rags.
Opposing wise men humble themselves and become friends.
Empress sews and shows she is not too noble to work.
Noble and ugly holy man embraces man who calls him ugly, saying he loves those who see him as he really is.
Ass in lion’s skin unmasked when he raises his voice.
Crow tries to prophesy like raven: detected by his voice.
Weasel paints self to deceive mice.
Painted jackal admitted neither to the peacocks nor to the jackals.
King of jackals captured because of his large banner.
Lowly animal tries to move among his superiors.
Large wolf, called by his companions “Lion”. Presumes to mix with lions but is only a wolf.
Ass follows after lion and is punished.
Ass and cock are surprised by lion. Cock crows and scares lion, who runs. Ass thinks that he has scared lion and pursues.
Ass who has worked with ox thinks himself equal to ox.
Frog heaps abuse on bullock, who scorns him.
Thinks that the clog on his neck is a decoration.
Bad singer thinks he is talented: driven from theatre.
Bad writer who praises himself reprimanded.
Flute-player thinks song meant for the prince is sung to him.
Ass who carried divine image thinks people bow before him.
Disdain of the wolf for the dog.
Is fleeing from dog’s master not from him.
Gnats think they have thrown horse down.
Crow thinks harvesters are stealing his grain.
Woman in finery in church thinks people are standing up to see her when they rise at gospel reading.
Spider thinks that it has held back the wind.
Gnats apologize for lighting on bull’s horn.
He had not felt their weight.
Raven riding on bull’s horns thinks he has brought bull home.
Crow alighting on falling tree thinks his weight made it fall.
Glowworm thinks he shines like stars.
Fox thinks his elongated shadow at sunrise makes him as large as elephant.
Jackal falls into dye vat, tries to pose as peacock: detected.
Animals each think moon shines for his benefit.
Owl thinks echoes of his hoots are sounds of praise.
Rat imagines himself owner of camel.
He is attached to camel by string.
Rag accidentally in king’s wardrobe thinks it is a ribbon.
Foolish boast of ancestry by lowly.
Mule as descendant of king’s war-horse.
Fox claims that certain statues are of his ancestors.
Ape shows that he is a liar.
Lowly tries in vain to be greater than he is.
Frog tries in vain to be as big as ox.
Fish swells with pride until it bursts.
Bird tries to puff itself up to look like peacock.
Titmouse ruffles feathers to seem big as a bear.
Servant asks master for arms of knighthood.
Is given a stalk of garlic.
Is told that he can be made rich but not noble.
Old simpleton resolves to become a senator.
He is made to believe that he is wanted as an archer and is so frightened that he dies.
Ambitious branch chosen king of trees.
Vine and fig tree have refused.
Presumptuous man before the works of Michelangelo says: “I too am a master”.
Mole pretends that he sees, smells, and hears.
His mother tells him to claim no more senses than he has.
Flies try to drink water from elephant’s ears.
One cock takes glory of another’s valor.
Victor in cock fight crows over his victory. He is taken off by eagle. A second cock then comes out from hiding and struts about among the hens.
Kid perched on house jeers at wolf.
Hare demands equal rights for all animals.
Day after Feast Day disputes importance with Feast Day.
After one day of schooling children are ordered by their father to cease associating with the unlearned.
Boaster of victory over a weaker person reprimanded.
Presumptuous smith chants the Divine Comedy.
Dante throws his tools in the street.
Dante beats a mule driver who chants the Divine Comedy.
She sees how a little bird by persistence pecks a hole in a stone.
The quarreling sons and the bundle of twigs.
Peasant puts twigs together and cannot break them. Separately they are easily broken. His sons apply the lesson.
Sons united make living; separated fail.
Preacher teaches beaten Genoese the strength of unity.
Lion succeeds only when bulls separate.
Dog leader fears defeat because his forces are of different breeds.
Quails caught in net rise up in a body with net and escape.
As soon as they quarrel they are caught.
Captured elephants pull all at once and escape from net.
When they quarrel they are defeated.
Cranes fighting as allies defeat all enemies.
If they quarrel they are doomed.
Cats unite in battle against a wolf.
Grain will be cut when farmer attends to it himself.

Lark leaves her young in the cornfield. They hear farmer tell sons to go to neighbors for help in harvesting. Lark tells young not to worry. Same when he sends for relatives. Farmer decides to harvest it himself. Larks move, for they now know that it will be done Pauli (ed.
Stag found by master when overlooked by servants.
Hides under hay and escapes until master himself comes.
Gardener who plants vegetable tends it best.
Gods help those who help themselves.
Ox driver must put his shoulder to the wheel before Hercules will help him.
One must act therefore without awaiting everyone’s approval.
Attempt to please everyone with weather unavailing. Weather given therefore without regard to men’s desires.
Miller, his son, and the ass: trying to please everyone.
Miller blamed when he follows his son on foot; when he takes the son’s place on the ass; when he takes the son behind him; and when he puts the son in front of him.
Warns man by loss of appetite, loss of desire for drink, and sickness. Man does not recognize the messengers.
Cranes disregard warnings and are killed.
Snake disregards warnings to improve his manners: eaten by crab.
Man disregards mother’s warning and is punished.
Man disregards priest’s warning and is punished.
The cock and the pearl: prefers a single corn to a peck of pearls.
Baldheaded man finds the comb: it is useless.
Foolish dog finds treasure and dies rather than leave it.
Frog as beauty doctor unable to cure his own ugliness.
Doctor unable to cure himself scorned.
Bald man tries to sell hair restorer.
Mother crab blames her children for not walking straight.
Drunk man makes sport of another man for being drunk.
Futility of trying to teach the stupid.
Raven killed by apes who will not receive his teaching that a shining stone is not fire.
Results of labor lost in a moment of procrastination.
After laboring to make a brazen head, artist loses labor in moment of procrastination.
Man to be judged by his own qualities, not his clothes.
Guests strike man who tries to interfere in their quarrel.
It is their host in old clothes. Guests are humiliated but forgiven.
Rich Brahmin wearing poor clothing is treated as a beggar.
Man who never does any piece of work so well that he cannot improve it.
Parson’s apology for not answering challenge: I have never regretted silence but have often regretted speech.
Philosopher does not join in with gossipers.
He is silent because he fears that some day he may talk too much and not be able to keep silent.
Man does not court ugly woman: she might say yes.
Woman tests enduring power of gossip by having a servant ride through streets on a flayed ass.
By the third day he has ceased to attract attention. She concludes that it will be the same way in connection with her intended marriage.
Fox is terrified on first seeing lion.
The third time she meets him she has no fear.
Man desirous of traveling sent six miles to deliver a letter.
It must have been an extraordinary bed to permit a man with so many debts to sleep on it.
Futility of trying to hide an obvious deed.
Thus answers goat to herdsman who begs her not to tell master that he has broken off her horn.
Money does not always bring happiness.
The happy friar becomes unhappier as he receives ever more and more money.
Gets rid of money and is happy as before.
Possession of gold turns humble servant into arrogant one.
King sees poor man far happier than himself.
Poor man returns to the emperor all save enough for comfort: wealth would take happiness from his simple life.
Wise man refuses to react to unpleasantness.
Futility of expecting stranger to have one’s interest at heart.
When the sweet fails try the bitter.
Man pleads with thief who is stealing his figs. When pleading fails he brings him down from tree with stones.
Illegitimate daughter of trickster inherits father’s ability to dupe others.
Makes gift to husband’s mistress so that she may receive him fittingly. Husband is shamed into reforming.
Disguised real wife orders motley wear for her husband when he goes to fetch new bride-to-be: prospective father-in-law takes him for a fool and real wife reveals herself to husband.
Wife dismisses maid who is husband’s mistress and tells him she has fled.
Clever wife advises husband how to succeed on adventures.
Wives prevent war by placing themselves and their children between two armies.
Clever wife obtains secrets from husband by questioning him.
Physician decides that there is no need of purging one who drinks so many liquids.
Physician removes pea from patient’s ear.
Knocks him down and pea rolls out.
Clever minstrel gets a new robe.
Has tattered robe mended with scarlet. Ridiculed “I wish the rest of the robe were of the same material”. Is given one.
Clever merchant profits by being robbed.
Monkeys steal his caps. Traps monkeys and sells them.
Maxims for use of law court.
Solomon able to detect truth without evidence of witnesses.
Guilty person deceived into gesture (act) which admits guilt.
Largest part of a prize to go to the guilty man.
In order to obtain the prize, he confesses the earlier crime.
“Thief has grease from stolen fowl on him”: thief begins to feel his beard and is detected.
Creditor: “The destroyed bond was a cubit in size.”
Farmer will not pay servant wages due.
“Guilty man’s stick will grow during night.”
Guilty man chops end off stick.
“Thief has the feathers sticking on his head”: guilty woman immediately passes her hand over her head.
To decide which is master and which servant they are to put heads through window and servant’s head is to be cut off.
Which is man and which demon in man’s shape?
Decision to go to whichever can go through end of reed.
Accused woman to go three times around building naked: guilty one begins to strip off her clothes.
Thief persuaded detective can read thoughts: confesses.
Queen flogs suspects telling them to produce stolen gem: thief promises to do so.
Confession of debt secured by having defendant dispute as to whether cat was present when debt was made.
B warns A not to tie his horse near B’s.
Horses fight and A’s is killed. In court B plays dumb. A says B could talk the day before, and repeats conversation. Judge blames A for not taking advice.
Magician assigned three places at a table.
He confesses to carrying two persons in his body.
Cheaters examined apart; first made to repeat paternoster.
Others think that he has confessed and truth is discovered.
Confession induced by bringing an unjust action against accused.
False message to thief’s wife to send the stolen jewel case as bribe to the judge.
Detection of theft by finding bag-repairer.

Two men are in a lawsuit and before witnesses seal the documents in a bag to await arrival of the king. One of the men cuts the bag open, changes the documents, and has a repairer sew it up again. On the king’s arrival the change is discovered. By having a fine carpet repaired the expert repairer is discovered.

A man buries gold and a thief steals it. The owner detects the criminal. He takes some money to the thief and borrows money scales “to weigh so as to bury with the other”. The thief decides that he is detected and hastens to return the stolen money.
Thief suspected of crawling through hole must take off clothes.
He is full of scratches and confesses.
Animals put to graze in man’s garden.
Confession obtained by making thief fear for his life.
Husbands ask suspected priest to talk to wives on tithing, and thus obtain sufficient evidence to convict him.
Guilty man freed of murder charge is tricked into making a false accusation for which he is sentenced.
Minister threatens divine punishment to thief in congregation.
The thief is tricked into revealing himself in church.
The thief is tricked into betraying himself in supposed ordeal.
Test of mother by weighing milk.
The one with the heavier milk the mother of the boy; the other of the girl.
A woman’s adulterous love detected through her pulse quickening at mention of her lover.
Adultery detected by spit marks on the wall.
Too high to have been made by husband.
Thief’s corpse carried through street to see who will weep for him.
Mother’s weeping for thief made to seem natural.
Clever son falls from tree, so mother’s tears over dead body of father being carried through street will seem natural.
Woman breaks milk jars so that weeping for thief will seem natural.
Thief detected by building straw fire so that smoke escapes through thief’s entrance.
The secret hole into the building is thus discovered and the thief caught.
Eaters of stolen food detected by the giving of an emetic.
Animal thief of eggs detected when he comes to a spring to drink.
All animals must tell why they are thirsty.
Murderer detected by actions of murdered man’s dog.
Trespasser (lover, mistress, ghost, fairy, etc.) leaves footprints in the ashes.
Pitch is spread so that footprints are left in it, or that shoe is left behind as clue.
Husband relates his wife’s adultery in pretended dream.
Feigned madness unmasked by threatening man’s child.
Cheater discovered by fishing in the street.
Man arouses the curiosity of the rascal who has swindled his wife.
Detection by disrobing in a dance.
A man masking as a maiden has committed adultery with the queen. A clever girl by challenging him to disrobe in a dance exposes the imposture.
Urinalysis reveals coition as cure for illness.
Buried money is stolen from blind man. Latter has boy watch and notify him when passerby smiles at him. The smiler is the thief.
Thief detected by his answer to question.
Thief posing as corpse detected by pricking soles of his feet.
Magistrate detects thief’s complicity by associating cut hand with companion’s severed head.
Magistrate finds thieving innkeepers guilty of arson.
Silver buckles are not melted by the fire.
Truth detected by spies listening to reactions of defendants at night.
Washing test: defendants given basin of water.
Ninety-nine wise men and one fool ordered to pour milk into a tank all at one time: only the fool obeys.
Cleverness connected with the giving of evidence.
Testimony discredited by inducing witness to talk foolishly.

Husband tells his talkative wife about treasure he has discovered. To discredit her report he tells her also of impossible things (woodcock in the fish net, fish in the bird trap, etc.). She repeats it all and whole story is disbelieved. Husband may keep his treasure.
Wife puts fish in furrow where husband plows them up (or like absurdity). At mealtime the husband says, “Where are the fish?”

(Or rain of figs, fishes, or milk.) A mother in order to discredit testimony of her foolish son who has killed a man makes him believe that it has rained sausages. When he says that he killed the man on the night it rained sausages his testimony is discredited.
Witness claims the borrowed coat: discredited.

Adulteress is surprised in intrigue by unsuccessful suitor. He threatens to tell her husband. She tells her husband that the scorned suitor has accused her falsely of indiscretion with many men. When the suitor tells the husband he does not believe him.
Witness cannot speak language of accusation: discredited.
Two parrots taught accusation of mistress in a particular dialect. They know nothing more of the language.
Separate examination of witnesses discredits testimony.
Susanna and the elders: separate examination of witnesses.
Testimony as to exact circumstances of her deed does not agree.
To which of two men does woman belong?
Only one can answer questions just as she has.
Witness discredited by inability to tell details.
Parrot unable to tell husband details as to wife’s infidelity.
Wife has parrot describe a storm very realistically. Husband observes contrast in the two tales.
Witnesses to make image of diamond they claim to have seen.
False witnesses cannot describe stolen jewel.
“Then I woke up”: man discredits his confession by declaring it all a dream.
Confession discredited by claim to be notorious liar.
Bribed witnesses nonplussed when judge asks wrong question.
Witness claims not to have seen crime.
Witness says that dust storm blew and shut his eyes so that he did not see.
Literal pleading: letter of law has been met.
The three joint depositors may have their money back when all demand it.
Money is left by three joint depositors subject to their joint order. It is stolen by one. When the banker is sued he agrees to give up the money when he receives joint order from all three.
(Fleischpfand.) Literal pleading frees man from pound of flesh contract. Contract does not give the right to shed blood. Impossible, therefore, to carry out.
Trespasser’s defense: standing on his own land.
Man has earth from his own land in his shoes.
Before swearing, the cheater hands a stick containing the stolen money to the man he has stolen it from. He then swears that he has repaid it.
For three years not to drink wine, not to lie in bed, nor sleep with a prostitute. He goes to a convent, sleeps on eider down, and sleeps with the nuns.
Barber paid to change color of woman’s face burns her with acid.
Ruler forbids blacksmith to reveal solution of riddle unless he has seen him 100 times.
Ruler orders doctor to wear his hair and his robe “not too long and not too short”.
Has both his hair and his cloak cut half short and half long.
Bishop orders priest to wear his beard and his robe “not too long and not too short.”
Drunk philosopher wagers that he can drink the ocean dry.
Agrees to do so if the other will hold back streams emptying into the ocean. Agreed to drink only the ocean.
Man tells servant that he may have anything he can take with his teeth (eat).
Servant takes master’s cape with his teeth.
Thief makes it fall out that he has but taken what has been given him (he has followed literal instructions).
Plea by admitting accusation and discomfiting accuser.
Nurse’s false plea admitted: child demanded.
A nurse falsely demands pay for caring for a child which she says is the hero’s.
Own name inscribed on a stolen object as sign of property.
Clever pleading: youth in court for calling king a fool, proves truth of statement because king allowed self to be duped by alchemist.
Pleading for accused by means of parable.
Clever pleading: fighting for King of Kings.
Knight hailed before king for fighting blasphemer, tells king that he would fight to protect the honor of the king’s name so why not for the name of the King of Kings?
Plea by showing great temptation to crime.
Thieves tell judge walls of houses were so weak they could not resist temptation of breaking in.
Plea by shifting blame to another.
Barber operating on child’s skin kills it: blames mother for child’s thin skin.
When royal mace-bearer is attacked he throws away mace: attackers accuse him of insult to king.
Physician called to doctor woman’s eyes bandages them and then steals things each day. She refuses to pay fee and is haled to court.
Lawyer declares unjustly that stolen horse has been bought and paid for.
Knight attacks enemy contrary to orders. Part of army helps him and is killed. He disclaims responsibility since he had not asked their aid.
King vows to sacrifice first thing he meets. It is a miller driving an ass. Miller pleads that the ass preceded him. They behead the ass.
King has trickster’s horse’s tail cut off. Trickster retaliates by cutting off part of upper lip of king’s ass. At trial the animals are brought forth. Everyone laughs at the ass.
A tailor makes a Jew a coat of stolen goods. Accused of theft, he says that the Jew has the cloth.
Man hires ass and driver for trip across plain. In the heat the traveler sits down in the ass’s shadow. The driver pushes him away.
Judge demands that a pseudo-prophet show a miracle. Latter offers to cut off judge’s head and resuscitate him. Judge agrees to be the first disciple.
Three unlawful acts in killing one sheep: two lambs were inside.
Series of wise judgments settles quarrels of village.
Two women claim a child. Judge offers to cut it in two. Real mother refuses.
The ring to be cut in two and divided between quarreling persons: real owner laments the waste of the gold.
Three suitors dispute over a woman. When it is proposed to divide her, true lover is discovered.
The woman with two husbands is to be killed.
One of the husbands refuses to bury her. She is awarded to the other.
Clever judgment: man must belong to the third wife because the first had buried him and the second did not protect him.
Which mare is mother of colt: colt taken in boat to the middle of river; mother will swim to it.
Judgment as rebuke to unjust plaintiff.
Not the same purse as was lost.
Payment with the clink of the money.
Man sued for payment for enjoyment of the flavor of meat when roasting.
A man rescues a serpent (bear) who in return seeks to kill his rescuer. Fox as judge advises the man to put the serpent back into captivity.
Unjust claimant of woman duped into entering jar.
Jackal as judge declares that real husband shall enter jar woman carries on her head.
Animals render unjust decision against man since man has always been unjust to them.
Turtle released by man to carry him across stream.
Series of clever unjust decisions: plaintiff voluntarily withdraws.
Judge orders woman’s second husband to return her to the first in the same condition as he received her (with child).
Novel settlement: snake’s wife must wait to kill prince till princess bears as many sons as snake has.
Clever decisions concerning kissing and rape.
Youth in court for kissing prince’s daughter pleads his love for her.
Woman is allowed to take one in return.
Man breaks promise to sleep chastely with woman.
The girl screams when she is robbed.
Accuses young man of raping her. When he tries to rob her of money she summons help.
Girls must pay for young man’s virginity.
Girls repulsed by man climb in his window at night. Become pregnant and demand marriage. Branded as prostitutes and must pay the man.
Man’s torn garment as proof of his innocence of rape.
If he were the assaulter, the torn garment would be woman’s.

One of four companions is left in a warehouse to care for a cat which has a broken leg. Cat scratches self near flame and sets warehouse afire. The three must pay the one left behind. Broken leg could not walk and it was the three legs belonging to the three traders which caused the fire.

Rich man wishing to get rid of a neighbor’s tree sets it afire. Neighbor’s house catches and burns. Must pay four times value of tree since fire is intentional, but only actual value of house, since that fire was accidental.
Soldier accused of stealing slavegirl from author. Girl told to pour water into an inkwell. She does it so skillfully that she must have learned it from the author.
Some full and some half-full wine casks left with man by neighbor, who accuses him of theft. Fraud of accusation detected by measuring the dregs.
Woman leaves honey-pot with neighbor to guard. It has gold below the honey. Neighbor steals the gold and substitutes honey. Theft proved by gold pieces sticking to sides of pot.
A two-headed man is only one man.
Two-headed man claims double inheritance. Hot water poured over one head. Other head cries out with pain. He is declared to be one man and to merit only one share.
True husband of woman determined by assigning superhuman task.
Thus god masking as husband is discovered.
None should interrupt or leave the room while story is told: treachery revealed.
Story told to discover thief: sundry tales.
Damages for the field devastated by a flock.
David says pay money damages. Solomon says let laborers have flock till milk and wool have paid the damages.
The hog belongs to whichever place he goes of his own accord.
The short blanket must be patched.
Weaver makes blanket shorter than ordered. Weaver ordered to add a piece to the blanket and then to receive full price.
Robber innocent because he is merely following traditions of his ancestors.
Servants would not have left the coats.

Merchants complain to nobleman that his servants have robbed them of money. Nobleman asks whether merchants had on those good coats when the robbery took place. When told yes, he said that the robbers were not his servants, for they would never have left good coats.
Thread awarded to disputant who knows what it was wound on.
Stolen necklace does not have same scent as defendant uses.
Tenant advised by landlord to steal in order to pay his taxes acquitted.
Tires of the bickering of two men over a trifling sum.
Man believing wife dead becomes a priest. Later finds her alive.
Those who furnish equal number of animals for plow share equally in crop (in spite of amount of work done by each).
Watchers could never have got her merely by watching.
Cardinal’s clever decision: that the monks who arise earliest may sound matins.
There had been a great argument over this privilege.
Eye of king’s foster-son damaged by sting of bee.
Boy’s friends demand eye of king’s son in forfeit; king decrees instead destruction of swarm of bees so that guilty one may perish.
Clever means of avoiding legal punishment.
Execution escaped by use of special permissions granted the condemned.
Execution: man induced to kill self.
King may not execute Brahmin, but gets him drunk and brings about his death.
Execution evaded by using three wishes.
King ordains that guest who turns his plate shall be executed, but orders that anyone so condemned shall have three wishes granted.
Execution evaded by having three wishes granted: to be emperor, judge and the emperor’s son-in-law during the last week of his life.
As judge he frees himself and is in reality freed.
Condemned man wins pardon by clever remark.

Fool is allowed to jump off cliff (balcony) as punishment. Master expresses surprise that in three trials he has failed to hurl himself from the height. The jester offers the prince four trials. Amused prince pardons the jester.
To be beaten by deceiver of husband.
Lady has her women ready to give a trickster a beating. He is allowed to make one request. The one who has most often deceived her husband shall strike first.
Execution escaped by invoking laws of hospitality.
Prisoner has drunk water furnished by the king and thus becomes king’s guest.
No second punishment for same offense.
Adulteress hurled from high rock escapes injury: she may not be punished again.
Ears not to be cut off a second time.
Executioner discovers that the prisoner’s ears are of stucco, having been clipped for a previous offense.
Scheherazade: story with indefinite sequels told to stave off execution.
Clever means of avoiding legal punishment—miscellaneous.
Youth will answer question only when king places him on throne: then youth calls executioners to punish cruel king.
Execution escaped by threatening with malediction.
King substitutes for condemned man when he is told that whoever is executed that day is destined to become king in his next birth.
Reductio ad absurdum: the decision about the colt.
A man ties his mare to a second man’s wagon. The mare bears a colt which the wagon-owner claims, saying that the wagon has borne a colt.
“The sea is on fire” not more absurd than the decision about the colt.
Suit for chickens produced from boiled eggs.
The funeral for the ineligible husband.
A king awards a young woman to a gardener, who is already married. The young woman performs a funeral ceremony for him. The king is pleased with the jest and takes her into the harem.
To return the dead elephant alive.
Hired elephant dies. Owner demands the live elephant. The god causes the elephant’s owner to break pots of the other. Is unable to make specific restitution.
Reductio ad absurdum of accusation: object-birth slander.
(Later children tell toy animals to drink.
Impossible to eat pearls: also impossible for woman to bear animals (objects).
Plaintiff in court beats thief since he had not warned him ahead of time to have witnesses to robbery.
Judge has refused to inquire for lack of witnesses.
Rice pot on pole, fire far away.
As easy to cook rice thus as to warm a man at a distance from a lamp on a balcony.
Judge awards decision to the greater bribe.
Judge favors poor defendant so he may obtain money from rich without begging.
Trickster takes jar filled with earth but with honey on top as bribe to the judge. He takes the decision in writing. Cheat is discovered and judge sends message that an error has been made.
Clever animal says in court that she drops dung on ancestors of judges who take bribes (unless they confess).
Killing the fly on the judge’s nose.
The judge has told the boy that he should kill a fly wherever he sees one.

A judge awards damages of a penny against a friend of his for giving a blow. The defendant goes to get the money and is gone long. Meanwhile the plaintiff gives the judge a blow and tells him to use the penny as damages.
Judge finds offense is not great when it is his own son who is guilty.
King promises thieves pardon for confession: pleased with their cleverness.
Clever man puts another out of countenance.
Putting out of countenance by telling evil stories.
Bishop has instructed him to tell the truth and spare no one when he preaches.

Bishop has fined priest for incontinence. Priest hides and witnesses amorous intrigue between bishop and abbess, hearing bishop refer to the abbess’s charms in biblical similes. Priest incorporates overheard references in his introduction to the Mass and is asked for an explanation. Bishop returns his fine.
He has seen his victim in a disgraceful position and is allowed the booty as a price for his silence.
Thief confronted by the officer tells all the circumstances of the drunkenness (with many shameful additions). The officer denies the ownership.
Courtier having observed king’s amour shields him and gains pardon.
Answers in clever proverbs when called on to say what he has seen.
One of the disputants keeps the hens he is to give the judge in his hand and when the decision begins to go against him makes the hens cry out.
A thief steals a calf and keeps the hide. The owner makes a hue and cry about a stolen ox.
Absurd pretence, when allowed, puts pretender out of countenance.

Two hunters, one with dog and other with dog-head, dispute. The claim that the dog-head captured the game is allowed and then the alarm is raised that the owner of the, game is coming to punish the theft.
Cheater put out of countenance by raising alarm.
Wine seller carries water into his cellar. Man raises alarm pretending that he thought the house must be afire.
Worldly man puts religious man out of countenance.
One dueller fights with God’s help; the other with his brother’s.
First claims that the odds are unfair; second agrees that he will fight without his brother if the first will fight without God.
Simple holy man puts philosopher out of countenance when he says to him that wisdom came before learning.
Thirty years old for twelve years.
Man claims to be thirty; has been doing so for the last twelve years.
Old man in love with young woman puts his critics out of countenance.
Rebuke for telling a poor and long-winded story.
Poet puts others out of countenance.
Poet (Dante) puts ruler out of countenance.
Ruler had instructed jesters to tease him. The poet cleverly answers his questioners pretending to have the impression that the questions are addressed to the ruler.
Clever dividing which favors the divider.
Dividing two sheep and a ram: trickster to divide with two friends.
You two take one sheep; the ram and I will take the other.
Dividing four coins among three persons.
Two coins apiece given to two; other is to wait till two more coins are found.
Dividing three fish among two men.
Fools submit problem to trickster who solves problem by taking third fish himself.
Division of the fat and lean fowls.
Two fat fowls and one lean one at meal. Hero is lean, his two hosts fat.
Dividing the eggs: one man’s hand in the pot at a time.
Trickster alternates hands so fast that the other man never gets to put his hand in. He finally puts his foot in the pan.
Hog’s head divided according to scripture.
To be divided among three students according to their skill in quoting.
Three men divide a large fish by quoting scripture.
Inherited gold ring divided between three by selling it and dividing the money.
Dividing five eggs equally between two men and one woman.
Three to the woman and one each to the men. Men already have two (testicles).
Humiliated lover in repartee with disdainful mistress.
Evading a direct answer which may trap one.
Repartee based on church or clergy.
Repartee based on levity toward sacred persons and things.
Priest consoles sick man by saying that God chastens those whom he loves.
Man barks his shins on dark night.
Farmer looks at his hay on ground after a rain: “If I was a God, I’d be a God and not a damned fool!” U. S.: Baughman.
Woman causes disturbance in church, is carried out forcibly.
She remarks. “Well I am more favored than my Lord.
Distrusts God when he can be brought by a man.
Priest offers to help peasant with “the body of the Lord”.
Sacrament too precious to be bought.
If that were so, says the apprentice, no one would have given it to you or me.
Dante is accused of not kneeling before sacrament.
Says that he had his mind on God and did not remember what his body did. If those who criticized him had had their minds on God they would not have noticed it.
Priest bringing Host to dying man sees thief on his fig tree.
Says that he thought that the owl had stolen the Host.
Priest carries the Host across a dangerous stream.
Priest tells condemned man after confession that he will dine with Christ that evening.
Beggar woman asks pope for shilling and, being refused, for a penny. Finally asks for his blessing, which he gives.
Will spend the funeral money now.
Priest may use his own mother’s mass money.
At his mother’s funeral a boy takes the money laid on the altar for masses. When the priest objects, the boy says, “When your mother dies you may take the money too.” Pauli (ed.
Judgment Day a long way off.
Thief told by monk that he must return stolen cloth on Judgment Day “If I have so long a period of grace, I should like to take the whole monastery.” Pauli (ed.
Monk’s cordon cannot stand the strain.

Franciscan claims that his cordon will save him from Hell. Benedictine answers that he once had a dream in which he saw St. Francis throw his cordon to save members of his order in Purgatory and so many clung to it that it snapped.
“Better a live confessor than a dead martyr.”
So answers a preacher when asked whether he preferred to stay at home and confess his flock or go to war against the infidels.
How does goddess with thousand faces blow her noses?
A Jew objects to the doctrine that God could exist in the Virgin Mary. A disputant asks if he believes God is everywhere; then if God is in a mud puddle.
A Jew slaps a Christian and tells him to turn the other cheek. The Christian beats the Jew, who says, “You do not act according to your Gospel.”
Parishioner hears preacher say that alms are returned “100 to 1”.
Chops down crucifix and takes money from box.
Whoever gives alms in God’s name will receive tenfold: preacher’s wife gives sweetmeats away.
“You don’t blame a toolmaker for making all manner of tools, both harmful and helpful, so why blame God for making bad beasts as well as good ones?”
Repartee: “If you can’t see the soul in the living man, how can you expect to see it in the dead?” retorts wise man to atheist.
Indian examines skeleton of man at museum, finds there is no rib missing, concludes that ministers have deceived him in telling him the story of Adam.
Ruler trying to confiscate Jew’s money asks him which is the true faith. “There are three, the one which the Lord knows is right and the two his children think are right.” (Cf.
They can always find patrons as ignorant as they are.
A bishop disgusted with priest’s ignorance says, “Who consecrated you as priest?”
Peasants complain of his ignorance. He says that they stand so close to him that he is afraid they might memorize and then pay no attention to his reading of it.
Two priests apply for the position of chaplain and argue as to which one can say the mass more quickly.
Christ’s disciples did not pass the examination.
Ignorant student unable to pass his examination thus consoles himself.
Rich man shakes ducats into pope’s lap.
Pope says, “Who could withstand such an armored army?” and decides for the rich man.
Priest refuses small bribe: only for large sum will he sell himself to devil.
Jew so decides when he thinks of the scandalous life of the court of Rome.
The abbot’s luxury and the cardinal’s.
Cardinal rebukes abbot for living in luxury beyond that of the founder of his order. Abbot asks cardinal if the cardinals of St. Peter traveled in the luxury he does.
Man calls Saints Peter and Paul fools for enduring poverty if rich abbots can reach heaven, too.
Clergy in no need of spectacles.
Peasant sees priest at work in the fields. Tells him he wishes to confess. He is told to put money in the box and take the same penance as the year before.
Priest accused of being too intimate with parishioners’ wives says that the church is his wife and that the men treat her far more shamefully than he treats any woman.
Father wears a crown but is no king.
Nun asked why she did not call for help when raped.
Youth says he is associating with a pious person.
Nun claims her child is by the Holy Ghost.
Priest is entrusted with reforming five dissolute nuns. Gets all five with child. The priest is rebuked for not using his “talents” when tempted.
Abbess has twenty-four nuns for twelve monks: twelve nuns therefore for the guests.
Bishop has parson to dinner in the seat of honor. The parson fears that the dinner precedes punishment.
Priest offers to exchange places with the bishop when he is told that he is unfit to care for his parish.
Repartee based on church or clergy—miscellaneous.
The parson’s share and the sexton’s.
Man absents self from church because he does not like to hear people slandered.
Would be first in all things.
Chaplain accused of being first to start all knavery thus defends himself.
Scolding priest says he is merely trying to get even for all the scolding he must undergo.
Bishop brought quail on Friday orders them cooked.
Bishop refuses a favor to an abbess on the ground that he does not love her.
Praying before the King of Kings.
Man while praying refuses to salute superior. While standing before the King of Kings he could not show respect to inferiors.
Robber’s defense for stealing from rich.
God will not permit them to enter heaven unless we take their ill-gotten goods from them.
Who bore the Savior on his back? (St. Christopher.)
Complaints against underpaid priest that he does not stay at home. Says he cannot stay at home for the mice are dying of hunger since he receives only forty florins a year.
Their own quarters need it more.
Such is the answer given monks who insist that quarters occupied by the king and his train be reconsecrated.
Youth announces fire in imitation of priest’s metaphorical language.
The fire set by cat’s tail gains headway.
Cannot leave court of God: reply of saint when king invites him to court.
Repartee concerning the parentage of children.
Eunuch visits augurer to see whether he is to be a father.
“When I look at the livers, you are to be a father.
Of three brothers the shoemaker makes shoes for the queen and princess; the tailor, clothes; the fool
Children by day and by night.
Artist paints beautiful children but his own are ugly. One kind, he says, are made by day, the other by night.
His father has been in Rome.
A young man comes to Rome who looks like the emperor. Latter asks him if he mother has ever been in Rome. No, but my father has been here often.
Child born one month after marriage.
Child born two months after marriage.
Repartee regarding the parentage of children—miscellaneous.
Mother of twelve on deathbed explains to family that not all her children are legitimate. Gives the paternity of each child.
Even God can overdo it! Returning sailor finds his hovel transformed into a fine house.
Suitor hesitates to marry girl as immature (or too delicate).
Girl’s father protests, saying that she has had three children.
The children of the Genoese are strong because there is more help.
“If I were a tyrant you would not say so.”
Answer made by emperor to one who calls him a tyrant.
To be rewarded by ruler with a coin, an ass, a sheep, or a vineyard. Answers that he will take the coin, mount the ass, drive the sheep into the vineyard, and there pray for the ruler.

A king gives a man a coin. “Is that all you give your brother?” “Are you my brother?” “Surely, we both pray, Our father, etc.” “If all your brothers give you as much as I you will be rich.” Pauli (ed.
Do not leave it to your successor.
A widow stops a ruler on his way to war. He may be killed and he should not leave the act of justice as a credit to his successor.
Show me how it is done.
Wronged woman thus addresses ruler, who is indifferent to insults directed at him. She wishes to be shown how to bear insults. This rebukes him.
A widow asks justice of a king. The latter says that he is too busy to hear her. “Then cease being a king,” replies the widow. Her bold reply wins an audience with the king.
A peasant goes to a judge and thinking to gain his favor addresses him with high titles. The judge calls him a fool.
A judge asks a pseudo-prophet to prove his powers by opening a difficult lock.

Peasant tells bishop, who rides by with forty horses, that he wonders if St. Kilian at Würzburg is also riding with forty horses. Bishop excuses extravagance by saying that he is also a prince and that it is the prince, not the bishop, who is using the horses. “If the prince should become a fool, what would the bishop do then?” Pauli (ed.
Will not try to correct them.
Pope calls persistent courtier a fool. Latter says that there are people who call the pope the same thing and that he for one will not try to correct them.
Philosopher asks ruler for money Ruler says that philosophers do not need money.
Shoemaker speaks ill of lord’s rule.
Lord takes his tools away from him. Shoemaker begs for them saying that he cannot carry on his business without them.
One ear saved for other litigant.
Judge stops up one ear while first litigant presents his case. He is saving one ear for the second litigant.
Seek harmony in your own house.
King brought to sense of duty by philosopher who tells him to seek harmony in his own house before inquiring about the harmony in his kingdom.
A philosopher of the city came to him asking mercy for it King said he would do nothing he asked. Philosopher then asked him to destroy the city. This saves the city.
Man, fined for sabbath-breaking, asks for receipt, explains that if God asks for it, he will not have to journey to hell to get it from the judge.
Man is arrested for drunkenness; he is so drunk that trial must be postponed.
When he is tried later, he is told how at the earlier trial he had kept repeating that the judge was a very wise judge. When he hears this he admits that he must have been very drunk.
Weaver hearing of tax for every doorway of weavers takes his door to the khan: will not return for the sidewalls of his house.
Gem offered by monarch to one who can first go around the kingdom.
Trickster goes around king and says king is kingdom.
Thief serves king buffaloes he has killed in hunt and lost; thus reproaches king’s wastefulness.
Hairless palms from giving and receiving gold.
Emperor: “What people have the biggest bellies?” Jester answers: “The landlords.”
Holy man asked by king for the heart of religion answers: “You are sitting on your throne and I’m sitting on the ground, so how can I tell.”
Tailor caught resting his head on royal robe while he rests tells king there is no better resting place for king’s robe, for “the head is the king of the body.”
King to smoker: “Even donkeys will have nothing to do with tobacco.”
Reductio ad absurdum of question or proposal.
Why is it that black cow eats green grass, gives white milk and yellow butter?
Theological questions answered by propounding simple questions in science.

Where was God before he made heaven and earth? and the like answered by “Why a louse bite raises a blister, a flee bite raises a swelling, and a gnat bite is unnoticeable?” If you cannot answer such simple questions how can you pry into God’s secrets.
How many priests should one have in one place?
How many fox tails will reach to heaven? All depends on the length of the tails.
How much cloth would it take to make God’s coat?
Just as much as for me, for what you have done for a poor person in my name you have done for me.
“In this sesame flower where is the oil?”
Tide inquires whether moon is up.
Minnow seeing absurdity of question (since tide could not be up without the moon) tells the tide to wait till he gets a drink and he will tell.
Little bird as large bird’s mate.
A large bird wishes to mate with a little bird. The latter says that she is going to swallow a large eel. The large bird sees the absurdity of his proposal.
Not more absurd than crow claiming swan as wife.
If his head is taken off other punishments do not matter.
Turning king into Brahmin like turning donkey into horse.
Pot full of milk as sign that city is full of fakirs; flower on top of milk not disturbing it as sign that one more will not matter.
Butcher buyer demands saddle and ornaments along with camel (or the like).
Women insist on knowing how a man wants to be mourned when he dies.
Priest complains that miller’s mule is overloaded.

Aesop goes for fire to a neighbor’s in the daytime and lights a lantern so as to bring the fire back. Fool asks him what he is hunting for with the lantern in the daytime. “I seek a man” (not a busybody).
A man goes forth in black clothes. People are curious as to the reason.
One who believes in auguries asks peasant woman if she has seen a bird.
Mother asks newly-wedded daughter if she approached her husband the first night.
Man asks naked Indian if he is not cold.
Indian asks if man’s face is cold. Man replies that it is not.
“How often do you kill your ducks?”
“Where did dirt go when canal was dug?”
What is wanted, not what is asked.

A servant is so trained that when the host asks for wine from a good cask he brings it from a cheap one. When the guest objects, the host says that the servant brought not what was asked for but what was wanted.
Serve the water and the wine separately.
Server of diluted wine thus taunted.
Server of diluted Rhine wine thus taunted.
Christ’s making wine from water has made all landlords try to do it too. Man prefers Jewish wine to the baptized kind.
Very small to be so old.
Guest criticizes host’s small serving of wine which he said was six years old.
Man asks that large jug be filled with wine. Is told to go to the river. Is accommodated when he presents small jug.
Wine gives ambassador courage to address Pope.
Man says: “I do love my enemies and I have great affection for them that hurt me.”
Where did he get the wine?
Father shows drunkard son a drunk man being mocked on the street.
Though old woman is made to believe she is in hell she calls for drinking companions.
Will take care of the thirst.
Priest blamed for large amount of wine he drinks tells people to consider his great thirst. He has slept on a sack of salt and has enough thirst for a week.
A beggar will not come in but insists on the man coming down to the door. When he asks alms the man bids him come upstairs.
A numskull tells his mother that a beggar is below asking for bread.
Beggar tells stingy to go beg.
Beggar claims to be emperor’s brother.
(All men are descended from Adam.) Emperor gives him small coin.
So says beggar who asks goldsmith to plate his club with gold.

Parents serve boy a small fish and keep back a large one for themselves. Knowing this, the boy puts the fish to his ear. He says that he has asked the fish a question; the fish cannot answer but tells him to ask the large fish under the bed.
A dog to scent the rice.

Widow serves tailor one egg. He sings, “One egg, one egg.” She decides one egg is not enough and serves him two next time. He then sings “Two eggs are two eggs.” He is next given two eggs and a sausage, etc.
Hungry apprentice attracts master’s attention by telling lies on him.
He tells of a cow with four teats who bore five calves.
Stingy innkeeper cured of serving weak beer.
She always gives the servants a pitcher of weak beer before meals so as to fill them up.
The little lumps of sugar are sweeter, says the hostess.
The servant says that he doesn’t like sweets and takes the large lumps.
He slaps another son, and explains that the other boy was saying that he would not get any of the father’s cherries. The father shares the cherries.
By telling a mewing cat that it could not yet have the bones because no meat has been served him, a collegian calls attention to an oversight on the part of a servant.
Hired men sing of displeasure with food; change song when food is improved (cante fable).
Hired man shows in saying grace how better food has resulted from arrival of unexpected guests.
The liking for food and drink.
What music do you like best? The sound of plates and spoons.
Unwelcome guest tells about the hidden food.
Having seen his hostess hide it, he tells about it in the form of a tale.
Why he did not eat the bread.
Maid rebukes pilgrim for eating too much.
A woman accuses another of being a harlot.
A king and his son hunting on a hot day put their fur coats on the fool’s back.
Young rival derides old one for his age.
There is someone carrying a goose. How does that concern me? He is carrying it to your house. How does that concern you?
Not in his line of business.
“You are a good man; there is not your equal on the earth.
Two men meet a homely girl.
Monk says that he is a stallion.
In reply to women’s taunts he boasts of his powers. A woman calls on the devil to come and ride him.
Too late for the same advice.
To be rewarded by his kind.
Man decides to spend 100 florins to become known.
Two men meet in narrow passage.
Person asks: “Whose fool are you?” Answer: “I am the Bishop of Durham’s fool; whose fool are you?” England: *Baughman.
Why soldier is silent before king: is always so when questioned by stupid person.
Safe since no white man is near.
White man asks Indian if he can safely leave some of his belongings inside the Indian’s lodge.
Where you got it last year.
Parson tells borrower to get the corn at the same place as he got it last year.
The one to blow the whistle.
Many persons request a man on the way to market to buy them a whistle.

To a man going on a voyage, various people give commissions for purchases, which he writes down on cards. Some give him money; some promise it on his return. On ship he looks the cards over, placing the proper gold on the proper card. A wind blows into the sea those not weighted with gold.
Stag tries to borrow grain from the sheep, using the wolf as security. Sheep says that they are both so swift that he does not know where they will be on the day of payment.
A three thousand year old debt.
Vegetable thief is caught in a garden.
A thief climbs over a wall by means of his ladder. When caught in the garden he says that he is a seller of ladders.
Two thieves caught with stolen sheep.
How he would act if he were a hawk.

A hawk steals a piece of liver from a trickster and flies away with it. The trickster likewise steals some liver from another man and escapes to a high place with it. He says that he is seeing how he would act if he were a hawk.
Fox pretends that he has been to the farmyard only to see if any of his kindred were there.
Lame excuse: one cannot drink because he has no teeth.
King demands that each subject bring small amount of milk to put in his new cup. They plan to cheat him by bringing him water.
A thief ransacks a man’s house and departs. The man gathers together the rest of his belongings and tracks the thief.
Owner advises thieves to return later.
Cynic helps robber steal his money so he and robber can get sleep.
Owner laughs at thief who finds nothing in house.
Bridegroom promises thief spoils later if he will not interfere with wedding.
A numskull caught changing meal from others’ sacks into his own. Miller asks him what he is doing. “I am a fool.” “Why then don’t you put your meal into their sacks?” “I am only a simple fool.
The king in order to correct the habit has him robbed. He says that robbers get up even earlier than he.
Was going to give it to him any way.
Thus a hunter answers a thief who steals his hare.
A king noticing that a student has stolen a capon, asks, “Does not the Bible say that you should not worry about tomorrow?” “Exactly.

A man takes a shirt to market for a friend who has stolen it. At market it is stolen from the seller. He tells his friend that the market was bad and that he was able to get back only the cost price (nothing).
A man complimented a hangman on the good job he had done in hanging a thief.
A parson hides his money in a holy place and leaves a sign, “The Lord is in this Place.” A thief takes the money and leaves a sign, “He is risen and is no longer here” Pauli (ed.
The hay wagon and the gate.
A parson arriving late at a city gate asks if he can get in. Guard sees that he is fat and in fun says that he doesn’t know.
(Peace fable.) The fox tries to beguile the cock by reporting a new law establishing peace among the animals.
A falcon reproaches a cock for fleeing from the master who has fed him.
“Do as I say and not as I do.”
Doctor forbids patient to drink wine.
Doctor throws patients into a pit of water. Servant warns queer-looking hunter to flee before master throws him into the pit.
When he killed animals he had to pay for them; but he did not have to pay for killing people.
Tells Alexander that the power of reason makes even a poor man as great as a king.
The cynic and the pale gold.
“Why is gold so pale?” “It is in great danger.” Pauli (ed.
Cynic asks that his body be exposed to the elements.
The cynic as judge of wine.
Asked which wine tastes best, he says, “That belonging to other people.” Pauli (ed.
The cynic and the big gates.
Coming to a little town with big gates, he says, “Close the gate so that the town won’t run away.” Pauli (ed.
The cynic and the bastard stone-thrower.
Hearing a man discoursing at great length about heaven, he asks, “When did you come down from there?” Pauli (ed.
The cynic and the bald-headed man.
His only reply to the baldheaded man’s slanders is to compliment the hair that has left such a horrible head.
When the deceiver calls him wicked, he says, “I am glad that you are my enemy; for you do good to your enemies and evil to your friends.” Pauli (ed.
The cynic and the fig tree.
Man tells friend that his wife has hanged herself on a fig tree.
Cynic is asked if widower should remarry.
The smallest woman makes the best bride.
A wandering actor rewarded by a city with a coat of their color gambles it away. When upbraided about giving away their present he replies that they hadn’t wanted to keep it themselves.
A man has been told by a seer that there are two ways in which a believer may be distinguished. But he has forgotten one of them and the seer had forgotten the other.
Dog reproaches sow that Venus will not allow those who have eaten swine to enter her temple. Sow says that it is because the goddess abhors those who kill swine.
Philosopher explains that with his own blood he was nourishing as large a population as that of the Roman Emperor (lice).
It’s better to fight in the shade.
Soldier tells captain that the enemy are so numerous that their arrows darken the sun.
A man points out the statue to show the supremacy of man.
Village called on to join in war deliberates in meeting. A man says, “We have taken oaths not to go to war.
A trumpeter captured pleads that he did not fight.
Must drink from the common cup.
A man always drinks out of his own cup. In storm at sea a sailor says, “Today we all drink out of the same cup (the sea).
Sailor prays for gods to sink ship during storm, since gods never do what they are asked to do.

A duke invites a notorious eater. The latter consumes eight fowls, forty eggs, and other things in proportion. In leaving he apologizes for eating so little as he had not felt well the night before. He will do better next time.
Reproached with his mutilation, the eunuch says that his ill fortune is no shame. The only shame is to merit what you suffer.
The fairest thing in the garden.
Three brothers asked by princess what is the most beautiful thing in the garden. The youngest replies, “Yourself.” He wins the princess.
He dreams that he receives nine coins. He demands ten. He wakes and finds that he has dreamed. He is willing to accept the nine.
A man prays for a thousand gold pieces and says that he will not accept one less.
A sailor says that all his ancestors have drowned.
A peddler scolds the dog who is waiting and tells him to get ready to go with him. The dog replies that he has nothing to carry, that it is the peddler who is late.
A hide is in the river.
A man boasts of his jump on Rhodes and says that if he were in Rhodes he could prove his boast.
Husband and wife burn their mouths.
A wife served overhot soup, forgets and burns herself so that tears come to her eyes She says that her departed father liked soup so much that she weeps when she eats it.
Says that he is crying because so many have left the monastery.
After her husband’s death a woman cannot find a hammer and anvil.
Man tells parson secret and asks him to keep it.
King and jester flee: the king’s swift horse.
An inexperienced rider borrows a horse, which runs away with him.
“Why didn’t you stay on the horse?”
An unskillful barber keeps cutting a man’s face. A noise is heard.
A bride slips up behind her husband and kisses him.
Husband mistaken for lover in bed.
Farmer has whiskers shaved off, hair cut short. He gets home late, slips into bed with his wife.
A lazy youth explains his late rising by saying that he lay abed to hear the argument between industry and laziness.
A man sends his two sons to schools and later enquires of their progress.
What the bear whispered in his ear.
Paid guide climbs tree and leaves traveler to mercy of a bear. Traveler feigns death and the bear sniffs at him and leaves.
Trickster artist hoodwinks king: cuckold’s eyes cannot see picture.
Daydreamer has lost his chance for profit.
He has broken his master’s pots while dreaming of future profits. He has therefore lost more than the master and excuses himself of blame.
Why captain takes lame and one-eyed soldiers into army.
Person runs from actual or supposed ghost.
Man runs from actual or from supposed ghost.

Man attempts to stay in haunted house all night. One cat after another enters, says, “Everything will be all right when Caleb comes, won’t it?” (or something similar). Man finally says, “When Caleb comes, tell him I was here and left.” He leaves.
A rule must work both ways.
Turnips called bacon: cat called rabbit.
A peasant compels his servant to call turnips bacon. Under favorable circumstances the servant compels the master to call a cat a rabbit.
Man bathing rich man uses sand instead of sandalwood: “Consider the sand of the Ganges to be sandalwood.”
A woman feigns periodic attacks of a sickness that can be cured only by eating a great number of delicacies. The husband feigns the same disease.
After dinner a servant feigns a fit and goes to sleep. The master thereupon feigns a fit and beats the boy, who is thus cured of his laziness.

A host spills his customer’s wine so that he must buy more. He consoles the guest with “It is a sign of the great abundance you shall have this year.” With the same remark the guest draws the spigot from the host’s wine cask.
The porter’s revenge for the three wise counsels.

A man offers a porter three wise counsels for carrying his goods. “When anyone tells you that hunger and satisfaction are the same, don’t believe him.” The second and third are similar and equally valueless.
No clothes needed for Day of Judgment.

Friends tell a man that the next day is the Day of Judgment and urge him to kill a lamb and give a feast. He apparently consents. He then burns up their clothes. They will not need clothes on the Day of Judgment.

A husband forbids a wife to think. During his absence she roasts a chicken, eats it, and leaves two drumsticks on the table. The husband asks for the chicken. “Since you have forbidden me to think, I did not think of you.” The ban is lifted.
Master says that he has eyes in back of head: servant cheats him.
Holds up food to master’s back and then not having objection raised, eats it.

A priest who has lent money to a Jew, but will not lend to a farmer, on being reproached by the latter, says that the money he lent the Jew was “false”. When the Jew gets to know of this, he claims that as soon as he heard the money was false he burnt it up.
Boy pretends to speak only Latin.
Father, chastising his lazy son, also speaks in “Latin”.
The man in place of a watch-dog.
The master orders his serf to watch the manor at night in place of the dog.
Oisin’s poor diet in Patrick’s house—pancake size of ivy leaf, measure of butter only size of rowan berry.
Later Oisin gives Patrick quarter of a wild boar, servant ivy leaf and rowan berry.
Things on highway belong to the public.

Man reproves another for picking his cherries that overhang the highway. He is told that things on the public highway belong to no one in particular. He invites the man to climb the tree for better cherries, drives off with his horse and buggy, giving the same answer about things in the public highway.
Can drink only one kind of wine at a time.

Priests come to an inn where host gives them good wine and bad. They insist on having all good since they must drink only one kind of wine. On their return he serves them with all bad. They claim to have had the rule changed.
“Eat spiritual food, not material,” say monks to lazy brother who criticizes them for working in the garden.
Ox bought; buyer also claims load of wood attached.
Later deceived man disguises and sells sharper another ox for “handful of coppers.” He is allowed by court to claim the hand as well.
Priests say dying woman’s unfulfilled request for mangoes must be paid in golden mangoes to them.
Priests burned with iron since she had asked to be cauterized.
Vizier advises doctor to give up his wife to love-sick prince since everything belongs to a sovereign. Doctor then tells him prince is in love not with his (the doctor’s) wife but with the vizier’s.
Goldsmith sells thinly plated gold; peasant retaliates: a pot of dirt with a little gyav on top.
A king demands a hundred men’s drink from the milk of a hornless dun cow from every house in the land. Wooden cows are made and bog-stuff substituted for milk; the king must drink it.
To return the eye to the one-eyed man.
“If he does not live, let him die.”
The student as healer hangs this sign around the neck of a sick calf. Later as parson he is sick. It is proposed to heal him with the same remedy.
You lead and I will follow: hard command thus evaded.
The father of an illegitimate child must walk in front of the cross.
Condemned man insists that the priest, who is guilty also, shall lead the way.
Rogues exchange objects and cheat each other.
Thieves deceived by prearranged conversation which they overhear.
Overheard conversation: “Mustard has advanced in price.”
Thieves steal mustard and leave all else.
Thieves take box filled with stone (or dig up field).
Overheard conversation: “My money is hanging in the tree.”
The shoes carried into the tree.
Tricksters induce a numskull to climb a tree, planning to steal his shoes. He takes them in his belt with him.

A monk at an old man’s deathbed asks if he hasn’t promised this and that to the church. The old man from weakness rather than understanding nods “Yes”. The son standing by asks, “Shall I throw this fellow down stairs?” The old man nods “Yes”.
Clever wife of king’s adopted son keeps king distracted on deathbed so that he cannot disinherit husband.

A ruler receives gifts from his subjects and later demands them as he due. The fool sets the nobleman’s bed on fire. When the nobleman commands him to put the fire out he refuses, since he would ever afterward have to be putting out fires.
A woman entrusts three coins to a headsman. He denies her claim which she fails to substantiate in ordeal. She now claims more and happens to succeed with ordeal.
Claimant has called dead cricket “something” and must be content.
Half price for half a shave.
A man asks to be shaved at half price. The barber shaves one side. He must pay the other half for the rest of the shave.
Stingy man rebuked when his children are feasted in his absence.
They think he has been responsible and honor him.
Poor girl outwits prince in fright-contest.
He frightens her and later mocks her with her words of fright. She plays the same trick on him.
Army major approaches sentry, takes away his rifle, and reproaches him for allowing himself to be disarmed. Sentry draws pistol from inside shirt, demands return of unloaded rifle.
Priests misinterpret raja’s dream and get his horses. Trickster advises raja to announce dream demanding cauterization of the priests. They return horses.

Borrower of golden pumpkin returns a brass pumpkin and claims that the gold has turned to brass. The lender takes the borrower’s son and returns with an ape. He claims that the boy has turned into an ape.
Mill has given birth to horse.
Trustee claims that mice have eaten the iron scales confided to him. The host abducts the trustee’s son and says that a falcon has carried him off.

Man keeps dog for boy, tells him when he comes for it that the chinch bugs have eaten it. The boy borrows a mule from the man, later tells him that a buzzard has carried it away. He gets his dog back.
The pot has a child and dies.
A borrower returns a pot along with a small one saying that the pot has had a young one. The pots are accepted. He borrows the pot a second time and keeps it. He sends word that the pot has died.
(Modus Leibinc.) A sailor’s wife bears a son in his absence and says that it came from eating snow. Later the husband makes away with the boy who, he says, melted in the sun.
Absurdities concerning birth of animals, or men.
Deer captured in bird-net: water flows upstream.
One partner claims a deer he has captured in his bird-net. The other pretends to be watching water flow upstream.
Absurdity of entrusting military mission to bishop.
Courtier rebukes king by asking that he be given an ecclesiastical post.
Absurdity of trying to convert king to Hinduism—like making cow of donkey or black dog into white.
Priest forbidden to have female servant ostentatiously washes his own clothes.

A scholar, showing his skill in logic, proves that two chickens (or eggs) on the table are really three. His father (or host) takes one chicken for himself, gives the other to the mother, tells son that he can have the third one.
A man pledged to give his wife only good words hits her with a prayer book.
Man pledged to do so with his wife follows instructions literally.
A man overcomes his quarrelsome wife by playing the flute as long as she is scolding.
He placates her by telling her that he wants a handsome child.
Husband and wife separate and divide property.
Man keeps the house, gives the wife the road.
A wife whose husband has beaten her sends a rumor to the sick king that her husband is a skilled physician but will practice only when he is well beaten. He is seized and whipped.

A husband disguises as a priest to hear his wife’s confession. She says that she has been mistress of a servant, a knight, a fool, and a priest; i.e., her husband when he was her servant, and later her knight. He had then been a fool for demanding her confession, and was a priest because he had heard it.
The wife has cooked so many dishes that when he complains, she can always supply another. Finally he says, “I had rather eat dung.” She produces some.
Wife shows that she does many more tasks in one morning than the husband.
Fault-finding husband threatens to hit wife with shoes.
Man who continually threatens to leave wife mortified when she tells him to go; pretends his buffalo is dragging him home (after he does leave).
A wife driven from home is allowed by her husband to take her one dearest possession. She takes her sleeping husband and effects reconciliation.
(Women of Weinsberg.) Permitted to carry from the city their dearest possession, they take their husbands.
Husband tells wife in indecent posture to “lock up shop”.
She retorts that he has the key.
Wife by cleverness wins back fortune overbearing husband has foolishly lost and humbles him.
Clever laughter and response of wife stops husband from fondling maid.
Corpse to be cut in two for easy carrying.
Husband who feigns death hears wife propose this.
Husband declares that he will drown himself. The wife shows him a deep spot in the stream.
Overcurious wife learns of the senate’s deliberations.
Husband (son) tells her that they have decided that each man may have many wives. Gullible wife believes it.
A woman demands money for a visit which she dreams of having had from a merchant. She is shown the money in a mirror.

A penitent confesses that a plan to sin had entered his mind. Priest tells him that the thought is as good as the deed. Assesses four florins as penance. Penitent says that he had only had it in his mind to give the florins; he must take the thought for the deed.
Singer repaid with promise of reward: words for words.
Directions for getting pay given in return for directions for healing.
Substitute for candle repaid with substitute for money.

A monk gives a man a stick instead of the candle the man has wanted to burn before a holy picture. The monk says that it will have the same effect as if the candle were burned. The man takes out his purse and lets the monk touch it.

A man receives a present of a hare. Later a crowd comes to him for entertainment saying that they are friends of the man who presented the hare. This happens a second time. He serves them clear water.
Imagined ownership: derived from a dream.
Man claims ownership of bulls because he has dreamed of them. He is given their shadows.
Clerk tells person to imagine that blue cloth is green. The customer walks out without paying. The clerk asks for payment; the customer tells clerk to imagine he has been paid.
Half of money thrown into tank.
The priest administers to a man sick with infectious disease.
“Here is half of picture and you must imagine other half.”
Jester later redecorates house in fragments of pictures.
The ass consulted about the loan.
A man wants to borrow an ass.
The ass is not at home.
A man wants to borrow an ass. The owner says that the ass is not at home. The ass brays and the borrower protests.
When told by servants their master is not at home, man says it is a fool that goes out in such midday heat.
A man asks for credit, although he has always paid cash before.
Man refuses to lend horse: sued for consequent damages.
The would-be borrower gets one from another neighbor. He overworks the horse and renders him useless. The owner of the horse sues the man who had refused to lend his animal.
Better to donate half of what is asked than lend all.
Two farmers ask a priest to lend two measures of grain to each of them. The priest refuses to lend them any but donates one measure to each. Thus he saves two measures.
Lender repays borrower for deceptive loan.
Borrower of butter receives pot of cowdung with little butter on top: repays by lending wooden sword covered with thin iron.
Miscellaneous retorts concerning borrowing and lending.
A present or a retaining fee.
An abbot presents a lawyer with a fine horse. Later the abbot comes to Rome and calls on the lawyer for help. The latter returns the horse. “I did not know that you had a lawsuit in Rome.” Pauli (ed.
God as surety; the abbot pays.

A young man is ransomed by giving God as surety for the ransom money. He fails to return as agreed. The creditor sees a wealthy abbot, who says that he is a servant of God. He robs the abbot and when the young man finally appears he tells the latter than the debt is already paid by God’s servant.
A student leaving the university sends back a small coin to pay for the knowledge he is carrying away, although he says that he is really paying too much.
Clothes thrown into the cooking food.
A trickster when told that food cooking is clothes being boiled retaliates by throwing his dirty hose into the pot.
An abbot has his innkeeper treat his guests with the most shameful neglect. A guest retaliates by telling the abbot that he has been very sumptuously entertained. The innkeeper is discharged.
A man at a banquet is neglected because of his poor clothes. He changes clothes, returns, and is honored.
Poor suitor served good supper prepared for rich one.
Hostess says that she has no spoons.
Otherwise she would be glad to give something to eat. A joker brings along the necessary spoons.
Father causes inhospitable daughter to spoil her feast by deceptive advice about cooking.

Man refused hospitality tells rich man he is a relative. Asked for the “connection,” he tells him there is a box connection. Rich man not understanding, man explains his cart is made of box wood and is tied to a rich man’s box tree. Rich man, ashamed, entertains him with all due respect.
Grace said in name of the host.
Neglected guest thus gets his portion of food.
A cuts the meat and puts all the good things on his side.
The peasant’s share is the chicken.
He serves small birds and a roast chicken to his guests. Guests each take a small bird, leaving only the chicken when the plate reaches the host.
Host hides meat in his clothing.
It attracts his dog and he is exposed.
The guest who could not keep warm.
He keeps calling for more bed clothes. The host finally piles a ladder, a trough, etc., on top of him until he calls for help.
Guests make impossible demands of host: host’s representative forces guests to leave by sending them on difficult quest.
Bread baked with onions for an undesirable guest.
Proper food for ox and ass.
Guests call each other ox and ass. Host offers green grass for the first and fodder for the second.
Tells guests husband uses it against guests.
Food being considered unclean then, guests depart empty but unwitting of true reason.
When hints do not get rid of unwelcome guests, force must be used.
A sham fight to frighten away the guests.
Tells them he has that morning confessed man with plague.

He is asked a question by his master each time he tries to eat a date, so that he always has to spit out the date. He revenges himself that night when the master tries to carry on an intrigue with his wife’s maid. He comes with his answers at embarrassing moments.
A rabbi who has been inhospitably treated is afterwards invited to dinner. He keeps the guests so amused by his jokes that they fail to eat and the feast is spoiled.
Fox and crane invite each other.
Fox serves the food on a flat dish so that the crane cannot eat. Crane serves his food in a bottle.
Bugs unable to eat honey at banquet of bees, and bees unable to eat dung at bug’s dinner.
Crop division between parrot and cat: they try to cheat each other by inviting to a dinner in turns every day.
It is the only place he can find at the royal table not covered with gold and jewels.
Ruler refuses hospitality from subject who spends more than he earns.
A step-ladder for setting the table.
Guest brings along cakes to eat.
Mother of girl tells suitor that she cannot have him burning her midnight oil. The next night he brings his own lamp and a can of oil, tells her he will stay all night if he wishes.
Answer of hungry man when host asks for suggestion for a picture to be painted of something that has not been seen.
Inviting to a feast only those whose households have never been touched by death.
Poem for poem: all for all.

A poet gives the emperor a poem, hoping for a reward The emperor later gives the poet a poem in return. The poet thereupon sends the emperor two pennies, saying that this is all the money he has. The emperor, seeing that he is defeated in the exchange, laughs and becomes the poet’s friend.
Reinforcement of the request for alms.
A clown asks for alms and receives nothing.
The penny baked in the wafer.

A peasant always puts a bad penny into the offering. The priest has a penny baked in a wafer and gives it to the peasant at communion. The peasant, unable to swallow it, thinks that he is possessed of the devil. The priest asks whether he has ever done wrong with a penny, secures confession and a pledge of reform.
Parishioners put base money into the collection. The priest burns sulphur instead of incense He tells them that their money will buy nothing better.
Stingy king insists on trickster asking any boon desired. By asking king to perform disgusting act, trickster compels king to give expensive gift.
