A man takes refuge from robbers in an open grave.
A numskull who has lain down thinking he is dead is carried off in a bier. The carriers lose their way.
The dead man in spite of himself.

Neighbors who have heard of the numskull’s death insist on the funeral although he is alive and well. He is persuaded and is carried on a bier. They meet a busy man whom they try to persuade to join them. He pleads business.
Supposed dead man on bier threatens his bearers.
Cold hands and feet for the dead man.
His wife has told him that one tells a dead person by his cold hands and feet. He freezes his feet and hands and lies down for dead.
Parents made to believe that they are dead and are married to each other again.
Foolish peasants carry couple to burial; when “corpses” speak they flee in terror.
Drunken man insists that he be beheaded.
Is struck with the flat of his sword. He thinks he is dead.
Idiot tells his mother he has been dead twelve years.
Supposed dead man roused with whip.
Naked person made to believe that he is clothed.
Layman made to believe that he is a monk.
Wife persuades husband that she has returned immediately.
She goes to a neighbor’s to cook a fish. She is gone a week. She gets a new fish and cooks it and returns home with the hot fish. She convinces her husband of her short absence.
Wife leaves home, offers self to lover.
Returning persuades husband that she has not been away.
Gullible husband made to believe he has cut off his wife’s nose.

She, in another house, has had her nose cut off by mistake. She makes him believe he has done it by making him angry enough to throw a razor at her. When he throws the razor she claims it has cut off her nose.
Husband made to believe that his house has moved during his absence.
The wife and her confederates transform the house into an inn with tables, signs, drinkers, etc. The husband cannot find his house.
Man cannot recognize his own house which has been turned into a mansion by emperor.
Well man made to believe that he is sick.
Man thinks that he has diabetes.
Rascals have sewed his trouser leg till it is too tight.
Numskull convinced that he is a thief.
An article is stolen. Declared that whoever does not eat all his cheese is the thief. A stone is put in the numskull’s cheese so that he cannot eat it all. He admits the theft.
Man made to believe that he is pregnant (has borne child).
Parson made to believe that he will bear a calf.
In having his urine examined by a doctor, a cow’s is substituted by mistake. (Or he dreams that he has borne a calf.) When a calf comes into the house he thinks that he has borne it.
Man thinks he has given birth to a child by letting wind.
Husband makes wife and mother-in-law believe he will bear a sheep.
His wife was pregnant when he married her.
Drunken man made to believe that he has been to heaven and hell.
He is dressed up as a rich lord and given rich food and drink. When put back into his own clothes he thinks that he has been to heaven.
Numskull believes that he is married to a man.
Two men’s hands joined in fun with words “I marry you.” Fool thinks that he must get a bishop to annul the marriage.
Wife persuades her husband to have a good tooth pulled.
Husband made to believe that yarn has changed to tow through his carelessness.
Thus his lazy wife is relieved from spinning.
Fool believes gold in bag turns to ashes because of child’s urinating on it.
A student tells a woman that he comes from Paris. She understands him to say from paradise and gives him money and goods to take to her husband.
Foolish woman gives swindler money for her parents in heaven.
Dream explained as a dead father’s demand for horses.
Emperor wants to travel to paradise.
Alleged messenger from relatives in distress given goods to deliver.
Man who asks for good weather given a box full of hornets.
He thinks that it is filled with the weather.
Numskull with unimportant office boasts of it.
Proud sheriff has only nine farmers in his jurisdiction.
Fool appointed to fictitious office boasts of it.
Fool locked in dark room made to believe that it is continuous night.
The sledges turned in the direction of the journey.
At night turned around by a joker.
Master persuaded to buy big fish since small ones creep out of all parts of his body.
Hunters shoot a stag and hide it. Another who sees puts a dead ass in the bag instead.
Jewess makes parents believe that she is to give birth to the Messiah.
Dupe persuaded that he is invisible.
Adulteress makes husband believe that the birth of her mulatto child has been due to suggestion.
Near-sighted man persuaded by doctor that he can see.
Husband refuses to believe in wife’s infidelity.
Husband refuses to believe that his wife is unfaithful, even when she is caught in the act.
Husband away three years accepts children born in his absence as his own.
Woman gives birth to child fourteen months after husband’s departure.
The latter is made to believe it is legitimate.
Woman tells husband that she has become pregnant during his absence according to his own instructions.
She knows best: woman denies accusation of adultery.
Husband dismisses the truthful accusers saying that she knows her shortcomings better than anyone else, and she denies it.
Rascal tests it and finds it lacking.
Only husband remains ignorant about his wife’s infidelity.
Dreams he is being kissed by fairy. Is really a pig.
An apprentice, or newcomer or ignorant person, etc., is sent for absurd or misleading or nonexistent object or on a ridiculous quest.
Dupe is persuaded that money will grow if he buries it.
Dupe is made to believe horse will fly.
Wife makes husband believe that her paramour is Death.
Credulous king reads about ocean of milk and its properties.
The woman who asked for news from home.
Gets many impossible answers, which she believes. E.g., “The cock has become sexton.”
Animal betrays himself to his enemies by talking.
Fox holds conversation with his members, attracts attention, and is caught.
He scolds in turn his feet, eyes, ears, and tail. In his excitement he sticks out his tail from his hiding place.
Hidden wolf gives himself away by talking.
Wolf (bear) boasts of having eaten horses.
When the horse strikes sparks with his hoofs the lion is frightened and picks up the boastful wolf to show him the horse. He squeezes the wolf to death.
When his faults are pointed out he maintains that he is better than his companion, who is immediately investigated.
One brother receives the sacrament; the other is refused it because he cannot pray. He replies that his brother cannot pray either and thus deprives him also of the sacrament.

To prove that a woman cannot keep a secret the man tells his wife that a crow has flown out of his belly (or that he has laid an egg). She tells her neighbor that two crows have flown. Soon he hears from his neighbors that there were fifty crows.
Foolish boasts get man into trouble.

Man boasts to boss that his brother can do twice the work he does. The boss hires him. The two brothers tell him their father can do as much work in a day as the boys can do in a week. The boss fires them, tells them to send their father to work for him.
Numskull talks about his secret instructions and thus allows himself to be cheated.
Told not to serve a man with a red beard or to keep sausage for the long winter, etc.
Fool loses magic objects by talking about them.
Boy talks about his secret instructions and brings his father’s theft to light.
He is to avoid his companions lest they smell what he has been eating.
Fool’s talking causes himself and companions to be robbed.
Tortoise speaks and loses his hold on the stick.
He is being carried through the air by a bird.
Young heir too frank in celebrating his father’s death.
He says to the mourners, “When your fathers die, I too will come and lament their departure.” They brand him as a fool.
He gives them twice-threshed straw to eat as punishment.
Numskull amuses with his discursive nonsense.
Incognito mistress breaks off relations when she overhears the lover discussing the adventure.
Fool discloses woman’s adultery; lover kills him.
Wishes his enemies to know that he is not afraid. Enemies go there before him.
Fool points out hiding place to evil spirits.
Children ask parents too difficult questions.
Scientific query: why does not the sea get larger when it rains in it and nothing flows out?
Scientific query: why does the sea stink when it is full of salt?
Scientific query: why don’t rats stick their eyes out in the straw?
Scientific query: why don’t the poor, being in the majority, kill off the rich?
The judge wants to know how the theft was committed.

Just lain down to sleep, a man is awakened by a neighbor announcing that his she-ass has borne a young one without ears or tail. The man lies awake all night wondering how the ass will keep the harness on.
How the first man killed himself.
The second fool imitates the first who leaps from a palm tree by means of a looped rope. The first kills himself.
Curiosity satisfied: riding the ox’s horns.
As his ox, who has enormous horns, is asleep, the fool gets on the horns. The ox wakes and throws him off.
Testing the evidence by experiment: biting the ear off.
The accused pleads that the plaintiff bit his own ear off. The judge takes time for consideration, tries to bite his own ear, but falls down and breaks his head.

A master sets his servant to keep watch over his horse at night. He soon asks the servant if he is asleep. “No, I was thinking of who created so many stars in the sky.” The second time the servant answers, “No, I was thinking of who dug the sea.
A man curious as to what a robber is going to do waits to intervene and goes back to sleep.
Question: did the man ever have a head?
How did the cow get on the pole?
A fool hides his purse on a pole on a cliff. A rascal substitutes cow-dung for the money. The fool is interested only in how the cow could have reached the purse.
Fool experiments with shut eyes and gets lost.
Which has greatest attraction to earth, cup or contents? Father shows great attraction of fool’s back and a stick.
Foolish imitation of sham death and return (= resuscitation).
Unsuccessful imitation of a god: lions fall out of the furnace instead of men covered with gold and silver.
Christ takes off a horse’s foot to shoe it and then successfully replaces it.
Unsuccessful imitation of magic production of food.
Alleged return from land of dead with bags of gold persuades dupe to try to imitate.
Imitation of jumping into fire without injury: dupe burned up.
Sister of goddess tries to imitate her feat of being cooked without harm and dies in the attempt.
Imitation of magic production of garden and lake unsuccessful.
Obedient woman’s pestle remains magically suspended in air.
A friend has cured his foot with this remedy.
Pulling out the eye so that the pain will cease.
He has had a tooth pulled and the pain ceased.
A peasant envying a doctor’s fee for giving him a plaster and predicting a son, poses as a doctor. He predicts a son for a eunuch and gives a plaster for heart disease.
Imitation of diagnosis by observation: ass’s flesh.

A doctor tells his patient that he has eaten too much chicken, and this the patient confesses. The doctor’s son wants to know how the diagnosis was made. The doctor says that as he rode up he observed chicken feathers and made his conclusions.
Imitation of diagnosis by observation: stick under table.

A man whose wife refuses to talk remembers that a priest drank black cherry juice whenever he lost his voice. He cannot get the cordial but concluding that a limb of the cherry tree will have the same effect beats his wife with is.
Sick woman hung in well to cool off: drowned.
Foolish physician cauterizes “sick” cartwheel to stop it from creaking; burns it up instead.
Fool claims to cure goitre by striking.
Has seen melon thus dislodged from camel’s throat.
Tries to go beyond his powers.
Ass tries to caress his master like the dog.
Ass imitating dog brays so as to wake master when thieves are robbing him.
Ass tries to jump on the roof like the ape.
Daw tries to carry off lamb like eagle.
Is caught in the lamb’s fleece.
Thinks he is imitating another animal.
Fowl makes another animal believe that he has had his leg cut off.
Says that he has received large pay. He has his leg hidden under his wing. The elephant (hippopotamus) cuts his off and bleeds to death.
Fowl makes another animal believe that he has had his neck cut off.
He has his neck hidden under his wing. The hare cuts his off and dies.
Monkey cuts his throat, thinking that he is imitating the cobbler.
Monkey sneezes in king’s presence like rabbit.
Crane tries to catch fish like hawk.
Jackal tries to roar like lion at elephant.
Raven tries to imitate dove’s step but breaks his bones.
Because one man has had good luck a numskull imitates and thinks he will have equal luck.
The two presents to the king: the beet and the horse.

A farmer takes an extraordinary beet as present to the king and receives a large reward. His companion is eager for a reward and leads a handsome steed to the palace. The king rewards him with the beet.

Ruler rewards the gift of a clever donkey. Greedy nobleman seeking a like reward sends ruler two donkeys in rich trappings. Ruler advises the donor that he is sorry that his gift will deprive him of worthy companionship.
The two presents to the king: two poems.
A famous poet presented to the king some poems and was richly rewarded. Another poet likewise gave the king some poetry. The king gave him the first poet’s verses.
Picking the louse and the flea.
One man rewarded with forty crowns for picking louse from king’s robe. Imitator given forty lashes for picking flea.
Crab tries to imitate bird who lays egg in pot of boiling water.
Falls in instead of being rewarded.
Fairies help forgotten child, but strangle child trying to imitate good luck.
Brahmin goes to heaven, ascetic to hell.
Pig sees goat return decked with ornaments and plenty of food; goes out and imitates trick played by goat but is beaten instead.
A snake for the real daughter.
Stepdaughter, married to a snake, appears decorated with jewels. Stepmother desires a snake be procured for her daughter. She is swallowed instead.
When his foot is caught in a wheel, they keep repeating his call for help as a song.
He slips and all fall to floor.
The fool spits in the hot porridge.
He has seen the smith spit on the hot iron.
The scythe cuts one man’s head off.

A trickster sees a man throwing his eyes into the air and replacing them. He also receives this power but he must not use the power beyond a specified number of times. When he does so, he loses his eyes. He usually gets animal eyes as substitutes.

A trickster sees a man with a sharpened leg. He also receives the power of sharpening his leg without harm if he will use it but four times. He breaks the tabu and is left with his leg sticking in a tree.

A trickster (animal) visits various animals who display their peculiar powers in obtaining food (often magic). He returns the invitation and tries to provide food in similar ways. He fails and usually has a narrow escape from death.
Numskull wants to be shaved too.
He sees another man being shaved and thinks that the man is having his ears cut off. He orders his wife to cut off his ears.
Numskull praises his daughter as being pregnant.
He tries in vain to sell his cow and succeeds only when he says that she is with calf. When suitors come wooing his daughter, he tries the same plan disastrously.
Numskull puts money into the exchange so as to participate in the business.
He hears that great lords take a part in the business of the exchange where he sees great heaps of money.
A man undertakes to do his wife’s work.
Men exchange duties: each wants to get better of the other, but is cheated, finding the other’s work more difficult.
Man saved from well by rope.
Disastrous attempt to save him from tree in same way.
Man has had stork protect him from rain by covering him with his wing. Man tries to protect his wife from rain with his arm.
The mother teaches the boy (the man his wife) what he should say (do) in this or that circumstance. He uses the words in the most impossible cases and is always punished.
Literal following of instructions about actions.
Literal numskull drags jar (bacon) on string.
He has sent a pig home alone. Told that he should have led it by a string.
Literal numskull is gay at a fire.
He has wept at a wedding and been told to be gay.
Literal numskull sings entertaining songs on approach of death.
Literal numskull throws water on roasting pig.
Told that he should have thrown water in the fire when the house burnt.
Literal numskull cuts peas into four parts.
Told that he should have cut up the pancakes which he has eaten whole.
Literal fool is told to cook a few peas for five persons.
Cooks five peas. Next time he is told to cook an abundance.
Literal fool puts three empty measures in pot.
Told to put in three measures of rice to boil.
On last trip he has lost the gloves and has been told that he should have put them in his bosom. He puts the hawk inside his shirt.
Literal fool carries the harrow in his hand.
He has killed a sparrow by his stupidity and has been told that he should have carried it in his hand.
Numskull told to steal something heavy brings millstone.
Numskull as thief: tries to carry off grinding-stone when told by confederates to bring out heavy things.
Told to bring shiny things; brings out looking glass.
Literal numskull destroys inherited property since his sister has instructions not to object to his actions.
Literal following of instructions about greetings.
Numskull gives wrong greeting and is told how to give the correct one. When he tries it, however, the conditions are wrong.
Told that he should have kissed the old woman.
Fool learns to repeat commonplace expressions: by chance thus scares off wife’s suitors.
Literal numskull laughs at his child’s death.
Master tells servant (sarcastically) to take a year to do errand.
Servant stays away a year and then returns to claim salary.
Numskull told not to forget to get the handsel (a little token extra in the bargain); brings it but leaves what he has been sent to buy.
Literal fool: fool told to follow his nose in a journey, runs head against tree, climbs it.
To sell some cloth for four rupees.
Fool refuses to take six rupees for it.
Asking favor when master is in good humor.
Fool waits till master is laughing at servant’s stupidity.
Numskull told to attract girl’s attention by throwing pebble at her flings large stone which breaks her head.
The dog Parsley in the soup.
The foolish bridegroom is told to put parsley in the soup. He throws in his dog, which is named Parsley.
Casting sheep’s eyes at the bride.
The foolish bridegroom is told to cast sheep’s eyes at the bride. He buys some at the butcher shop and throws them at her.
Foolish husband puts out wife’s eyes at night because he heard that a beautiful wife is an enemy.
While her parents are away from home, a matchmaker and a suitor come to the foolish girl. By following her mother’s advice literally, she gives away her dower to the tricksters.
The servant to improve on the master’s statements.
The wooer makes boasts to the girl and the servant always doubles the master’s boast. Finally the master says, “I have poor eyesight.”
The wife throws the meal into the well and the pigs after it.
Watering the cow (by pouring water on it).
The woman breaks the pots into fragments and piles them up.
Fool feeds it steaming food and kills it.
Numskulls, told to shove the boy along if he is lazy about weeding, do so with their weeding-knives and kill him.
Fool uses boiling water and kills it.
Heating water for woman to wash in.
Fool throws out all the furniture.
Oh bother! put it on my head! Numskulls asking old woman where to put grain obey and smother her.
Literal fool told to cut at plow if it sticks on roots cuts at bullock’s legs.
Fool takes threat to child as an order.
Told to plow above a certain tree (on the hillside), numskulls haul oxen and plow into tree and destroy them.
Fool plows them out of ground.
A man cannot remember the number of his sins. The priest has him put a pebble in a sack for each of his sins. He comes to confession with three large sacks of pebbles.
A man counts the days of the fastmonth by throwing a pebble each day into a pot. His daughter throws a handful of pebbles in.
You said you wished a lentil soup; so I put one in. If you had wished more lentils you should have said so.
The fool eats the paper with the prescription on it.
So advised, they cut their beds, houses, etc. in two.
Boy asked to do something to cool women’s ears breaks vessels they carry so milk in them can cool their ears off.
Literal fool—something you have never experienced.
Literal fool feeds dogflesh to visitor to follow father’s advice: “Feed him on food you have never eaten in your life.”
Literal obedience: soldier breaks woman’s oil pot in two with sword when she asks him to show her something she never has seen in life.
“Taking a pattern (picture) of conduct” from other people.
Fool steals a picture from the church.
A master tells his servant that he is going to skin some farmers (i.e., cheat them). When a farmer inquires for a tanner, the servant directs him to his master.

He tells his wife about the good things he gets to eat at the rich man’s house. The wife says, “Open your mouth for me once so that I may get some too.” The peasant gets up after the next large meal and opens his mouth to the astonishment of all present.
A count instructs his chaplain to read a hunter’s mass (i.e., a short one). The chaplain searches the prayerbook in vain for a hunter’s mass.
The woman puts butter on his hands.
The literal host: bread and salt.

Guest finds that his host spoke literally when he invited him to share his bread and salt. Later, when the host threatens an importunate beggar, the guest advises the beggar to flee since the host means what he says.
The numskull buys water at market.
The horse that went like a ship.
Men have been assured that a horse will “go like a ship”. When they spur the horse, it will not move. A man takes a pole and hits the horse. It goes. “See, it goes like a ship.
The fool is told that his son has given up the ghost.
The house without food or drink.
Father tells son that he has been scratched by “hairy rascals” (monkeys).
Woman tells husband she has cooked what is behind him. He sees the door there and tries to cook it.
Numskull wants to see an abstract quality.
Numskull dragon wants to see courage.
Sultan tries to prove to Adversity he cannot be seized at specified time and hides in a sewer.
He thus experiences adversity in his very effort to avoid it.
Fool interprets metaphors (or slang expressions) about drink.
“Keep locks of everyone in your hand” (keep control of them).
“Cutting the paper of the accounts” (falsifying accounts).
Giving half of savings away: “Whoever gives charity gets double in return.”
Fool covers his mistress with straw and suffocates her. Should have thatched roof.
Foolish son seizes an ass by tail and gets kicked.
“Don’t allow paint to wear off my daughter’s feet.”
Bridegroom carries her upside down across river and drowns her.
“Rupees make more rupees.” Stupid peasant sticks his sole rupee in hole and loses it.
Jester soon appears with large pot over head.
The master is to clothe the servant (at his expense). The servant insists that his master shall put on his clothes for him.
A plaintiff insists that the judge shall put some fear into the defendant debtor. The judge puts his fingers over the eyes of the defendant and cries, “Boo!
The names are “The Shepherd” and “Get the stick”. When the man calls his dogs to dinner, the thief thinks that he is telling the shepherd to get a stick.
Getting a box on the ears.
The man, advised to cure his wife with a box on the ears, goes to the pharmacy and gets one. He cures his wife.
Religious words or exercises interpreted with absurd literalness.
One man prays to the Virgin of Aix-la-Chapelle.
Did not want to be Christ.
An actor representing Christ in a Passion Play is beaten by Jews.
An artist, ordered to make a crucifix, asks peasants if they want a living God.
Numskulls believing that God has reposed on a leaf want to cross river on one.
“I don’t know” thought to be a person’s name.
A man in a country that cannot speak his language hears “I don’t know” so frequently that he thinks it must be the name of the owner of all the places he inquires about.
Boy who worked for “nothing at all” goes to town and demands “nothing at all.”
Misunderstandings because of lack of knowledge of a different language than one’s own.
A wayward son, asked by his mother to give her a sweet word, thus answers.
Fool told to repeat part of the ceremony at baptism persists absurdly in repeating every remark.

Minister tells congregation that he has forgotten his spectacles, that he cannot line out the hymn as he customarily did. The choir sings his words. He tries to explain, apologizes. The choir repeats the apology in song.
Man sent to priest for religious service to repeat priest’s words.
A mother orders her daughter to knead the dough until the front of the oven (stirn) sweats. She does so till her forehead (stirn) sweats.
Not naked but with a hood on.
She confesses that she has had relations with the priest.
Fool admits crime but pleads mistakes in the details of the accusation.
Brings back all stolen cattle possible.
Simple monk eats all he can of abbey’s stolen cattle so as to bring them back home.
Fool therefore trusts that he is in angry elephant.
Conventional greeting phrase taken literally: “Come and share it.”
Three stupid sons sent out into the world to learn trades: hunter kills his father; musician plays and dances at his father’s death, etc.
A man and his wife make a wager as to who shall speak first (close the door). The man (woman) becomes jealous and scolds; loses the wager.
Wager as to who shall rise (speak) first in morning (last up to get reward).
They are carried to funeral pyre before they will give in.
Husband to spite wife plays dead.
When she tells neighbors that they may come and take dead man’s property he gets up.
Silence wager: man and wife taken for dead.
Stand up when king offers reward for information about their death.
The fool and the visitor’s large nose.
The fool asks where he got the large nose. Is removed from the room. He comes back to mend matters. He says, “What a small nose you have!” He is again taken from the room.
A fool hearing of the effectiveness of holy water for the forgiveness of sins pours the whole supply over himself.
Sickle bought at great cost given back.
In a land where the sickle is not known the new sickle cuts off the head of a man and is thereupon given back to the original owner.
Directions followed literally to the sorrow of the giver.
The youth obeys literally the precept even when he sees the master’s coat on fire.
The youth so instructed picks up too much. The master then tells him to pick things up only when the master gives the signal. The master falls into a hole and cannot give the signal.
Fool loads his master with horse dung.
“Do nothing but attend to the horse.”
The youth obeys the command to such extent that he almost lets his master drown.
She is to follow instructions which the husband has written down on a card. He falls into a brook and is about to drown.
Pupils are taught to clap their hands and say “God bless you” when one sneezes. As they are rescuing a drowning man by a rope he sneezes. They all clap their hands and he falls back into the water.
Command to use only one phrase.
Fool allows the house to burn down.
To tell nothing else than “very good news.”
The youth obeys the command to such an absurd extent that he is a nuisance to his master.

Officer calls to householders to hang out lanterns. One hangs out lantern but does not light it. The next night the officer calls to them to hang out lanterns and candles. He hangs out a lantern with a candle in it but unlighted. The next night the officer calls out to hang out lanterns and candlelight.
When lizard comes in fool burns house down to drive it out.
Sleepy servant removes master’s turban while still in council meeting.
To draw out fence stakes and throw them down.
Asked to call a doctor when his master falls ill, fool also calls the undertaker.
Fool kills himself in despair because a sparrow has taken one grain from his field.
Fool kills himself in despair because an ox has been killed.
The man is accused of maintaining a brothel.
He has a bull for breeding purposes.
Rebuke for going with a naked head in public.
The woman rebuked has lost her hair in sickness. Forthwith she covers up her head with her dress and exposes her body.
Girl marries man so she will not be ashamed undressed in his presence.
Breaking the glassware to prevent others from doing so.
A king thus removes temptation from his subjects.
The obedient husband: the leave of absence.
His wife says, “You may go away for a little while.” He stays away for days and then sends a messenger to his wife asking if he has been away long enough.
Wife had wished only to test her husband’s love for her.
Arrives home after dawn when wife’s lover has gone.
Fool liking salt decides to eat nothing else.
Fool will not drink from a river because he cannot drink it all.
Wishing to prove their equality twelve fools sleep on the ground and put their feet on the one bed provided for the chief.
Thief out of habit robs from his own purse.
Fool believes letter apparently reporting his uncle’s death, though he has just seen uncle.
Bureaucrats debate as to who shall put out palace fire: meantime palace burns.
Fool starves himself at table. Later hunts food in house and gets into trouble.
Fool thanks God that he was not sitting on the ass when it was stolen.
Thankful that the recipe is left.
A hawk steals the fool’s meat. He is grateful that the recipe remains.
A man plans to take peaches as a present to the king. He is persuaded rather to take figs. They are green and the king has them thrown in his face. He is thankful that they weren’t peaches.
“Thank God that camels have no wings.”
They might fly about and kill people.
Fool thankful that God has built a palace without columns.
Else the stones might fall down and kill us.
A man carries blind men over a stream at a certain price per head. One falls down and drowns. He comforts the others that there is one fewer to pay for.
Man who has been promised a beating lives in constant dread. Is eventually beaten.
Philosopher loses all his wealth at sea. Thanks Fortune for taking him out of business. Can now devote his life to philosophy.
Man contends that melons should not grow on slender vines but on tall trees. He is hit on the nose by a falling nut. Is thankful it wasn’t a melon.
Heart may not be able to stand winning mistress.
Man told it is well he did not obtain girl he loved because his heart might not have been able to stand it.
Person frightened into falling down a cliff.
Seven men make strenuous plans for the attack on the fierce animal. One screams with fright and the animal runs away.
Fools frightened by stirring of an animal.
Fools are frightened at the humming of bees.
Fools frightened at the flight of a quail.
When they hear “whirr!” the army flees.
Lions flee because of the crowing of white cock, elephants because of swine’s grunting.
Fright at the creaking of a wheelbarrow.
The hawk frightened at the snipe’s bill.
A man awakes with his knees in the air. He thinks the knees are a lion and splits them with his axe.
The sleeper answers for the dead man.

A man falls asleep by a gallows. A company of wags come and invite the dead man on the gallows to accompany them. The sleeper awakes with a start and says, “I’ll come at once.” The wags flee in terror.
The dead girl frightens father and lover.

The girl dies. The lover, thinking that she is asleep, talks to her. When he hears the father speak of her as dead he is frightened that he has talked to the dead. The father hears the lover talk and thinks that it is the girl’s spirit.
Fool frightened by stirring of the wind.
Falls on a knife and kills himself.
Tailor puts on thimble as protection from slug.
Fright at animals’ eyes in the dark.
Coward is frightened when clothing catches on thistle.
Coward boasts of what he would have done after danger is over.
Boastful coward frightened when he sees strong adversaries.
Hides in trousers of plowman who fights the men.
Fools try to frighten one another, but get scared themselves and both flee.
Tiger frightened of leak in house.
Fool worries lest earthquake make him fall against an open knife.
Bungling fool has succession of accidents.
The fool accidentally kills his child and loses the body.
Accidentally strikes the dog dead, drowns the midwife, and kills the child.
One woman to catch squirrel; the other to get the cooking pot.
One falls from the tree and kills herself; the other breaks the pot.
Foolishly kills his horse and throws his axe into the lake to kill a duck. Undresses to recover axe.
Sent back for the rest of the money.
A fool finds a treasure and takes some of it to a judge so as to purchase influence. The judge sends him back for the rest.
The cup with two and three handles.
When the servant girl presents the cup to the emperor she holds the handle herself. When there are two handles she holds one in each hand, and when there are three she holds the third one toward her.
Servant injures master while shampooing him.
Gives him a slap and breaks his skin.
“I am as good as you are.”
The fool testifies: “I had been drinking and was lying on the bench asleep.
They escape but he is captured and stupidly betrays their hiding places.

A servant is sent by his master to find a girl for him. If he returns with one he is to say, “I have a fox”; if without, “I have a hare.” When he returns he has forgotten the agreement. “I don’t know whether it is a fox or a hare, but the girl is down stairs.
Fool keeps repeating his instructions so as to remember them.
Fool’s talking to himself thought to be inappropriate greetings.
He keeps repeating a word to remember it but changes it so that it seems to refer unfavorably to people whom he meets.
Bungling fool forgets what elephant is called.
Says it is an “earth egg” (confused with name for potatoes).
A man hears a noise outside the house at night. He wraps a bed cover about him and goes to investigate. The robbers take the bed cover and flee. The wife asks what the debate was about.
He tries to rescue woman caught by crab. Is caught himself and found in embarrassing position.
Buyer draws picture of grindstone on his order list.
The grocer sends him a cheese. The buyer has forgotten to draw the hole.
“What do I hold in my hand?”
Guess what I have in my hand and I will give it to you to make egg-cake with.
What does it look like? What outside and yellow inside. It is a hollowed turnip filled with carrots.
Guess how many eggs I have and you shall get all seven.
How to find if it is raining.
Men must go to look in the pool to see if rain is falling.
Man put out tubs to see if rain is still falling.

One fool docks the tail of his horse; the horse of the second gets tail caught in gate, is docked too. One notches ear of his horse; the second horse notches its ear on the fence. Finally they measure heights of their horses. The black horse is two inches taller than the white.
Trickster’s greed while hunting causes him to be deserted.
Magic animal wins contest for man.
Magic bullock wins fight for master.
Fortune to go to direction cat jumps.
King will give wealth to person toward whom the cat jumps. Clever woman has brought mouse along and thus entices the cat.
Young knight substitutes for old man in tournament.
Supernatural substitute in tournament for pious warrior.
Woman substitutes for husband in combat.
Wise man disguised as monk beats learned heretic in debate.
Contest with magician won by deception.
Race won by deception: relative helpers.
One of the contestants places his relatives (or others that resemble him) in the line of the race. The opponent always thinks the trickster is just ahead of him.
Race won by deception: riding on the back.
One contestant rides on the other’s back.
Hare and tortoise race: sleeping hare.
In a race between the fast and the slow animal, the fast animal sleeps on the road and allows the slow animal to pass him.
Race won by deception: chariot disabled.
A rival in a chariot race inserts linchpins of wax instead of those of bronze in the hero’s chariot. The latter is dragged to death.
Race won by deception: sham-sick trickster.
The trickster feigns lameness and receives a handicap in the race. He then returns and eats up the food which is the prize.
Race won by deception: rabbit as “little son” substitute.
A man challenged by an ogre to a running race persuades the ogre to race with his little son instead. By this he means a rabbit.
Race won by deception: blinding opponent by spitting pepper into face.
Race won by deception: bow and arrow.
Certain goal to be touched. Man shoots arrow and wins.
Obstacle race between deer and hare.
Hare accused of removing obstacles from his course.
Wrestling match won by deception: where to throw the ogre.
The ogre squeezes the man so that his eyes bulge out.
Wrestling match won by deception: bear as “grandfather.”
A man challenged by an ogre persuades the latter to wrestle with his old grandfather instead. By this he means a bear.
Giant invincible in wrestling because with each contact with earth his strength is renewed.
Wrestling match of man with fever.
Man places stone image at wrestling-place; fever enters image and shatters it.
Deer defeated but always pleads illness.
All comers are challenged and all are killed until the hero defeats the challenger.
The boat is already sawed through.
Rowing contest won by deception: magic boat.
Climbing match won by deception: squirrel as “child”.
The ogre agrees to contest against the man’s young one, i.e., a squirrel.
Diving match won by deception: breathing under brush.
Trickster comes up and breathes under some floating brush, where he is not detected.
Diving match: trickster eats food while dupe is under water.
A hole is already dug and covered with boughs.
Contest: who can go deepest into the earth?
Contest in jumping from the church tower.
The devil is not to look behind him. The man runs downstairs (or otherwise cheats).
Contest in jumping into a trap.
He is trying to warn the people beyond the sea with his cry. The ogre is intimidated.
Throwing contest: trickster addresses Angel Gabriel.
Throwing contest: trickster addresses Angel Gabriel or St. Peter, warns him to get out of way of missile trickster is about to throw.
Throwing contest: golden club on the cloud.
Trickster shows the ogre the club he has thrown. (Really only a bright spot on the cloud.) (Cf.
Throwing contest: bird substituted for stone.
The ogre throws a stone; the hero a bird which flies out of sight.
Small animal challenges two large animals to a tug-of-war. Arranges it so that they unwittingly pull against each other (or one end of rope is tied to a tree).
Flying contest won by deception: riding on the other.
One animal chooses cotton; the other, seeing that a rain is coming, chooses salt and wins.
Tournament won by deception on borrowed horse.
The man sends his wife on all fours in tar and feathers. The ogre has never heard of such a bird.
Shooting test won by deception: proof of good sight.
A man puts a dead hare under a tree and shows it to his dog. He tells people to look at the hare under the tree.
Shooting contest won by deception: bird substituted for arrows.
Plowing contest won by deception: hare exchanged for horse.

God and the devil contest in plowing. The devil plows with a horse, God with a hare. While the devil is asleep, God takes the devil’s horse and plows the field. When he wakes, the devil thinks the hare has plowed so much and gladly trades his horse for the hare.
Pig plows while dog sleeps. Then dog runs back and forth in furrow to claim victory.
The man calls out, “The wolves are coming!” The ogre is intimidated.
The man takes the center of the field. The ogre is given a dull sickle and mows around the outside of the field.
God mows with a chisel, the devil with a scythe. God deceives devil into changing scythe for chisel.
Deceptive contest in chopping: iron in bamboo.
Hero challenged to cut down bundles of bamboo suspended in air but a strip of iron is treacherously inserted in each.
Sewing contest won by deception: the long thread.
The ogre sews with the whole length of the thread. When he returns from the first stitch, the tailor has his task finished.
Contest in bridge-building won by deception.
Waking contest won by giving opponent soporific.
Contest in seeing sunrise first: sun on the trees.
The fox places himself on a hill facing the east; the hog in a lower place facing the high trees to the west. The sun shines on the top of the trees, and the hog wins.
Contest in seeing sunrise first: sleeper wins.
One keeps awake, the other sleeps. The first thinks that he sees the sun and cries out prematurely, thus waking the other, who wins.
Contest in pushing hole in tree: hole prepared beforehand.
Hero and ogre to vie in pushing a hole in a tree with their heads.
Contest in squeezing water from a stone.
The ogre squeezes a stone; the trickster a cheese or egg.
The ogre bites a stone; the man a nut.
Contest: pulling on steak with teeth.

Two men take an end of a steak in their teeth; each attempts to pull it away from the other. After each has a good hold, the Irishman says (with clenched teeth) “Noo’re ready?” The Dutchman says, “Yah!”, loses the steak.
Contest with magician in bringing grain out of closed bamboo: trickster brings culm-borers to make holes.
Contest in strength won by deception.
Deceptive contest in carrying a tree: riding.
The trickster has the dupe carry the branches of a tree while he carries the trunk. He rides on the trunk.
Deceptive contest in carrying a horse.
The ogre carries it on his back and soon tires; the man carries it between his legs (rides).
The man has an iron glove on.
The man has an iron finger.
Contests in other physical accomplishments won by deception.
Deceptive eating contest: hole in bag.
The hero slips his food into a bag and makes the ogre believe that he is the greater eater. (In many versions the hero cuts open the bag; the ogre imitates and kills himself.) (Cf.
Trickster wins with the aid of substitutes.
Hero can produce unlimited food which opponents must eat.
Food secretly furnished one, but plan detected and foiled.
Deceptive drinking contest: hole for water.
The trickster lets the water run out through a hole; the dupe drinks himself to death.
Deceptive drinking contest: rising and falling tide.
Buffalo and heron wager as to which can drink the sea until the water falls. The buffalo drinks as the tide is coming in; the heron drinks in the falling tide and wins.
Attempted intoxication avoided by boring a hole in the bottom of cup.
The man drinks water, the devil is given vinegar.
One bullock keeps mouth in water. Other drinks self to death.
Scratching contest: man’s wife shows wounds.

The man sends his wife to meet the ogre with whom he is to have a scratching contest. She tells the ogre that her husband has gone to have his nails sharpened. She shows him deep wounds that her husband has scratched on her body (obscene). The ogre leaves in terror.
Scratching contest with devil: man’s wife shows scratches in her oak table.
Contest in scratching skin off each other: covering self with several ox-hides.
The ogre tries to laugh as long as the dead horse with a grinning mouth. Laughs till he dies.
Gambling contest: coin which attracts fly first to win.
Winning coin had been rubbed on a pear.
Girl distracts opponent’s attention so that gambling lover wins.
Three daughters are to wet hands; the first to have hands dry is to be the first to marry. The youngest waves her hands, exclaiming, “I don’t want a man!” She wins.
Boar in duel with tiger cakes mud on body: defeats tiger.
Combat won by means of substituted weapons.
Beauty contest won by deception: other contestants covered with leaves.
Pseudo-magic formula for making gold sold to king.
Gold required for its manufacture carried off by manufacturer.
It needs only the addition of a few vegetables and a bit of meat.
It already has the ingredients in it.
Dupe kills his wife (mother) and is unable to resuscitate her.
Seven devils’ wives imitate ritual of death and resuscitation done over hero; not having the real water of life and death, the seven enemy devils are killed.
The dupe takes it. “It is dog’s dung,” he says and spits it out. The trickster says that he is telling the truth and demands pay.
Sale of alleged oracular bamboo cup.
Woman sold a letter to wear around her neck which will prevent eye trouble. It helps only so long as she believes in it.
Alleged healing letter (charm) sold: to aid in childbirth.
Pseudo-magic letter is found to contain insulting remarks.
Pseudo-magic charm (letter): to ward off plague.
Pseudo-magic letter (charm): to aid in engendering offspring.
A sailor boy sells a seasick Jew “Babylon stones” as a cure. They are pieces of coal.
Betrayal through pretended fountain of youth.
Sale of tree with alleged magic fruit.
Sale of tree alleged to produce clothes.
Fishing-rod alleged to take fish to fisherman’s home.
Pseudo-magic acorns: to protect holder’s pigs.
Sale of gilded (plated) ware as gold or silver.
Trickster, as watchman, exchanges worthless bag for bag of gold at night.
Alleged to be a swift deliverer of letters.
Alleged speaking hare sold as messenger.
Horse which will not go over trees.

Salesman tells buyer that he is selling the horse because it eats too much and will not climb trees. On the way home the horse bites everyone and refuses to cross a bridge. Seller is literally correct.
The horse swifter than the rain.

Caught in the rain, a trickster finds that his horse will not budge. He undresses, puts his clothes under the horse’s belly and keeps them dry. When he reaches the king, he reports that his horse has run so fast that he has had no time to get wet. The king buys the horse.
Trickster grooms master’s old mule and then sells him back without detection at huge profit.
Trickster in disguise regains possession of his own horse by trading with man whom he has duped once before.
He gives a description that is literally correct.
Selling or trading a balky horse.
Trickster temporarily lames valuable horse and buys him for trifle.
Said to swallow up the cold so that if he is near, one may sleep comfortably in the cold.
Dog alleged to chase hare and bring it to hunter’s home.
Sale of dog supposed to excrete sweet dung: dupe deceived.
Sale of dead buffalo by making him seem alive.
Two jars full of live black wasps sold as interpreters of foreign language.
Parrot knowing only two words sold as speaking foreign language.
Animals made by magic exchanged for real ones.
Deceptive exchange: useless for magic object.
Sale of a sausage filled with blood.
Sale of worthless glass as diamond.
Pot of cow dung covered with cheese sold as cheese.
Exchange of alleged ghee (liquid butter) for goat (cow).
Pus from sore sold as ghee.
Earthen pot with rice water on top of which clarified butter had been poured sold as a pot of clarified butter.
Green plantains sold as matured plants.
Cheaters sell each other valueless articles.
Trick exchange: basket of stones for one of bread; a few pieces of money shown through slit in basket-cover to dupe.
A beggar tells the bishop how to stay warm.
For a gulden he tells him that he should wear all his clothes when he goes horseback in winter.
Thief masked as devil bought off by frightened owner.
Dupe persuaded to pay for learning this dance (really moving toward and away from a fire).
Trickster feigns ability to influence the sun; sells services.
Sun to shine on fools’ backs as they go to town in morning and return in afternoon.
Man collects toll fraudulently, stamps “Brass Gate” on receipts he gives.
People think this is some Government phrase.
Trickster persuades dupe to sacrifice animal and give it to him as payment for supposed services.
Deceptive partnership between man and ogre.
Giant cheated in division of spoils of the chase.
Jackal cheats other animals of elephant they have killed together.
Deceptive crop division: above the ground, below the ground.
Of root crops the ogre (stupid animal) chooses the tops; of other crops the roots.
Deceptive grain division: the corn and the chaff.
The bear chooses the chaff because of its greater bulk. At the mill the fox’s grain makes a different sound from the bear’s.
Deceptive nut and olive division: inside and outside.
The clever man chooses the kernel of the nuts and the outside of the olive.
Deceptive sacrifice of nuts and dates.
Trickster sacrifices only the shells of the nuts and the inside of the dates.
Deceptive division of pigs: curly and straight tails.
All with curly tails belong to the trickster, others to the dupe.
Deceptive division of animals for shearing.
The trickster shears the sheep; the dupe the pig.
In dividing the fish, the dupe gets the bones.
Evil takes lower half of wife, Good takes upper half. Child begotten by Evil not permitted to nurse the top half which belongs to Good.
The common cow and bull: one gets front of cow and back of bull.
Evil chooses lambs, leaving milk to Good. Lambs drink up all milk.
Barber’s and jackal’s common garden: jackal pretends that garden has not yielded any fruit at all.
Monkey cheats fox of his share of bananas.
Climbs on a tree and tosses peelings down upon fox.

The trickster makes a bargain with his master that the first to become angry must submit to punishment. He thereupon heaps abuses on his master till the latter breaks out in anger and must take his punishment.
Anger bargain: may God give you a penny.

A servant and his mistress agree that when they are angry with each other they shall say, “May God give you a penny!” When the master says this, the servant says, “May he give you two!” They keep increasing the amount till those who hear wonder at the performance.
Deceptive bargain: as much bread as he wants to eat.
The baker fixes his price at the rate for twenty loaves. The trickster eats thirty.
Deceptive bargain: a sack of corn as reward.
Trickster has an enormous sack made.
Deceptive bargain: as much grain as will go in a rope.
The ogre is to fulfill three wishes of the peasant. The latter wishes for all the tobacco and brandy in the world and then some more brandy in addition. The devil must admit failure.
Deceptive bargain: first to say “Good morning.”
The first to give the greeting shall have the disputed property. The trickster is early on the scene and witnesses the other’s adultery. He may keep the property without saying good morning.
First to greet the other in morning will lose beauty contest.
Dispute is to be settled thus.
The servant girl eats secretly; the miser starves.

The ogre and the trickster agree to fell a large tree. The trickster purposely dulls his axe on a stone and then asks the ogre to exchange. Rather than work with a dull axe, the ogre does all the work.
Deceptive bargain: a peck of grain for each stack.
The man who is to receive this share of the crop makes very small stacks.
Deceptive bargain: an ox for five pennies.

A woman who has been left the ox on condition that she give the proceeds to the poor offers it for five pennies, but it must be bought along with a cock at twelve florins. She gives the five pennies to the poor and keeps the twelve florins.
Small niche in house brings large price.
House sold reserving niche. This becomes such a nuisance that buyer pays heavily for it.
Deceptive bargain: the ogre and the copper coins.

Every time the copper coin is paid out, the ogre must make a new one. The man buys an extensive property and pays with a large number of copper coins. He threatens to buy another and the ogre goes back on his contract.
As much land bought as can be surrounded by an ox-hide. The hide is cut into very small strips.
Deceptive land purchase: as much land as Vishnu can lie upon (or can step over in three steps).
His worshippers claim for him the whole earth.
Deceptive land purchase: boundary fixed by flight of a goose.
Subject given as much land as a goose can fly over without lighting. The man carries the goose with its wings extended over an enormous territory.
Deceptive land purchase: as much land as a shawl will cover.
Deceptive land purchase: as much land as can be covered by saint’s hood.
Only by snatching up hood does seller prevent it from covering whole territory.
Land grant: as much land as can be covered by saint’s mantle.
Deceptive land purchase: bounds fixed by a race.
Deceptive land purchase: bounds fixed by throwing object (axe, spear).
Deceptive land purchase: as much land as can be surrounded in a certain time.
Land bargain: land surrounded by a horse (cow) in one day.
Land bargain: land ridden around during a sermon.

Deceptive land purchase: king, as reward for help in winning battle, promises wounded chieftain as much land as his chariot can travel around; bribes charioteer to turn back whenever chieftain faints from loss of blood.
Land purchase: as much as can be plowed (fenced) in a certain time.
Deceptive land purchase: fields that crackle when burnt are to be his.
He puts bamboo on the fields before they are burnt so that they crackle.
Deceptive land purchase: as much land as can be shadowed by a tree.
Deceptive land purchase: enough to raise certain plant.
This is a rapidly spreading weed which overruns the country.
Deceptive land purchase: saint’s enemy promised as much land as he can see from certain point.
Saint causes cloud to obstruct vision.
Land grant: as much land as can be seen on a clear day.
Land grant: as much land as can be seen from certain eminence.
Deceptive land bargain: saints agree that the one who casts his staff far enough to reach distant island shall be owner of land.
Staff of one contestant transformed to spear (or dart) and so alone reaches island. When saint touches weapon, it becomes staff again.
Land grant: as far as ox can be heard.
Deceptive bargain with ogre: buying trees.
Trees to be neither straight nor crooked.
The boy promises the soldier what the king has promised to give him. The soldier receives a beating in place of the boy.
A man promises in confession to steal only a small amount. He steals a rope with a mare on the end of it.
As hostages the dogs are handed over to the wolves; the young wolves to the sheep. The wolves then attack and kill the sheep.
The man helps the horse against the stag.
The horse must agree to be saddled and bridled. The man then refuses to release him.
Deceptive bargain based on an unusual name.
This is the name of an estate, which the king unwittingly gives away.
Bargain: if the sun reverses its course.
Because of an eclipse the sun is held to have done so, and Atreus becomes king.
A ribbon long enough to reach from ear to ear.
The rascal has had an ear cut off and this is in a distant city.

Man boasts of hog so big that a man could not reach its back if he holds his hand as high as possible. A stranger buys the hog, sight-unseen. The seller takes him to the hog, shows the buyer that the hog’s back is much below his hand when he holds it as high as possible.
Trickster lends bamboo on condition that it is returned exactly as it is.
Until the log burns out: time given servant for Christmas holidays.
Soaks the log so that it burns a week.
Cheater is forced to eat excrements.

Gentleman agrees to exchange his good horse for the peasant’s jade, provided the peasant will eat its excrements. The peasant finds no difficulty in the task, whereas the gentleman, put to the same condition when he wants to get back his horse, finds it impossible.
Deceptive bargain: as much gold in reward as sticks to poet’s hair when poured over him: he smears it with tar.
Devil cheated of his promised soul.
The man saves it through deceit.
Devil cheated by imposing an impossible task.
Devil is cheated by giving him task: counting the letters in the church Bible.
He is unable to read the holy words.
Man whispers in devil’s ear that his wife is approaching with her broom again.
Devil pounded in knapsack until he releases man.
Devil’s magic power turned on himself.

The hero who is riding the devil as a horse receives supernatural strength from plucking a hair from the devil’s mane. He then spurs the devil until he agrees to forego his bargain for the man’s soul.
The man has promised himself to the devil in return for money. He stuffs his clothes with straw and hangs them up. The devil thinks the man has hanged himself and is satisfied.
Devil to release man for performing seemingly impossible task.
The task is performed by trickery.
The evil woman in the glass case as the last commodity.

The man is to belong to the devil as soon as he has sold his goods. If he has any goods that no one will buy, he is to be free. The man puts an evil old woman in a glass case. When the devil sees her, he recognizes her. “Whoever knows her will refuse to buy her.” The man goes free.
Bringing the devil an unknown animal.
The man sends his naked wife on all fours in tar and feathers. The devil has never seen such an animal.
Guessing name of devil’s secret plant.
The man’s wife in tar and feathers overhears the devil tell the secret name of the crop he has discovered (tobacco).
Not to sleep for three successive nights.
Devil gets another soul instead of one bargained for.
The devil bargains with a man for his soul, but the man fulfills his contract and escapes. In envy two persons commit suicide. The devil rejoices that though he lost one he has gained two.
Devil cheated by religious or magic means.
Devil cheated by having priest draw a sacred circle about the intended victim.
Devil cheated of his victim by boy having a bible under his arm.
Devil cheated when his victim becomes a priest.
Devil cheated of promised soul by intervention of Virgin Mary.
The picture of the Virgin Mary saves the priest.
Penance of priest saves him from devil.
The priest, who sold his soul to the devil, orders his servant to cut him (alive) up into pieces, to crucify him on a tree (and the like), thus saves his soul from the devils.
Devil is unable to take man contracted to him when friends pray over the corpse.
Other ways of cheating the devil of his promised soul.
Devil cheated of his promised soul by making the intended victim drunk.
The devil may punish the drunk man’s body but has no power over his soul.
Devil cheated of his promised soul when the victim sells his to a comrade.
The latter says, “The devil can take only one soul from each person. I bought the soul so that when he comes I can give him one and still save my own.” Pauli (ed.
God cheats the devil of his promised soul.
The devil is to fill a cask full of money. God knocks the bottom out of the cask.
Devil is to get soul of man whether he is buried “inside or outside of church, above or below ground.”
The man has himself buried in the wall of the church, partly in and partly out of the ground.
Man cheats devil by giving him sole instead of soul.
Devil gets an animal in place of a human being.
Devil gets a flea instead of man’s soul.
Payment precluded by terms of the bargain.
Payment to be made at harvest of first crop.
Payment to be made when last leaf falls.
The last leaf never falls from the oak tree.

The student is to come into the devil’s power if at the end of a year he does not at least return for the heaping bushel of gold a level one. The student forthwith hands back the level bushel and keeps the surplus.

Horse bought on condition that the buyer pay ten florins and owe sixteen. In court the buyer insists on the bargain and shows that if he pays the sixteen florins which he owes he will break the bargain, for then he would no longer owe.
The debt will be returned to the devil when the pigs walk instead of run home.
Other deceptions in the payment of debt.
Debtor refuses to pay his debt.
Refusal to perform part in mutual agreement.
Mutual agreement to sacrifice family members in famine.
Trickster refuses to carry out his part of the bargain.
Trickster eats other’s food and then refuses to divide his own.
The dog refuses to help the wolf.

A farmer plans to kill a faithful old dog. The wolf makes a plan to save the dog. The latter is to rescue the farmer’s child from the wolf. The plan succeeds and the dog is rewarded. The wolf in return wants to steal the farmer’s sheep. The dog refuses his assistance.
Reward for accomplishment of task deceptively withheld.
Dancers given one coin instead of ten and have this taken away.
Interpreter says they are complaining that the coin is bad.
Refusal to make sacrifice after need is past.
In distress a person promises a sacrifice to a god (saint) but disregards the promise when the danger passes.
Sailor offers saint a candle as large as a mast.
But he knows that after the storm he will not try to find such a candle.
The sacrifice of the cock is at last carried out.
Postponed until a hawk carries off the cock. Then the woman says, “O holy St. Martin, I have long owed you a living sacrifice. Take the cock as sacrifice, and may it be pleasing to you.” Pauli (ed.
Horse withheld as sacrifice to a saint refuses to move.
The deceiver takes the horse to the church planning to remove him again, but the horse will not stir until a money equivalent has been paid.
Sick man offers deity 100 bulls for recovery.
When reminded that he does not own so many bulls he explains that he doesn’t expect the deity to come to enforce payment.
Payment of money to the devil impossible, since debtor learns that the devil is dead.
When the debt is due he offers the creditor his loyalty.
Hogs used as a mortgage collateral.
False offer to return goods in place of payment.
Milk bought on credit poured into one container.
The trickster buys it from various women. After it is all poured together he says that each may have her own back.
Order to put a small vessel of milk into huge container.
Shrewd group each by himself pours water thinking this will not be detected if the others pour milk.
Trickster gets strong drink by trickery in returning goods.
Trickster returns a bottle of water instead of the bottle of rum he has just purchased.
Trickster fills his gallon jug half full of water, then has it filled with rum at the store.
When seller refuses credit, he pours back half gallon of the liquid
Debtor tells creditor that he has had his reward in the hope of payment.
Toad receives water from frog; refuses earth in return.
Servant refused payment because of single mistake.
Man refuses to pay murderer for killing and kills him.
Fish promised in return for bacon.
The devil keeps calling daily until the gate with the inscription rots. He then claims his debtor.
Agreement to leave sum of money on coffin of friend.
One puts on his share in cash; other makes out a check for the total amount and takes cash left by the other.
To pay beggar for standing in tank all night.
Beggar sees lights in temple. Payment refused since beggar has thus warmed himself.
Palm rat, when asked to throw down nuts according to bargain, replies that he is deaf when eating.
By using verse with double meaning man appropriates borrowed goods.
One day and one night: object borrowed for a day and a night retained.
Fairy (god?) loses stronghold by consenting to lend it for “a day and a night.”
Bird has new clothes made: flies away without paying.
Drinkers argue about who is to pay.
They blindfold the bartender who is to catch one of them; the one who is caught will have to pay. While the bartender is blindfolded, the drinkers leave the tavern.
Trickster sends one of each pair back to be stretched, leaves town with pair of boots made up of the remaining boots.
Man orders a bottle of beer, then returns it and takes a loaf of bread instead.
He refuses to pay for the bread because he has returned the beer undrunk. He refuses to pay for the beer because he has not drunk it.
Jackal refuses payment for being carried.
Healer to take payment in satisfaction at patient’s recovery.
Woman promises marriage for pair of earrings: she escapes with them.
Trickster summons all creditors at once, precipitates fight, and escapes payment.
King promises valuable dog to each of two powerful and mutually hostile tribes.
At feast prepared by king the two tribes get into fight and king escapes.
Fox is promised chickens: is driven off by dogs.
Husband promises a cow to tiger; wife frightens the tiger away.
Thor is to give his hammer in return for Freyja as wife.
He masks as a woman and kills the giant who is to receive the hammer.
Man cheats devil of reward: to have man if he gets him at first grasp.
Man holds cat which flies in devil’s face.
Conquered warrior kills victor instead of paying.
Forty-nine are moulded out of earth.
A woman having thus sworn keeps buying and selling the same mule many times a day.
After payment, snow takes proper form.
Saint ransoms prince for much gold and silver.
Later all the money vanishes. Saint replies that since the money had been created from nothing, it had simply to return to that state.
Man to be released when earth is placed at his head (buried).
Trickster disguises himself and escapes notice of creditors.
Creditor to wait till debtor is shaved.
The debtor refuses to finish shaving.
Man who owes 1000 ducats has his creditor arrested for owing him ten.
Thus he hopes to postpone payment of his own debt.
Refusal to tell about the Rhine treasure, though condition demanded is fulfilled when the only one who knows where it is is killed.
The trickster castrates the dupe and is to come the next day and be castrated himself. He sends his wife as substitute.
Creditor falsely reported insane when he demands money.
King promises beggars new clothes: burns their old and gets much gold and silver.
Death feigned to avoid paying debts.
Customer takes invitation to buy as invitation to receive the goods free.
Devil loses his grain and gets thistles.
God grants the devil one grain crop, which he can create by calling its name. The devil is tricked into forgetting the name and calling “Thistles”. Hence his crop is of thistles.

A man dreams of an egg hanging under his bed. An interpreter demands half of what he finds as his fee for interpreting the dream. The man finds that the egg is a silver cup filled with gold crowns. He gives the interpreter part of the cup but none of the gold.
Pseudo-magic money-dropping ass beaten to death by buyer; cheat says: “Return my ass, I shall return your money.”
Payment in worthless goods which are alleged to be valuable goods transformed.
The eaten grain and the cock as damages.
A trickster has only a grain of corn; this is eaten by a cock, which he demands and receives as damages. Likewise when a hog eats the cock and the ox eats the hog.
Trickster demands return of food guest has just eaten: gets damages.
Damages claimed for loss of a charm.
Princess lets trickster’s fly (alleged to be a charm) escape.
Horse concealed by owner in loft of stable at inn.
Damages for accidentally broken water pot: to pay for elephant.
Payment to lame man who claims that man’s father lamed him.
Deceptive sale of another as slave.
Profitable league made with both parties to a quarrel.
Dog as wolf’s shoemaker eats up the materials.
Devours the cow, hog, etc. furnished him.
Charging thirty cakes for cooking twenty-five.
Crab demands seven patas as payment for four patas of paddy frog has borrowed.
Crow demands young swan in payment for helping swan find feed for its young.
Camel has offered one pound of flesh to jackal for help.
Deceptive wages: as much rice as will go on a leaf.
Deceptive wages: two grains and land to plant them on.
Grain multiplies and takes up all of dupe’s land.
Stolen property sold to its owner.
Trickster steals farmer’s cow and then sells her to the farmer.
Merchant buys the same article several times from the same or different seller.
The price of a lump of gold.
A trickster asks a goldsmith what he would pay for a lump of gold of a certain size. Believing that the man has such a lump, the goldsmith pays him a large sum.

Man asks peddler what he pays for mink skins. Peddler says he will pay ten dollars. The man tosses a skin into the cart, receives ten dollars. The next day the peddler protests that the man has sold him a cat skin.
The priest made sick of his bargain: three words at the grave.
A poor man in return for a steer gets permission from the priest to speak three words at the burial of his enemy, the rich man.
Devil is made sick of his bargain.
Devil helps shepherd boy become a minister on condition that he mention Satan by name each time he enters pulpit. Boy consents but does so in such a way that devil begs to abolish the agreement.
In talking the trickster makes gestures and scratches without detection.
Deceptive wager: whose horse will jump highest.
The trickster has his worthless horse jump out the window. The duke will not let his run the risk.
Deceptive wager: cat to carry lantern into room.
The fee used up before the main question is reached.

A man with an unsolved question seeks the help of a wit. The latter refuses to answer unless paid. He takes small fees for each easy question leading up to the principal question. Before reaching that point the fee is exhausted, and the question remains unanswered.
New bags for old! Recovery of the old bag (containing money or having magic power) which the stupid wife has given away.
The husband exchanges a new bag for it.
Hole in the hat and hat over a pit.
Dupe denied food until hands are clean.
Grass burned around food makes continued washings unavailing.
Trickster sells what is not his to sell.
Man contracts for load of hay on the road (without making any payment), orders the seller to deliver it at a certain inn.
He then goes to the inn, sells the hay to the innkeeper, and pockets the money. The owner of the hay delivers it at the inn, tries to collect at the inn; the trickster absconds.
Trickster persuades girl to reveal hidden gold by promising to make it into ornaments.
Man undertakes to steal various closely guarded things.
Youth learns robbery as a trade: boasts of it.
Courtesan runs away with men’s goods.
Thieving contest: first steals eggs from under bird; second meantime steals first’s breeches.
Youths execute a series of clever thefts.
Two thieves steal a ham from a former companion who has married, have it stolen back, and resteal it.
Man is robbed of gold chain while with prostitute.
He swallows her string of pearls in revenge.
Blind man steals from neighbor who in turn steals from him.
One thief hides in money bag; other carries it off.
One thief entrusted with other thieves’ money cheats them.
Youngest brother surpasses elder as thief.
Means of entering house or treasury.
Thief dressed half white, half black.
His father’s corpse is guarded by twenty knights in black and twenty in white. By disguising he steals back the corpse.
In the shroud of the supposed dead man is hidden another robber.
Sham dead man brought in sack by confederate.
Is killed by his intended victim.
Thief disguises voice and is allowed access to goods (children).
Thief becomes monk in order to rob monastery.
Robber disguised as bear is killed.
Man allows himself to be carried off by monkeys, who mistake him for cow: steals their magic cups.
Magician transforms self into crocodile to steal.
Theft by disguise as son of owner.
Thief in disguise as long lost son-in-law.
Thief pretends to be girl’s bridegroom and calls for her.
Theft by disguise as owner’s grandmother.
Thieves disguised as fine gentlemen steal provost’s purse.
Are admitted to court without question.
Theft by disguising as palace official.
Theft by disguise as woman servant.
Theft by disguise as merchant (or peddler).
Thief in the clothes of robbed bride kills bridegroom.
In one cask is oil; in the others the robbers are hidden. The girl kills them.
Thief hidden in cage that is carried into house.
Entry by master thief into closely guarded city in wood-gatherer’s basket.
Trickster feigns being pursued by drunken husband to obtain entrance.
Thief enters treasury through secret passage.
Underground passage gives entrance to closed chamber.
Thief enters treasury through passage made by him as architect of the building.
Thief bores hole in house wall, then introduces blackened pot as a feeler.
Thieves enter palace through hole in wall and abduct new bride.
Theft from giant by fishing through chimney.
Thief copies key by making wax impression.
Thief enters by burning off locks.
Entrance into wine cellar by removing lock during absence of mother.
Trickster brings rabbit under his coat. When the king’s watchdog gives chase the trickster enters and robs.
Thief learns location of dupe’s food supply by strewing ashes.
Fills the dupe’s bag with ashes and cuts a hole in the bag.
Girl made to carry shell from which ashes fall: she is thus followed.
Theft of gold hoard by spying on secret hiding place.
Thief pretends to return grass that has stuck to his clothes to ground where it belongs.
Theft by use of coat of invisibility.
Thief feigns illness to be taken in victim’s house.
Means of hoodwinking the guardian or owner.
Man gulled into giving up his clothes.
The man claims to sleep thus and beguiles the ogre into sleeping, so as to rob him.
Owner put to sleep and goods stolen.
Master thief puts watchers to sleep and cuts off their hair.
Theft after putting owner to sleep by lousing her.
Master thief puts guards to sleep and steals meat.
Guards fatigued by trickster so that they sleep while goods are stolen.
Worthless object (animal) substituted for valuable while owner sleeps.
Mouse’s tail in mouth of sleeping owner causes him to cough up magic object.
Trickster steals magic doll while owner is asleep.
The foolishly concealed money: A man hangs a bag of money in the top of a high tree.
Servant sleeping with him steals it.
Thief lies down in the space between the king’s and the queen’s bed and steals jewelry from both.
Theft by giving narcotic to guardian of goods.
A blind man’s arrow is aimed for him by his mother (or wife) who deceives him into thinking that he has missed his aim. She eats the slain game herself.
Theft from three old women who have but a single eye among them.
Buzzard steals coyote’s eyes, while he is throwing them up in the air.
Blind beggar overheard telling that his money is kept in a stick.
Owner gives up goods through flattery.
The raven with cheese in his mouth.
The fox flatters him into singing, so that he drops the cheese.
Goat induces the camel to talk and meanwhile eats all the food.
Owner frightened from goods by report of approaching enemy.
Owners frightened away from goods by report of deadly epidemic.
Poor parson thus rids himself of unwelcome guests; they leave food they have brought.
Thieves steal pig and make it impersonate person with plague.
Trickster quarrels with owner of goods, feigns death, and frightens owner away.
Owner frightened away from goods by a bluff.
Dupe, made to believe that trickster becomes a wolf when he yawns three times, flees and leaves his clothes behind him.
Porcupine, made to believe that rabbit’s ears are horns, flees and leaves food behind.
Owner frightened from goods by apparitions of the dead.
When they are turned loose in the churchyard the parson and the sexton think that they are the souls of the dead. Meanwhile the thief steals from them.
Thief frightens priest as the latter crosses cemetery.
Meanwhile a confederate steals his chickens.
Owner frightened from goods by trickster’s ferocious animal.
Pretended dog is really a lion.
Thief frightens away guards of his father’s corpse by impersonating demons.
Town crier is frightened by the voice of a cleric robbing a grave.
Delivery boy is frightened into giving up his chickens.
Trickster upturns his eyelids and puts on boar’s tusks.
Trickster lights torches and bluffs old woman into giving him money.
Torches alleged to belong to man coming to collect damages from her.
Servants frightened by ferocious actions of robbers; give up masters’ food.
Owner frightened away by thief disguised as devil.
Owner frightened from goods by trickster’s summons of wild buffalo herd.
Frightened robber leaves his coat behind.
Object falls on robbers from tree.
Door falls on robbers from tree.
Cow-hide falls on robbers from tree.
Person falls from tree on robbers.
Robbers frightened from goods by the dead.
Corpse thrown among robbers frightens them from treasure.
Robbers frightened from goods by sham-dead man.
Robbers frightened from goods by man’s outcry.
Trickster hits a slain ox and cries out, “Those others did it!” The thieves flee and leave their treasure.
Animals climb on one another’s backs and cry out; frighten robbers.
Robber frightened from his goods by playing of bagpipe.
Robbers frightened from goods by hidden man.
Thieves steal chest containing hidden paramour.
Are frightened away by his outcry.
Robbers frightened from goods by Thumbling.
Other thieves come to steal the bees, take the heaviest hive to the forest and make a fire under it. They flee when they hear a man screaming in the beehive.
Guardian beast overcome by hero’s mirrors.
Robbers frightened from goods by man in tar and feathers.
Robbers coming to steal from stable frightened away by bear staying the night there with his keeper.
Tricksters threaten to cook a robber. All the robbers flee in terror, leaving them their booty.
Sons of thief frightened by threatening to bring the three strongest men to punish them.
Thieves frightened by ghosts who tie fruits to their hair, which they think are missiles thrown at them.
House filled with smoke so that owner gives trickster lodging.
Fire set to village so that robbers can steal goods.
Trickster fills house with smoke so that partner cannot see to eat.
Oversalting food of giant so that he must go outside for water.
Thief sends owner for water in leaky basket.
Thief ties owner’s hair while he escapes with goods.
Owner’s interest distracted while goods are stolen.
Trickster reports lost money; searchers leave him in possession of premises.
Unable to find a place by the inn fire the trickster mentions that he has lost money on the road. One by one the guests slip out to search and leave him the fire.
Animal feigns death repeatedly and then entices owner from goods.
Man feigns sickness in order to go back to steal hidden gold.
Thief distracts attention by apparently hanging (stabbing) himself.
Thief persuades owner of goods to dive for treasure.
Owner persuaded to climb tree while goods are stolen.
Owner of horse climbs tree after thief, who drops down and rides off on owner’s horse.
Owner enticed to chase game while goods are stolen.
Theft of horses (cattle) by letting loose a rabbit so that drivers join in the chase.
Partridge pretending to be wounded entices woman from food while jackal eats it.
Shoes dropped to distract owner’s attention.
The thief drops two shoes in different places and steals a ram while the shepherd goes after the shoes.
Animal’s cry imitated to distract owner’s attention from his goods.
Baby’s cry imitated to distract owner’s attention from his goods.
Cattle let loose so as to distract owner’s attention from his goods.
Cat made to mew so as to distract owner’s attention from his goods.
Golden deer sent to entice girl’s guardians away, so she can be abducted.
Thief pretends to show how horse can be stolen; rides it off.
Trickster pretends to ride home for tools to perform tricks.
