Thief pretends to horse dealer that he wishes to buy a horse.
Thief shows knife-maker use of purse-cutting knife: cuts his purse and robs him.
King loses signet ring while endeavoring to learn from a thief the art of stealing.
Thief tells his pursuer that the thief has gone to heaven by way of a tree.
While the man lies on the ground and looks up, the thief steals his horse.
Thief persuades owner to take his place so he can go and catch thief: really steals owner’s horse.
Trickster bribes guards to start a fight.
While the master goes to investigate, the trickster enters his bed with his wife.
Owner’s attention distracted by man fishing in street.
Meanwhile the man’s confederates rob the dupe.
Guard (owner) sent to see a cat which fishes for her master.
Trickster falsely announces marriage celebration and distracts owner’s attention.
Tailor throws piece of cloth out of the window.
The stingy woman has the tailor come to her house to cut cloth. He throws a piece out of the window, “the devil’s share”. While the woman has gone after it he cuts off a piece for himself.
Master thief pretends to throw needle and thread in anger at his son.
Thief steals belongings of his wife’s paramour while the latter is calling on her.
One thief distracts attention of owner while other steals.
Thief steals pastries while confederate makes a purchase.
Stone thrown to attract attention of shark guardians.
Man then slips in cave and steals lobsters.
Trickster entices children to dance and steals their food.
Thieves ask nurse maid to dance while they steal prince.
Helpful animal amuses princess with tricks and secures key to treasury.
Trickster poses as entertainer: steals meat while host assembles friends.
One thief steals, the other relates the situation, in the form of a tale, to the gentleman who is being robbed.
While singing and dancing in the farmer’s house, the thief gives hints to his friend in the loft, how to steal the bacon.
The thief orders the farmer to crawl into a tub and to sit there quietly and not look about, while he makes a magic spell (cure him of childlessness). Meanwhile, he steals all the farmer’s property.
Fire set in order to distract attention.
Man stands on pillory to attract attention.
Confederate picks pockets of men who come to jeer.
Fox drops goldsmith’s child to get him away from gold bench he is working on and thus steal gold.
Partridge plays hide-and-seek with girls while fox eats the curds they are taking to market.
Trickster starts argument and steals from arguers.
Miser enticed from his money by report of “money tree”.
Man lures fox-husband of girl away by means of cock-decoy and runs away with the girl.
Three men are quarreling over the possession of a rescued girl. The umpire will give her to the one who soonest returns with the arrow he shoots. While they run, he takes the girl.
Thief advises owner to go away; meantime steals the goods.
Innkeeper deceived into going under the floor of the granary; meantime robbed.
Owner sent on errand and goods stolen.
Bread dropped in mud; messenger returns for more.

A youth poses as a rich man’s servant and gets a sack of bread from a baker. The baker boy is to go along and collect. The rascal drops two loaves in the mud and sends the boy back for fresh ones. Meantime he runs off with the rest of the bread.
Woman falsely told that her father is wounded leaves her water pot with jackal.
Thief advises that slaughtered meat be hung up over night.
The stingy parson and the slaughtered pig.

The stingy parson does not want to give any one a part of his pig, which he has just slaughtered. The sexton advises him to hang the pig up in the garden over night so as to make everyone think that it has been stolen. The sexton steals it himself.
Thief advises that new cloth be hung in the open overnight.
Companion sent away so that rascal may steal common food supply.
Monkeys lure tortoise into a tree and carry away his load of salt.
Cheat induces dupe to go get food reported found and steals clothes as soon as they are left behind.
Owner persuaded that his goods are spoiled.
Trickster gives a woman a knife to cut him a slice of white bread.
He gets the whole loaf when he says that he has just cut a dog with the same knife.
Servant places his one fish with Brahmin’s entire catch; receives all since Brahmin considers all polluted.
Servant eats all of master’s anchovies. When master asks for some, the servant brings in a covered dish, and tells him that the fish smell very bad. The master tells the servant to throw them away.
Trickster cuts up partridges with his knife.
He is given all of them when he tells his companions that he is an executioner.
Dupe persuaded that the dung has spoiled the field. He gives the field to the trickster.
Son-in-law steals father-in-law’s pants by making latter believe he has dirtied them.
Sympathetic helper sent for remedy and robbed.
Thief sent into well by trickster.

A weeping boy tells a passing thief that he has lost a silver cup in a well. The thief takes off his clothes and goes after the cup, intending to keep it. He finds nothing. When he comes up, his clothes have been stolen.
Dupe left to care for child while his goods are stolen.
Antelope sends leopard for fire, eats game while leopard is gone.
Thief guards his pursuer’s horse while the latter follows a false trail.
King persuaded to change clothes with thief disguised as old woman.
Herdsman slaughters animals entrusted to him.
Woman persuaded to go after her forgotten comb.
Thief trusted to guard shawls during prayers.
Cloak as surety that owner will return.
Thief takes mistress’s ornaments across river on pretense of keeping them safe, and then deserts her.
Trickster’s claim of relationship causes owner to relax vigilance.
Prostitute claims to be intended victim’s daughter.
Trickster causes owner and another to fight over goods.
Trickster permitted to try on clothes.
Trickster persuades tailor to leave his goods.
Makes him believe he will get order to clothe fifty poor. Trickster makes away with goods.
Thief borrows cloak so to carry food.
Trickster permitted to try on ornaments.
Trickster advises wife to slaughter pig and have the trickster eat it all.
Trickster claims to be working magic spell over food and eats it.
Trickster asks hospitality: expels owner and appropriates house.
Crow asks hospitality of sparrow and gradually takes possession of nest and kills young.
Trickster pollutes house so that he is left in possession.
He is in upper room and throws filth on those below (Cf.
Trickster pretends to have spit in wine accidentally.
Tricksters feign death of their father.
Pickpockets strike man on leg so that he takes his hand off his purse.
Signal for theft given in foreign language.
Means of hoodwinking guardian or owner—miscellaneous.
Theft by means of magic invisibility.
Thief beguiles guardian of goods by assuming equivocal name.
Thief of sweetmeats says his name is Fly.
Child shouts to father, “Fly is eating,” etc.
Trickster dupes woman into putting him into basket.
He thus learns where food is kept.
Crow makes friends with pigeon so as to be able to steal food in household to which he belongs.
Objects stolen by means of magic impersonation.
Jackal ordered to take meat to lion’s family takes it to his own.
Man calling self “her husband” abducts child.
Tricksters eat up food given them for bear.
Man eats up food given him by tiger as bait for deer.
Monk entrusted with care of getting husband for girl, takes dowry himself.
Uncle entrusted with niece’s patrimony slanders her so marriage will be broken off and he will not have to part with her money.
Covetous husband desiring wife’s jewels tells her he has vowed to offer them to deity.
Theft by presenting false order to guardian.
Unique weapon got by misrepresenting to guardian use to which it is to be put.
The numskull has been told to keep the sausage “for the long winter”. When the trickster hears this, he claims to be Long Winter and receives the sausage.
Ring to put on corpse’s finger.
A thief holds a corpse up to a lord’s window. The lord shoots the corpse and leaves to bury it. The thief goes to the lady and gets a sheet to bury the corpse in and a ring to put on his finger.
A thief poses as a messenger from a husband to his wife asking that a certain silver cup be sent for repairs.
Stealing the platter for the intended gift.
Thief asks for silver platter saying that it is needed for an intended gift of confections. Servant carrying platter is told to wait until it is filled. Thief disappears with it.
Theft by posing as master of the house and learning where goods are hidden.
Hare in lion’s skin gets meat from lioness.
Fox drinks the milk of a tiger’s mate by giving her a misleading message.
Deposit money secured by false order to banker’s wife.
When banker refuses to redeliver deposit the owner presents false tokens to wife.
Theft by forgery: signature forged to obtain money.
Clerk mistranslates order given by master to maid, so that pie goes to clerks.
Thief steals lawyer’s scarlet robe. Later he returns and tells lawyer’s wife that her husband had sent him for the hood for the robe. He obtains the hood and escapes.
Hero reports to king that his ancestors (in heaven) want him rewarded with gold.
Confederate allows self to be sold as slave.
Rent a room at an inn and empty the mattresses of feathers, take fire wood, etc. Throw goods out of the window where confederate picks it up.
Wife tells him secret of buried money.
Thief feeds stolen money in flour to animal, then asks for ass.
The trickster has a cow that leads the parson’s cows to him.
Brothers are given the choice of a cow or a calf. One chooses the cow and thinks that he has the best of the bargain. The cow longs for the calf and returns to it.
A cow allows itself to be sold; then returns to its master.
Animal shams death and is sold.
Speaking goat swallows gold coins in temple and voids for master.
Trickster hides in food and eats it.
Trickster throws fish off the wagon.
The fox plays dead; a man throws him on the wagon of fish. The fox throws the fish off and carries them away.

By pretending that he has been invited to be godfather, the trickster makes an opportunity to steal the provisions stored by him and the dupe for the winter. When he returns on successive occasions he reports the name of the child as “Just Begun,” “Half Done,” etc.
Trickster eats food left by tiger (his trapping partner) at snare.

A rascal steals a priest’s watch. He tells the priest that he has stolen a watch and offers it to him as a payment for a past favor. The priest refuses to accept stolen goods. Commands the thief to return the watch to the owner.
Trickster pretends to teach dance: flees with valuables.
Thieves steal chickens and have mock funeral to cover theft.
Trickster kisses pile of money, taking some in his mouth with every kiss.
Fire stolen by swallowing it and then escaping.
Blame for theft fastened on dupe.
Thief accuses his companion of having stolen the gold they have both stolen.
Dupe’s food eaten and then blame fastened on him.
Trickster eats the common food supply and then by smearing the mouth of the sleeping dupe with the food escapes the blame.
Trail of stolen goods made to lead to dupe.
The crane in revenge for the loss of her young ones strews pieces of fish from the dwelling of the mongoose to that of the snake. The mongoose follows the trail and kills the snake.
Stolen goods taken to dupe’s house so that he is accused.
Crow causes serpent to try to swallow a stolen collar and thus be accused of the theft.
Necklace dropped by crow into snake’s hole leads men to kill snake which had eaten the crow’s fledglings.
Surreptitious transfer of stolen object to innocent person’s possession brings condemnation.
Stolen goods left in suitor’s room.
Impoverished lover falsely accused so as to be rid of him.
Thief makes believe that he has been robbed of money entrusted to him.
Thief successfully accuses owner of having stolen property he covets.
Accused of eating the lamb’s heart, the thief maintains that it had no heart.
Accused of eating the goose’s leg, the thief maintains that it had no leg, and cleverly enforces his point by showing geese standing on one leg.
Thief maintains that the bird had no tail.

The ass as toll-gatherer is killed by the lion for asking for toll. The fox eats the ass’s heart. When the lion asks for it, the fox replies that the ass could have had no heart since he was such a fool as to ask the lion for toll.
Thief claims to have been transformed into an ass.
While the owner sleeps the thief steals his horse, hitches himself to the wagon, and claims that he is the horse transformed into a man.
Thief escapes by leaving animal’s severed tail and claiming that the animal has escaped and left his tail.
Thief steals animals and sticks severed tails into the ground, claiming that animals have escaped underground.
Stolen sheep’s tails severed and put in tree.
Owner made to believe that they have escaped through the air.
Thief successfully claims that stolen goods are his own.
Grain-thief’s wagon falls into ditch: duped owner helps him.
The thief makes the owner believe that the grain belongs to the thief.
The stolen pot pawned with the real owner.
The thief gets a receipt from the owner and thus defends himself when accused of theft.
Thief successfully claims that stolen image has been given him by the saint himself.
Stolen animal disguised as person so that thief may escape detection.
Stolen sheep dressed as person sitting at helm of boat.
Stolen sheep dressed as baby in cradle, so that thief may escape detection.
Stolen animal magically transformed so that thief may escape detection.
Thief has his companion cut off his head so that he may escape detection.
Companion’s arm allowed to be cut off so as to prevent detection.
Thief has had his arm cut off as he enters a hole in a wall. He lets his companion also enter and have his severed.
Thief’s confederate cuts off own arm to furnish alibi for family’s grief.
Elephant cuts piece from own leg and puts it on shelf, lest he be accused of stealing meat.
In one night a thief pawns a cow four times, always stealing it immediately and finally delivering it back to its owner.
Plays all night for dance while confederate commits actual theft.
Detection of theft of bull escaped by putting boots on bull.
Thieves stretch chain across road and evade pursuers.
Quartered thief’s body sewed together to escape detection.
Marked culprit marks everyone else and escapes detection.
Many persons admit theft so that it is impossible to find real thief.
Repentant thief pretends to have found stolen cow.
Upbraids owner for not guarding her better.
Thief pretends to have recovered stolen horse.
Returns it to owner after using it all he desires.
Thief swallows stolen goods to escape detection.
Flower thief eats flowers to escape detection.
The owner is duped by thief who gives him the task of solving a riddle about the theft just accomplished.
Thief cannot remember whom he delivered the goods to.
Though he has eaten the food trusted to him, he claims to have delivered it, but cannot remember the person who opened the door.
Thief avoids detection by disguising as a woman.
Umpire awards his own stolen coat to thief.
Stolen bacon offered to the owner.
Making off with bacon, thief accidentally enters farmer’s living-room.
Thief paints horse black on one side and leaves other side white.
Hoodwinked guardians make conflicting report of theft.
Husks replaced in granary so theft of grain is unnoticed.
Goldsmith as thief in king’s treasury.
Makes golden human figure and says it is a corpse.
Thieves escape detection by carrying woman on bier and drowning her outcries with wailing.
Blame for theft fastened on inanimate objects.
Blame for theft fastened on fairies.
Thief loses his goods or is detected.
Robber mistakenly carries off worthless goods and leaves valuable.
Thief hoping to gain bigger booty, loses smaller.
Thieves directed to a hornet’s nest as supposed money hiding place.
Two cheats exchange articles as genuine and both find themselves cheated.
Stolen object magically returns to owner.
Thief condemned when witnesses of theft are able to find the stolen goods.
King’s daughter put into brothel to catch thief.
Apparently dead woman revives when thief tries to steal from her grave.
Horse catches arm of thief and holds on until help comes.
Magic statue betrays a thief by indirection.
He has threatened to smash the head of the magic statue if it betrays him.
Mouse’s tail in mouth of sleeping thief causes him to cough up swallowed magic ring.
Person being robbed deceives robbers and calls help.
Clever woman being robbed makes excuse for screaming and summoning help.
Clever husband being robbed induces wife to make outcry and summon help.
Owner pretends to help burglars to divide booty: handles weights so loudly that police are summoned.
Thief steals pig. Slaughters it together with one of his own and takes both to market. Puts little pig inside large one to avoid paying tax on two. Boy notices three hind legs.
Clever girl discovers robber and cheats him.
The girl seizes the robber concealed under the bed by the beard and says: “What a coarse bundle of flax.
Disguised robber in night-lodging tries to pull up confederate on rope: princess discovers him and catches him.
Girl tells the thief money is in chest.
When he looks in chest, girl drops lid on him.
Husband makes rhymes about cakes wife has stolen.
Blind thief trying to steal dates from withered tree killed by slipping of rope.
Robber with hand of glory killed.
A robber disguised as a beggar gets night’s lodging at a farm house.
Man scares robber with sausage; later boasts of event at inn. Robber hears this. Innkeeper secretly lends man a real revolver; robber is shot down when boldly attempting a second attack.
Conqueror of robber discovers his money-stick.

Thinking that he has killed the robber, the man takes his stick or knife with big handle. The robber recovers and, disguised as a beggar, inquisitively looks at the stick. The man is suspicious and by examining finds much money inside it.

Youth told by two robbers to go to town and sell bracelet for each. He goes and offers to sell two slaves. Goes back with buyer and cries out “Did you say both?” “Yes.” Youth is paid; robbers are enslaved.
Thief loses his goods or is detected—miscellaneous.
Betrayal through exchange of stolen goods.
Thief claims that stolen goods are his own: detected by master.
He has placed a coat on the goods to be stolen. His associate changes the place of the coat.
Thief leaves food untouched when owner pretends to be poisoned by it.
Sheep thief pretends to buy wethers from the ram, names the price himself.
Owner overhears, takes the ram to the thief to collect.
Robber induced to give respite and come to man’s office to get promised larger sum.
Tortoise asks greedy man to give him first ruby it has given him to be sure second one will be perfect match: disappears into water with it.
Owner pretends to think thief is family god and binds him.
Owner feigns madness and thus raises alarm: thieves captured.
Hidden person sees robbers concealing treasure and takes it.
Thief hides in large bottle to get into room: bottle put into water to boil.
A husband and wife are jointly under a pension from the king. She reports her husband dead and gets the whole pension. He likewise reports her dead and gets the whole money.
A lawyer takes a car as fee from a widow and an ox from her adversary. He pleads for the latter saying that the ox draws the car.
Dishonest notary invents debt and collects from both parties.
Fee from two persons for the same monopoly.
Man to furnish goods exclusively to animal. Bargains at same time with another to do the same thing.
Trickster collects from both husband and wife.
Estranged couple both pay him to effect reconciliation.
Money (or other things) acquired by blackmail.
Hidden paramour buys freedom from discoverer.
Clever wife gets money from those who attempt to seduce her.
Clever wife gets husband appointed to position occupied by man who attempts to seduce her.
Money exacted from watchers who permit goods to be stolen.
Money exacted from watchers who permit chest to be stolen.
The chest is said falsely to be full of money and the watchers subject to severe punishment.
Money exacted from watcher who permits theft of wooden cow supposed to be real.
Trickster entices wolves out of a stable by music: exacts money from their watcher for his carelessness.
Trickster exacts promise of marriage as price of silence after having seen a princess naked.
Trickster exacts beautiful wife from curious people.
They look into a carriage in which it is falsely said there is a princess. Trickster’s dead wife is in the carriage.
Trickster exacts money as price of silence after lying with princess (queen).
Fox eats his fellow-lodger: accuses another and demands damages.

He spends the night with a cock in a house. He eats the cock but in the morning accuses the sheep of having eaten it. In the next inn likewise he says that the ox has eaten the sheep, etc. In compensation he demands a larger animal each time.
Priest induced to betray secrets of confessional: money then exacted from him for silence.
The trickster confesses that he has had intimacies with the priest’s maid and then overhears the priest scold the maid.
Women lead man into intrigue and then shout for help.
Rascal extorts money for silence about companion’s poverty.
Princess has brought ill luck to bridegroom.

When palace and retainers disappear after wedding and only humble hut remains, clever fox tells king his daughter’s feet have brought ill luck to the groom, his master. King gives half his kingdom in compensation.
Rascal extorts money for silence about breach of food tabu.
Dream bread: the most wonderful dream.
Three pilgrims agree that the one who has the most wonderful dream shall eat the last loaf. One eats it and declares that he dreamed that the others were dead and would not need it.
Egg as reward of appropriate saying.
Bag of cakes said to be full of cobras.
The bag with the rice for the road.
Boy eats rice and throws empty bag on the road.
An impostor feigns to make clothes for the emperor and says that they are visible only to those of legitimate birth.
God to reveal self to those of legitimate birth.
All afraid to admit not seeing God.
Whoever hears singing snake must die.
The heller thrown into others’ money.

A rascal sees robbers dividing their booty. He puts a red string through his only coin (a heller) and slips it into the others’ money. He claims the money as his and says that he has marked it with a heller having a red string through it. The robbers divide.
Trickster drops half a grain into grain cellar then demands half of the grain supply.
Contraband gold discovered when king offers large price for gold.
Cheater marks coveted object with his name and later claims it.
Unjust umpire decides a religious dispute.
His confederate thus wins an absurd wager.
The wager that sheep are hogs.

A trickster wagers with a sheep driver that the sheep he is driving are hogs. The next man to overtake them will act as umpire. The trickster’s confederate now arrives and declares that they are hogs.
A rascal who has hidden with a simple man a treasure found by them carries it away secretly, trying to have his associate condemned on the witness of a tree in which his father is concealed.
Trickster’s confederate gives fabulous appraisal to worthless piece of glass.
Priest is duped into buying it as a diamond.
Man poses as returned heir to dead man; pretends to address corpse for identification.
The umpire takes the oyster itself as fee and gives each contestant half the shell.
Unjust umpire keeps the stakes when contest cannot be decided.
Cheating through knowledge of the law.
Supper won by trick: the mutual friend.
A parasite makes the host believe him to be a friend of a certain guest and the guest to think him a friend of the host.
Supper won by disguising as an invited guest.
Old beggar disguised as gentleman: much money borrowed on his credit.
The other man to pay the bill.
Three feast at an inn and each makes the host believe that one of the others will pay. None has money and the host is cheated.
Trickster buys chickens telling owner that priest will pay.
When owner comes to collect, the trickster tells the priest that a heretic has come for confession.

Feasters are imprisoned because of failure to pay for the food. They name the priest as surety and are released. The priest has been told that the host is possessed and agrees to come to heal him in two weeks. The host loses the money.
While the servant in the inn is bringing a glass, the trickster drinks the wine and then complains that he has been given an empty bottle. The servant must bring another.
Greatest liar to get his supper free.
Forged letter used to obtain credit, consideration, and entertainment.
Forged testament used to dupe host.
Worthless chests offered to obtain credit.
Trickster receives huge sum on trifling credit by chain of borrowings.
Pays small sum in advance for first sum borrowed. Pays this borrowed sum in advance for larger, etc.
Trickster takes goods given in charity to his family.
The bear helps the fox’s mother get berries: the fox eats them.
Monkey causes girl to cry as if from hunger: eats food given her.
Eavesdropping sexton duped into giving suppliant money.
The trickster prays to the Virgin for a certain sum of money and promises repayment of double at the end of the month. The sexton throws the money to him, but never receives it back.
Owner bids on his own goods at auction.
In cooking dinner fox’s porridge is light, bear’s black. At dinner fox steals spoonful of bear’s porridge and lets bear taste it. Bear believes that fox’s porridge is as bad as his own.
Fox covers his head with milk and says that his brains have been knocked out.
Trickster cheats rescuers into digging his well.
The well that he has dug falls in. He throws his clothes into the hole and hides. People going to church think that man is drowned and dig the well out.
The thief hands it to his confederate.
Two prisoners are made stable boys on their promise not to escape secretly.
Why go all the way to fair?
Man robbed of his plate of cakes half way to fair asks another vendor, “Why go to the fair, when half way up people come demanding your plate?” Vendor goes on and meets with same fate.
Cheating by substitution of worthless articles.
Prometheus divides slain ox so that bones and entrails seem to be choicest part.
Rock substituted for ham by trickster.
Tortoise cheats leopard by substituting bundle of resin for bundle of meat.
False articles used to produce credit.
Nugget of supposed gold (lead) given to help build church: money then borrowed.
Reward for the bag of lead.
A man sews up lead in a bag and feigns to have found it. A merchant claims it and thinking it filled with gold pays him a large reward.
Innkeeper serves sweetened water for wine, cat for rabbit, mule for beef.
False set of rings to offset genuine.
Priests substitute gilded images of calves for those of solid gold.
While swimming with the lizard, toad exchanges own ugly daughter for lizard’s pretty one.
Lean geese substituted for fat by trickster.
Woman gives friend dried comb while she herself eats the honey.
Cheating by substitution of common cow for magic one.
Audience secured with the pope by rudeness.

A woman bribes a man to get her an audience with the pope. By turning his back to the sacrament and saying that the woman had instructed him to do so, he brings it about that she is summoned into the presence.
He secures the audience’s attention by beginning a tale. He then launches into his speech.
Entry into enemy’s presence by pretending to be a messenger from a relative.
The peasant weighs the butter which he is selling to the baker along with the bread which he is buying.
Demi-coq by means of his magic animals and magic water collects money.
Blackbird to avenge capture of his wife carries rope, club, cat, ants and river in ears.
Money received to bury sham-dead person.
Husband and wife each receive money (from different persons) to bury the other, who is supposed to be dead.
Trickster reports treasure’s owner dead: receives it from children.
Color of devil’s cows changed while he sleeps so that he does not know them.
Only those not changed (all black, all red, etc.) belong to the devil.
Trickster gets money from a bank by raising an alarm and demanding “what is owing to him.”
Host with overstock of sour wine spreads rumor of dragon at his house.
A crowd gathers and he sells all his wine.
False alarm of robbery causes cheated man to be imprisoned.
The devil gets into the ark.
The devil wants to know what Noah is doing when he is building the ark. He forbids Noah’s wife to enter the ark until Noah has also invited him.
He confesses that he has an oversized measure and agrees to get a smaller one. He measures back the grain in the smaller measure.
Counselor accuses conspirators in order to confiscate their estates.
The lawyer tells the butcher that the dog’s owner (himself) is liable for damages. He ask double the amount of the damages as fee.
Trickster paid to educate an ass.
He gets paid in advance. He gradually starves the ass.
Trickster paid to teach monkey to talk.
Horse to be taught to speak.
Girl serves her father with piece of her own flesh in place of chicken.
Woman serves beggar with coals instead of food.
Dupe betrayed by asking him ambiguous questions.
They are phrased in such a way that he understands them differently from the way they are intended.
Wolf announces dawn prematurely to collect debt.
The contract is to be fulfilled at daybreak. The wolf imitates the cock and crows, but is caught.
Trickster shams sickness so that partner does all the work.
Foxes persuade man to plant cooked plants.
Persons deceived into eating meat in Lent, the meat being disguised as butter.
Trickster sells mother’s wine to merchant without asking her permission.
Mother saves part of wine because purchaser is dilatory in removing casks.
Object with a hollow as instrument of cheats.
Saint who desires broth containing no butter receives broth into which butter has been poured surreptitiously through hollow mixing-stick.
Saint who desires pottage of nettles containing no milk receives pottage into which milk has been poured surreptitiously through pipe.
The secret is revealed, and the saint blesses the cook’s successors.
Old man cheats crocodile by playing on its ignorance of agriculture.
Trickster breaks cat of taste for milk by overheating its milk.
Trickster unwilling to pay for burial fee of aged cow, gives cow to unwitting Brahmin as gift. Cow dies soon and Brahmin must pay.
God cheats birds by giving false description of tamarind fruit.
Gullible king gives large sums to minister for construction of imaginary weapon and then more to have it destroyed.
Trickster dupes rival by exchanging beds: receives his food.
Overhears maiden tell rival she will bring food at night, waits until rival is asleep and carries him to another bed, takes his place, and is fed by maiden.
Treacherous friend drinks out of other’s flask to save the water in his own.
Fox pretends to go to work, but goes out to sleep.
Escape from death or danger by deception.
Falsified order of execution. A messenger is sent with a letter ordering the recipient to kill the bearer. On the way the letter is changed so that the bearer is honored.
Death evaded by persuading executioner that another victim was ordered.
(E.g., boy has been ordered to kill hare.
Ogam inscription on shield orders that bearer (who does not know meaning) shall be killed.
Poet (who recognizes the meaning) reports to king that inscription means a request for honorable treatment.
A servant charged with killing the hero (heroine) arranges the escape of the latter.
Slaves charged with killing (drowning) the infant heroine are touched by her “laughing smile” and put her in a calfshed (hollow tree), where she is found by cowherds, who rear her.
Executioner persuaded to let hero go.
A servant charged with killing the hero smears the latter’s coat with the blood of an animal as proof of the execution and lets the hero escape.
Compassionate executioner: bloody knife (sword) from slain animal substitute.
A servant charged with killing the hero (heroine) substitutes an animal, whose heart he takes to his master as proof of the execution.
Compassionate executioner: substituted brains (other animal for helpful animal).
Eyes of animal substituted as proof for eyes of children.
Eyes, ears, fingers of corpse substituted for those demanded of victim.
Animal substituted for child served at meal.
The servant charged with sending the hero to executioners sends his own child instead.
Executioner makes substitution when victim escapes.
Compassionate executioner: substituted head (made of clay) as proof of execution.
Compassionate executioner: mutilation substituted for death.
Boy’s sixth toe cut off by compassionate executioner as proof he had been killed.
Compassionate executioner: feigns to torture victim.
Compassionate executioner: sleeping potion supplied instead of poison.
Disguise as girl to avoid execution.
Girl substituted for boy to avoid slaughter by father.
Children hidden to avoid their execution (death).
Girl escapes by hiding in huge harp.
Sleeping persons covered with oxhide and so saved.
Escape by hiding in the earth.
Death escaped through disguise, shamming, or substitution.
Escape by dressing in animal (bird, human) skin.
Man sewed in animal’s hide carried off by birds.
Escape by dressing in bear’s skin.
Escape by putting on old woman’s skin.
Change of bodily appearance so as to escape.
Disguise by shaving off beard so as to escape.
Disguise by mutilation so as to escape.
Ears cut off, eyes put out, etc.
Disguise as king with mask in order to hide from enemy who has ruined warrior’s face and torn his beard off.
Disguise as farmer so as to escape.
Disguise as carpenter so as to escape.
Disguise by painting (covering with soot, etc.) so as to escape.
Covering self with clay so as to escape.
Clothes changed so as to escape.
Disguise in clothes of other sex so as to escape.
Man in danger of life dressed by hostess as woman and set to baking.
Man in danger of life dressed by hostess as woman and set to grinding corn.
Man in danger of life takes his wife’s place in the bed with her night-cap on.
Disguise as musician in order to escape.
Musician in danger puts on his musician’s attire as if about to play; escapes.
Escape by disguising as a washerman.
Disguise as waiter in inn to escape.
Adulteress escapes prison disguised as an old woman.
Escape by making sheaths of bark for fingers: hero leaves without awakening nymph wives who make him sleep with fingers in mouth.
Abbot escapes from his paramour’s husband in disguise of priest.
One animal escapes by shamming as another (jackal as goat).
Goat escapes from jackal by being covered with flowers.
Women escape from enemy’s camp disguised as ascetics.
Hare escapes lion by being bundled in brushwood.
Hare and bride travel in pot to escape tiger, answer “Ruined pot” when challenged.
Death feigned to escape unwelcome marriage.
Escape by shamming death: blood and brains.
The trickster covers himself with paint (or the like) so that he will be thought to have bled to death (or with milk so that it will be thought that his brains have been knocked out).
Woman covers fleeing man with placenta of goat and with blood to convince pursuers she has just given birth and thus prevents their capturing him.
Death feigned to escape from husband’s death plot.
Captive parrots in net play dead and are thrown out: escape.
Escape by shammed drowning; wrecked boat or coffin lands.
Sham murder: trickster attacked by angry mother causes her to spear ox guts and believe she has murdered him.
Illness (madness, dumbness, etc.) feigned to escape unwelcome marriage.
Illness feigned to escape rendezvous with undesired mistress.
Illness feigned to escape unwelcome meeting.
Escape by use of substituted object.
The object is attacked rather than the intended victim.
Substituted object left in bed while intended victim escapes.
Woman puts figures of paramour and herself in bed.
Husband attacks them. Woman uses it as a lesson to “reform” husband.
Bride substitutes wooden picture while she herself escapes sleeping groom.
In order to save child from death, maid substitutes block dressed to resemble it.
Man steps aside so that only his shadow is caught.
Object substituted for murdered person so as to allay suspicion.
Animal jumps out of skin so that only skin is caught.
Man leaves mantle so that only mantle is hit.
Dog buried instead of foster son, who is falsely reported killed so that he can safely be taken away.
Girl escapes from ogress by substituting pig.
Destructive magic object tried out on something inanimate.
Destructive magic belt tried on tree.
Cock’s blood given spirits instead of human blood.
Escape by leaving behind false images made of spittle.
Captor’s bag filled with animals or objects while captives escape.
Escape by substituting another person in place of the intended victim.
Poisoned food (drink) fed to animal instead of to intended victim.
Escape by substituting brother for intended victim, namely self.
Exchange of clothes between master and his servant.
Two rival parties of fifteen each on ship.

When food is exhausted, it is agreed that half the company be thrown overboard, “every ninth man as they stood to be selected.” Clever sister of leader of one party arranges men so that enemies are chosen and so drowned.
Man calls animal by his son’s name so he can sacrifice it instead of his son.
An ordeal (usually dangerous) is escaped by deceptively providing a substitute.
The hero is compelled to smoke a fatal pipe, but the helpful insect which he carries on his head smokes the pipe for him.
Escape by substituting self for another condemned to die.
Holy man substitutes self for deacon held by heathen.
Two wicked men put to a fiery test ask for a third (pious) man to be tested together with them.
Escape from battle by magic invisibility.
Thief makes magic storm in order to escape.
Fugitive disguises successively in different forms and deceives pursuer into self-injury.
Hero walks backward to leave misleading trail.
Escape by rowing boat stern foremost.
Captors deceived into believing captive is planning to stay with them: vigilance relaxed.
Captured general orders heavy boxes taken into the temple. These are thought to be gold and it is concluded that he will not try to leave.
Girl escapes by making man captor think preparation is being made for wedding.
Princess cuts hair to escape captor who holds her hair in hand while sleeping with her.
Escape by reporting oneself invulnerable and overawing captor.
Escape by falsely reporting one’s ability to escape.
“I should be caught if there were not an escape at the back.” When the captors run to the rear, the captive escapes.
Fox to crocodile who has caught him by the tongue: “Those are the dirty clothes I’ve been washing!” She lets go.
Escape by alleged possession of external soul.
Monkey caught for his heart (as remedy) makes his captor believe that he has left his heart at home.
Escape by falsely reporting approach of rescuers.
Pope escapes captivity and death by dressing in full regalia and overawing captor.

The wee cock, lost in the woods, orders the fox, the bear, and the wolf to get into his belly. Overawed, the beasts make their apologies promising never to annoy him again. The bear even carries the cock home.
Man takes off wig, takes out false teeth, takes off wooden leg, overawes Indians.
Man hides in hollow log, fires rifle while Indians are sitting on the log, scares them away.
Jackal escapes by telling farmer he is jackal king and will call upon his subjects.
Ferocious animal (ogre) misunderstands victim’s remark: flees in fright.
Ogre frightened away by beating tom-tom.
Goat trembles so hard from fear of tiger that shaking of his beard frightens tiger away.
Shepherd threatened by tiger says he will report matter to ass: tiger flees.
Threatening tiger challenged to strength contest.
Beguiled into holding wood for plow and is injured.
Queen hiding king disguised as child tells ogress she has borne child with moustache: ogress frightened.
Hero threatens tiger with plowshare and leads him into village.
Escape by frightening tiger into thinking goat in cave is the ghost of his father.
Witch frightened by seeing victim cleave boulder with one blow of sword.
Trickster claims to be holding up sky.
Leopard, afraid to let sky fall, leaves him.
Escape by making attacker believe there are many defenders.
Woman alone in house rolls cheeses down the stairs after calling names of men in the house.
Attackers think the men of the house are rushing down the stairs.
Man convinces robbers that house is fully occupied by beating drums all over the house; they flee.
Sham calling to helpers frightens robbers away.
A captive makes a request or proposes an action that permits him eventually to escape.
Respite from death granted until particular act is performed.
Respite from death granted until prayer is finished.
Respite from death granted until confession is made.
Respite from death until mass is said.
Respite from death until prisoner has finished drinking his glass.
Iguana persuades jackal to let him go so he can finish his drink.
Respite from death until victim has blown on a horn (three times).
Respite from death while one plays the fiddle.
Respite from death while captive plays music (whistles).
Respite from death while one sings song.
Three cries allowed maiden about to be murdered.
Wild boar given permission to squeal before wolf eats him.
Respite from death while one plays the bagpipe.
Respite from death while victim dances.
Girl to dance for robbers asks to bring her party (strong men in disguise) who overcome robbers.
Mare is allowed to dance before being killed; it dashes off to jungle with persecuted boy hidden in belly.
Men ordered to dance before being killed.
Dance figure arranged so as to defeat captors.
Titmouse receives permission to sit on branch and sing before being sacrificed.
Respite from death until toilet is made permits escape.
Respite from death until clothes are changed.
Devil must wait for man to tie his stocking before the man comes into his possession.
Robber insists on disrobing woman before throwing her from precipice. She pleads to have him turn his face while she disrobes. She pushes him off.
Respite from death until hero bathes and drinks.
Escape by pretending to go to river and wash clothes.
Respite from death until mouth is washed; crow slain with arrow as he goes to wash mouth.
Escape by pretending to go for bath.
Escape by pretending to return for hair ribbon.
Girl makes toilet and calls help.
Escape by asking to die on a horse.
Escape by asking to ride on sacred buffalo.
Captured animal asks respite while he gives war alarm.
Wolf kept at door until children have been christened.
Let me live as long as this candle lasts.
Man who has sold his soul to devil thus escapes.
Escape by asking a last kiss.
Uses the opportunity to attack adversary.
Ten (five) year respite given captive while he undertakes to teach elephant (ass) to speak.
Captive explains to friends that in that time the captor, the elephant (ass), or himself is likely to die.
Respite from death until muddy victim may dry self in sun.
Respite from death until one pays a last visit.
Respite from death until visit is finished.
Respite from death until captive has taken six steps toward God.
Respite from death until prisoner is healed by magic object.
Woman escapes by ruse: must go to defecate.
Respite from death for drink of water.
Kidnapped woman escapes by asking for drink of water.
Jackal persuades woman to untie his legs so that he may get a drink.
Respite from death granted until wolf reads horse’s passport.
Respite from death granted while wolf counts hairs in horse’s tail.
Wolf is requested by tailor to be measured for suit of clothes; wolf beaten.
Respite from death until minister shows king how to reap pearls.
A year’s time granted to settle affairs before death.
God grants man twenty years more of life provided he plays no tricks.
Crocodile grants boy five days respite from death.
Escape by false plea: jackal asks to be able to clasp tree before crocodile kills it.
Respite from death until hero climbs tree.
He flies away in machine stored there.
Escape from threatened captivity by pretending to send for object for captor.
Turtle allowed to go to pool to pick flowers before death.
Respite from death until victim can fall asleep.
Captors give captive respite in order to witness alleged marvel.
Captured person (animal) persuades his captor to wait and fatten him before eating him.
“Wait till I am fat enough to race you.”
Hero to be eaten by cannibals when he is fattened enough to beat them in a race. He runs away.
Captured animal pretends to help captor bring more desirable victim.
“Wait till men come to take me from trap, then eat them.”
Troll lets the first two goats pass on the bridge so that he may eat the biggest one. He is thrown in the water.
Dwarf persuaded to wait for ram.
Ram promises to jump into wolf’s belly.
Gives him a hard knock. The stunned wolf thinks he has swallowed the ram.
Wolf is requested by horse to start eating from the rear; kicked to death.
“Soak me in the pond so that I will be juicy.”
Trickster, cornered by leopard, leaps into swamp, then says he is too dirty to eat. Leopard smells of him and agrees.
Executioner kept busy or interested until rescue comes.
Sometimes until he changes his mind.
Respite from death gained by long-drawn-out speech.
Respite from death gained by tale of the preparation of flax.
Respite from death gained by tale of the preparation of bread.
Respite from death gained by long-drawn-out song.
Escape by singing an endless song.
Tiger persuaded by jackals to settle argument.
The man who has chosen Death as his godfather has his bed turned around when he sees Death standing at the foot of his bed. He thus escapes death.
Man allowed to pick out tree to be hanged on.
Escape by asking to die falling from a tree.
Man asks to be beheaded standing in tank of water.
He ducks and executioners kill each other.
Escape by persuading captor to talk.
Attempted escape by persuading captor to talk fails.
Animal captor persuaded to talk and release victim from his mouth.
Usually cock and fox, fox and wolf, or mouse and cat.
Cat fails to be beguiled into releasing mouse.
The mouse tells the cat a tale.
Frog escapes after telling crow to sharpen his bill before eating him.
Sheep persuade the wolf to sing.
Crocodile persuaded to open his mouth.
When he does, he shuts his eyes automatically and monkey escapes.
Rat persuades cat to wash face before eating: escapes.
Captive trickster persuades captor to pray before eating.
Hare persuades cat to perform two gallops before eating him: escapes.
Escape because of plea that leaves means of egress open.
Jackal in tiger’s house has permission to sit with tail hanging down between bamboo stems.
Enlarges gap thus made and escapes.
Tortoise persuades tiger captor to put him in pocket with hole, escapes.
Thumbling in animal’s belly persuades latter to go to his father’s house for plunder: rescued.
Boy swallowed by fish that is thrown up on shore persuades tiger to cut it open with injunction not to look at him.
Jackal entrapped in elephant’s carcass tells passing God to show his magic power by making it rain.
Ass begs wolf to pull thorn out of foot before eating him: kicks wolf in mouth.
Escape by pretending to perform errand (do work) for captor.
Prince to giant: “Don’t eat me up, and I’ll prepare you a good dinner.”
Man persuades robbers to postpone killing him until he can show them his treasure.
Leads them into marsh and escapes.
Escape by pretending to dance so as to be untied.
Hare promises to dance if doorway is left free: escapes.
Escape from captor by means of flattery.
Escape by asserting that captor will have ill luck after killing victim.
Escape by asking girl about to murder him if she will have to assume all the guilt.
Escape by false prophecy: if corpses are buried in city, it will become a ruin: king releases condemned man.
To get out of thieves’ clutch, man reports high prices in another town.
Wife accused of plan to escape weeps and threatens suicide so as to allay suspicion and escape.
Monkey in danger on bridge of crocodiles pretends that the king has ordered them counted.
Escape from robbers by pretending to be going the same way but separating at the first opportunity.
Escape from pursuers by pretending to be one of them.
Monkey saved from trap by feigning marriage.
Respite while captor acts as umpire between captives.
Wolf acts as judge before eating the rams.
They are to go to the end of the field and run to him. They run at him and kill him.
Tiger to help foxes divide their young.
Knight is refused permission to leave city. He rushes to city gates and pretends that he has just killed a public enemy. Is aided in his escape.
Thief is jailed for stealing a quarter of veal. Sends man named “Calf” to captor. “I took only one quarter of veal, but I am sending you a whole calf.” Is set free.
A plea for a larger audience.
Fox asks cock to come down from a tree and sing for him. Cock asks fox to awake his companion, a dog, first. Dog kills fox.
Animal “punished” by being placed in favorite environment.
By expressing horror of drowning, he induces his captor to throw him into the water
By expressing horror of being thrown into the briar patch he induces his captor into doing so. He runs off.
Men double up hare’s legs and throw him on the ground as punishment.
Bird punished by being thrown into air.
Birds caught in net fly away with it.
He expresses horror of that punishment. Sets fire to village from his burning tail. Why he has burnt tip on tail.
Thieving insect put in closely woven basket asks to be put in a loosely woven one so he cannot see.
Punishment which proves fatal to captor.
Turtle persuades an animal to swallow him: causes the animal’s death and escapes.
After debate it is decided that marriage is the greatest punishment.
Thief begs for any punishment except the luxury of two wives.
Throwing the thief over the fence.
Escape by posing as member of murderer’s family or tribe.
Escape by posing as preceptor of tiger’s deceased father.
Escape by assuming an equivocal name.
Fairy child injured by man who says that his name is “Self”.
Man has eaten sweets and says his name is B.
By hiding under the belly of a ram the hero escapes under the legs of the blind ogre.
The three teachings of the bird (fox).
In return for release from captivity the bird (fox) gives the man three teachings. These usually mock the man for his foolishness in releasing what he has.
Cannibal sent for water with vessel full of holes: victim escapes.
Cannibal sent for water which magically recedes from him: victim escapes.
Captive gradually moves away and at last escapes.
Pursuer persuaded to sing while captive escapes.
Escape by teaching song to watchman.
Trickster, pretending not to see attacking enemy, sings song of friendship.
Captor is compelled to dance while victims escape.
Escape by singing watchmen to sleep.
Musician in hell playing for the devils, purposely breaks fiddle strings.
Must return to earth to repair strings.
Witch put off guard by playing on jew’s harp.
Escape by persuading captors to dance.
Enemy in ambush (or disguise) deceived into declaring himself.

(“Hello, house!”) An animal suspecting the presence of an enemy in his cave (house), calls and receives no answer. He then says, “Don’t you know, O cave, that we have agreed that I must call you when I come from abroad and that you in turn must answer me?” The hiding animal answers and the other flees.
Crocodile masking as a log obeys suggestion that he move upstream.
Crocodile in ambush betrays self by talking.
Sham-dead man deceived into making gesture.
Obeys suggestion as to how dead man should act and betrays himself.
Sham-dead tiger betrayed by his live penis.
Sham-dead deceived into moving by absurd action.
Leopard concealed in bundle betrays self when threat is made to run spear through bundle.
Escape by laughing and crying at same time.

Captured bird cries in thinking of her little ones and laughs under pretext that the hunter is wasting his time instead of taking the treasure which she pretends is in her house. The hunter leaves her.
Escape by putting captor off guard.
Captive pretends to louse the captor but deceives him by cracking berries in the teeth (or the like).
Escape from madman by sending him for cooking water.
Escape on ship on wheels after having deceived the captor into laying away sword and helm to receive pretended gift.
Man in devils’ power makes them believe he will return and is permitted to leave.
Prisoner released on promise to wed guard (captor).
Prisoner released on promise of life-long allegiance.
Animal captor appeased by being fed captive’s family.
Boy in hole escapes descending log by digging hole.
Cannibals advised to be absent while hero is being cooked; else he will not taste right.
Cleanest girl to be eaten by ogress: clever girl shakes sesame into fire to simulate sound of burning lice.
Pursuer persuaded to put oil on a tree when he wants to climb after fugitives.
Trickster persuades pursuers to play fatal deceptive game.
Pepper or tobacco thrown into his eyes.
Red ants’ nest broken and thrown down on ogre’s head.
Escape from animals by blowing ashes into their faces.
Captive plays further and further from watchman and escapes.
Escape by pretended debate as to which must be judged.
Jackals thus induce leopard to permit them to enter their cave, while he waits in vain.
Escape from captor by throwing objects to great distance which captor tries to procure.
Watchman outwitted by having rope stretched across the road while fugitives escape.
Abductors tricked into running race while captive escapes.
Escape by giving narcotic to guards.
Escape of girl foiled by hero’s refusal to take narcotic.
Escape by making the watchmen drunk.
Escape by throwing money (treasure) so that guards fight over it.
Escape by pretended bathing of guard.
Man and woman escape by sending the she-bear to bring the woman’s “forgotten” comb.
Tiger enticed away to gather berries: victims escape.
Tiger enticed away by slain pig.
Captive dodges when captor tries to cut off his hand; the hatchet sticks in a log and the captor is disarmed.
The captor is thus induced to fire all his shots.
Person holds hat just outside shelter; enemies shoot at it, either giving away their position or putting themselves at a disadvantage in having to reload.
Mice gnaw enemies’ bow strings and prevent pursuit.
Army of mice save kingdom from enemy invading force by gnawing their provisions, ammunition, etc., to shreds.
Captor’s powder is removed, ashes substituted: gun does not discharge.
Escape by arranging captor’s clothes so as to delay him.
Escape by throwing captor’s clothes on the fire.
Master thief persuades captors to dive into water: steals their clothes.
Sleeping enemies’ hair tied to an object prevents pursuit.
Hair of sleeping maiden tied to tree so that she is not able to rise.
Holes bored in enemies’ boats prevent pursuit.
Paddles broken in enemies’ boat prevent pursuit.
Cutting thongs of sleds prevents pursuit.
Captive tied to captor escapes by tying end of rope to a post.
One animal saves another by frightening enemy away.
Free animal saves its captured friend.
Crow and rat release deer from snare.
Confederate sings and delays pursuers so that fugitive escapes.
Monkey attracts attention of mowers until young birds can fly away from the harvest field.
Monkey saves condemned birds through feigned dream.
Confederate cuts rope almost in two so that prisoner breaks it and flees.
Bird’s call attracts attention of pursuer so that trickster escapes.
One animal swallows another to save him from pursuer.
Tiger-mother hides concealed guests in jar.
Confederate sits on hero and saves him.
Rescuer disguised as officer gains custody of prisoner.
Boys scolded in order to conceal their identity.
Son mentioned as daughter in order to save him from enemy’s pursuit.
Boys warned by dogs’ names to escape.
Sons warned by talk to oaks to hide.
Confederate in disguise helps man escape.
Confederate in disguise as beggar helps to escape.
Helper dressed in bear’s skin helps to escape.
Confederate in disguise as “troll” frightens king’s men, while his daughter helps prisoner to escape.
Confederate saves fugitive by shammed pursuit.
Confederate causes confusion so that prisoner can escape.
Prisoner escapes by means of wolf which he lures near by smearing honey on the feet.
Escape by cutting fetters on stones, etc.
Confederate persuades captor to throw away disguised trickster.
Wolf descends into well in one bucket and rescues fox in the other.
Fox climbs from pit on wolf’s back.
Prisoner kills his watchers who enter to torture him.
Fool’s brothers substitute a goat for the body of the man he has killed: thus save him.
Statue mourned and buried in order to account for murdered person.
Insect in nose of murdered person simulates snoring and allays suspicion.
Waxen statue left instead of abducted queen.
Captive throws his hat to lions who fight over it while he escapes.
Captive throws his shoe at serpent who chokes while he escapes.
Sleeping potion given to man who is to pass the night with a girl.
Is thought dead and placed in a chest.
Trickster persuades pursuers to ride in his basket.
Leaves basket on limb of tree and escapes.
Hero tests the rope on which he is to be pulled to upper world.
By placing stones on the rope he discovers his companions’ treacherous plan to cut the rope.
Hero hides in treasure box and thus circumvents plot to leave him below when companions pull up box.
Cutting rope to kill ogre who is climbing the rope to reach his victim.
Small animal in mouth of larger causes captor to spit him out.
Escape by catching hold of limbs of tree while passing under it.
Escape by announcing great catastrophe (end of world or the like).
Birds escape death by flying away with net.
Victim enticed into voluntary captivity or helplessness.
Deception into magic bag which closes on prisoner.
Leopard persuaded to enter bag in order to see trickster perform marvel.
Miser induced to thrust his head into bag; noose pulled by thief afterwards.
Ogre frightened into rolling self in mat: burned.
Witch tells boy to pass down some of fruit from tree, catches hold of him and puts him in her sack when he bends down.
Deception into allowing oneself to be fettered.
Deception into allowing oneself to be tied.
Animal allows himself to be tied so as to avoid being carried off by storm.
Animal allows himself to be tied to another for safety.
Animal persuaded to be tied by promise of food.
Animal persuaded to be tied through curiosity to learn secret names.
Ogre allows self to be tied so as to learn magic.
Animal allows self to be tied so as to learn music.
Faithless wife ties sleeping husband’s hair to bed, allowing lover to kill him.
Women bind warrior’s hair to wall of hostel while he sleeps.
Deception into putting on a collar.
Hare persuades wolf and fox to put their heads in loops on rope and thus strangles them to death.
Victim tricked into prison and kept there.
Trickster persuades policeman to take his place in the stocks.
Then tricks policeman’s wife into giving him jewels.
Victim tricked into jumping in a box by making him think he is going to heaven.
Dupe tricked into entering hollow tree.
Woman persuaded to hide head in jug: she is caught.
Victim lured into following deer sent by demon to cave.
Fish enticed into trap (promised new skins).
Deceived lion stuck in cave entrance; becomes food for hare.
Fox deceives lion into entering pit.
Deception into allowing oneself to be hanged.
(“Show me how!”) Executioner must show the hero how to use the gallows. The hero hangs the executioner.
Insects (or a spirit) having escaped from a bottle are told that they cannot return. They accept the challenge and go back into the bottle.
Cock persuaded to crow with closed eyes.
Dupe persuaded to close eyes and open mouth; then hot stones are thrown down throat.
Dragon enticed into pot while in its child-form, boiled, so it can see “courage”.
Dupe induced to waste his bullets, then seized.
Dupe lured away from protection of friends: captured.
Dupe persuaded to ride on trickster’s back: captured.
Foxes crawl into whale’s house and are killed.
Animal trapped through curiosity as to what the trap is.
Claim that a trap is a prayer house.
Frog causes deer to dance into snare.
Leopard traps lion by having two doors to cave, one large, one small.
Lion enters large entrance and leopard leaves by small and attacks back of lion.
Tortoise leads elephant down wrong trail into trap.
Birds led into trap by promise of a feast.
Knight captured in pitfall while his horse escapes.
Capture in trap bed: victim dropped into dungeon.
Dupe tricked into well: left there.
Tiger enticed into pit by being tempted to leap after boar-leader.
Capture by closing entrance to victim’s home.
Dupe lured into hole and entrance closed.
Tiger persuaded to walk into house: locked in.
An image covered with tar (or other adhesive substance) captures the intruder who addresses it and finally strikes it so that he sticks to it.
Capture by tarring back of a horse.
Small animal lures large one, who cannot get loose.
Capture by hiding in animal carcass.
Animal who comes to eat of carcass caught.
Man plays dead and hides in money chest: catches thief.
Capture by hiding under screen (grass, leaves, etc.)
Capture by hiding in disguised objects.
Capture by hiding in disguised ship.
Capture by hiding in artificial animal.
Permits capture of the city by concealing soldiers.
Capture by hiding in artificial elephant.
Capture by hiding in artificial bird.
Abduction by fraudulently giving signal of husband’s return.
Capture by imitation of animal’s voice.
Birds captured by imitating their song.
Attempted capture by causing animal to make noise.
Attempted capture by causing owner’s pig to squeal at night.
Attempted capture by ringing cowbell to sound as if cow has wandered far away.
Bird catches fishes by imitating voice of friend.
Capture by hiding in baskets of food.
Capture by putting on the clothes of slain enemy.
Stranger asks woman for fire: abducts her.
Capture by hiding in hollow tree.
Witch pretends to be starving beggar woman in order to capture child.
Hare carries disguised lion covered with honey, thus luring animals into trap.
Unicorn tricked into running horn into tree.
Lioness enticed into putting head into wall to pursue hare who escapes through hole.
Crabs induced to take moonlight walks: eaten.
Deception by having victim pick trickster’s teeth.
Capture by sight of women’s breasts.
Women with uncovered breasts meet hero. He averts his face and is captured.
Sight of women’s breasts used to appease enemies.
Sight of unclothed women calms rage of youthful hero.
Capture by luring merchant to look at supposed bargain.
Capture by taking aboard ship to inspect wares.
Capture with aid of sleep-bringing music.
Fortress captured as harper puts garrison to sleep with music while besiegers place fingers in ears.
Man is made drunk and left in temple at mercy of demons.
Capture of castle by pretending to surrender and entering.
Capture through the wiles of a woman.
Woman (Amazon) in disguise invites enemies singly into forest and overcomes them.
Amazonian woman disguised as leper seduces and binds enemies one by one.
Capture by luring to courtesan’s house.
Attack made on groom after he has been invited to female apartments to have meal with bride.
Adulteress lures husband so as to have him killed.
Castle captured with assistance of owner’s daughter.
Capture by lying in wait in enemy’s haunt.
Enemy blinded with chili powder and overpowered.
In duel with long poles the ogre is forced into the pig-sty.
Fairy wins kiss in game; embraces woman and flies off with her through skylight (smokehole).
Maiden sent to rendezvous with lover, who is captured.
Woman lured into the forest and captured.
Princess lured into the forest by harp-playing boy or thief.
Victim lured into house and killed.
Animal enticed into palace after it had long fed out of trickster’s hand.
Enemies invited to banquet and killed.
With help of captor’s daughter, prisoners slay many of his soldiers at a banquet.
Enemies invited to feast and poisoned.
Jackals persuaded to enter pit to escape coming storm.
Cruel king lured to enemy’s power by invitation to false execution.
Hostile visitors lured into iron house concealed by wooden walls.
Pretended friend puts food on far side of hidden ditch, victim falls in and is killed.
Victim burned in his own house (or hiding place).
Dupe’s house set afire so that he is burned in trying to put out fire.
Boy teaches giants how to lay a carpet of dried grass and naphtha over the hard ground floor of their cave, sets fire to it and thus suffocates them.
Men lured to their death when their fields are set on fire.
Monkey lures tiger into tree-top and sets fire to it.
Stag killed by lion into whose den the fox puts him.
Whimbrel sends his adulterous mate to meet him in cave.
He has arranged with lion to be there to eat her.
Hare tricks civet cat into being eaten by lion.
Overcurious dupe enters trickster’s basket and is killed.
Victim lured by kind words approaches trickster and is killed.
Fox persuades cock to come down and talk to him.
Fox tries to persuade cock to come down and talk to him.
Cock calls dog and fox flees.
Spider invites wasp (fly) to rest on her “white curtain”.
Dogs listen to wolves’ hypocritical words.
Cat invites hens to a feast and kills them.
Owl invites cricket to share his nectar.
Snake promises to do no harm to frog.
Cat acts as judge between sparrow and hare; eats them both.
Hawk persuades doves to elect him their king.
Tiger flatters cow into showing that she has few teeth.
Weasel induces cuckoo to tell him that it cries at night when asleep.
Wounded wolf persuades lamb to bring him a drink, adding that he will get his own food.
Boat lured to land with kind words and wrecked in order to take vengeance on the men.
When they have become friendly, he eats them.
Fish tricked by crane into letting selves be carried from one pond to another.
The crane eats them when they are in his power.
Fish, lured by kind words, are killed by old man.
Cat lures young foxes from den with music.
Jackal feigns holiness but seizes worshipping rats.
King of fishes eats his subjects as they pay him their respects day and night.
Serpent asks his victim to feed him with honey, then seizes and swallows him.
Victim told to stand ready by tree to catch bee nest as it falls; trickster throws club at him instead.
Dupe lured to supposed dance and killed.
Man killed with sword, which he himself is tricked into passing to captured enemy.
Giantess killed with the spear she herself has given hero.
Fairies in animal form persuaded they will hear music better in own shapes.
Women draw warrior aside so that confederate may kill him.
Victim persuaded to hold out his tongue: cut off.
Robbers induced by various excuses (to learn to sing, to learn foreign language, to have a hair taken off the tongue).
Cormorant’s tongue pulled out by putting louse on it.
Victim persuaded to hold out tongue: bitten off.
Elephant killed by cutting off trunk which is poked into cave after victims.
Man causes victim to bite his tongue off.
Man persuaded to hold out hand for alleged letter from king.
A trickster induces ducks to dance with closed eyes and kills them.
Dupe persuaded to relax vigilance; seized.
Fox persuades bird to show him how she acts in a storm: he devours her.
Cannibals persuaded to take snuff: killed.
Dupe persuaded to sing (dance) on trickster’s body.
When he approaches the mouth he is killed.
Fox shams death and catches crows that come to feed on him.
Cheese smeared on crab lures giant to smell him.
Crab pinches giant’s neck and kills him.
Bloodthirsty animal by trickery admitted to fold: kills peaceful animal.
Fox in sheepskin gains admission to fold and kills sheep.
Fox feigning illness admitted to hen-roost and kills the hens.
Wolf tries to cheat ewe by posing as ram.
Slave washing mistress’s back in stream pushes her into crocodile hole.
Trickster sends dupe to well for drink of water; pushes him in.
Monkey killed by girls who pretend to wash its buttocks.
Dupe induced to look about: seized and killed.
Jealous wife tells sister to look below: pushes her over cliff.
Victim persuaded to look into well or pond: pushed in.
Fencer calls opponent’s attention to something behind him: when opponent looks around he cuts off his head.
Female confederate disrobes before hero, who is attacked when he looks away.
Man gets bear off guard by telling her to listen for hunters: kills her.
Victim persuaded to look for certain tree: pushed over cliff.
Man asked to look at birds: pulled into pool.
Man lured into aiding trickster who has feigned an accident or needs help.
Victim killed while asleep in killer’s house.
Dragon deceived into listening to tale: hero cuts off its head.
Ferocious boar fed and put to sleep by rubbing.
Victim killed while load is being taken from his back.
Victim lured into trough: is pounded up with poisoned fish.
Victim enticed into eating: killed when off guard.
Victim lured into approach by false token.
Victim enticed into drinking by over-salting his food: killed when off guard.
King who demands milk from all hornless cows forced to accept bogstuff milked from wooden cows: he dies.
Camel lures wolf into looking at the writing on his breast.
Supernaturals tricked into (fatal) exposure to daylight.
Substitute for execution obtained by trickery.
Substitute for execution obtained by trickery.
Report that man executed just then will be king in heaven.
Dupe persuaded to take prisoner’s place in a sack: killed.
The bag is to be thrown into the sea. The trickster keeps shouting that he does not want to go to heaven (or marry the princess); the dupe gladly substitutes for him.
Dupe persuaded to take prisoner’s place suspended in air.
Dupe persuaded to take prisoner’s place in pit.
Tied animal persuades another to take his place.
Raja substitutes himself for condemned man.
Made to believe that this will take him to heaven.
Dupe persuaded to be killed in order to go to heaven.
Dupes persuaded to be burned, thinking they will be sent back with gifts.
Dupe persuaded to play for wedding party.
Takes place of trickster, who sets fire and burns him up.
Pursuer persuaded to take fugitive’s place in supposed swing.
Trickster being attacked by ferocious animal persuades dupe to take his place.
Spider throws its young; other animal imitates.
Old woman causes swing to break when her rival is swinging.
Deceptive game: bear cubs sway in tree.
Hero has power of resuscitation but fails to revive his enemy.
Fatal game: sewing each other up.
Hare is partly sewed up, but he sews antelope entirely up so that he dies.
Shooting game: blind man’s arrow aimed.
Jealous husband tricks blind poet into slaying wife’s lover with infallible spear.
Fatal game: putting heads in notches.
Fatal game: rolling down hill on barrel.
Fatal duel: brother kills brother in pretended game.
Deceptive game: butting one another like rams.
Deceptive game: fox wants to be frightened; titmouse whistles for dogs and the fox is nearly caught.
Hide and seek game proposed by seven demons so as to kill hero.
Deceptive game: “Eat me up!” Camel is killed by lion.
To trick spirits hero proposes a swimming race. As each spirit arrives, hero drowns it.
Slaughter of drunken enemies in banquet hall.
Judith and Holofernes: girl from enemy camp chosen to sleep with intoxicated general kills him in bed.
Girl kills man sleeping with her.
King given sleeping potion and then beheaded in his bed by his wife.
Groom murdered, while watchmen and bride are brought to sleep by music.
Boy makes adversary insensible by substituting opium for half of tobacco in pipe.
Drug introduced into half of fruit from enemy’s fingernail where it has been hidden.
Ape pretends to louse heron, but plucks out his feathers.
Fatal deception by pretended combing of victim’s hair.
Poor man deceives rich man, plays tricks on him, causes his death.
Dupe tricked into jumping to his death.
Intruding wolf tricked into jumping down chimney and killing himself.
Ape tricked into jumping on to stakes and killing himself.
Monkey tricked into jumping in water and drowning self.
Jackal hides in reeds which screen water.
Dupe tricked into jumping on supposed funeral pyre of beloved.
Dupe induced to jump over precipice.
Dupes persuaded to be thrown over precipice.
Dupes deceived into falling over precipice.
Dupe crowded into the water: drowns.
Dupe forced on to thin ice: drowns himself.
Man leads pursuers to edge of thin ice, swerves suddenly; they fall through the ice.
Cannibals enticed to climb slippery barricade: fall.
Animal left out of his element: dies or escapes.
Beaver and porcupine trick each other.
Beaver carries porcupine and abandons him in the center of a lake. Porcupine causes the lake to freeze and escapes. He then carries beaver and abandons him in the top of a tree.
Dupe tricked on to slippery road lined with knives.
Snake killed by putting knives in animal he is swallowing.
Animal killed by axes (knives) left in tree.
Giant impales self on javelin fugitive holds behind himself.
Robbers make stairs slippery so that bathing prince falls.
Dupe tricked into measuring boar whose bristles are poisoned.
Trickster lets himself be buried alive and stabs his enemies from the grave when they come to defile his body.
Man feigns death to stab brother who comes to grieve.
Sham dead king jumps up and kills the nearest slave.
Feigning deafness to lure enemy close and to kill him.
Robbers’ (giants’) heads cut off one by one as they enter house.
Robbers’ (giants’) noses cut off as they enter house.
Robbers’ (giants’) hands cut off as they enter house.
Giant’s (giantess’s) head cut off as he (she) looks out.
Men lured into serpent pit one by one and killed.
Ogre suitor persuaded by woman to bury her murdered lover: she cuts off his head.
Disguised hero attacks enemy at feast.
Disguised shipwrecked men admitted to the king’s house kill him at Yule feast in revenge for murder.
Bear killed from ambush as he leaves his cave.
Rock hurled down hill slays enemy passing below.
Uses one of the figures of the dance as a ruse.
Peacock helper dances before enemy army of hero; flame of fire from her tail burns them all to ashes.
He lets himself sink in water somewhat with a bundle of hay. The fleas gather on the hay-bundle and he dives into the water.
Murder by bleeding: taking more blood than victim realizes.
Hero entices enemies into building and sets fire to it.
Serpent transforms self to staff, is picked up and bites enemy.
One-eyed doe outwitted by approaching from her blind side.
Accustomed to feed on a cliff with her sound eye next the land.
Ruler promises minister that he will not kill him “on any day of his life.”
Murder by slipping gold coins into meat customarily demanded by enemy.
Men deceived into killing each other.
Hero, who has eloped with affianced wife of king, induced to return to court and treacherously slain during enforced absence of his sureties at drinking bouts.
Old wife provokes sparrow to speak and therefore drop new wife whom he is carrying in his beak.
Concealed weapons in food basket sent king: kills servant who opens it.
False message from other world causes man to go on funeral pyre.
Hare causes pursuing she-bear to stick between trees and kills her.
Treacherous murder of enemy’s children or charges.
Trickster employed to educate baby crocodiles: he eats them instead.
Trickster pollutes nest and brood of bird.
Trickster eats all of tiger’s cubs but one.
Counts that one many times and deceives tiger.
A woman in search of a shepherd tries the voices of applicants. The wolf and the bear are rejected, the fox accepted.
Deception into killing own family or animals.
Man betrayed into eating his own children.
Man betrayed into eating his own children and setting the village on fire.
Man betrayed into killing his wife or grandmother.
Trickster’s false report of high prices causes dupe to destroy his property.
Cows killed for their hides when large price is reported by trickster.
Wives killed when large price for his mother’s (wife’s) corpse is reported by trickster.
Dupe burns house because trickster reports high price paid for ashes.
Enemies each burn own houses to be able to sell ashes.
Angry man kills his own horse by mistake.
Trickster has shifted the places of his horse and that of the dupe.
Hermit (deceived by the devil) kills his own father, supposing him to be the devil.
Trickster shams the murder; dupe kills his.
Woman tricked into giving poison to her husband: thinks it a love-philtre.
Bird flies on head of dupe’s child.
Dupe strikes at bird and kills child.
King causes his own men to be burned and killed, by mistake or illusion.
King lured to send his sons on fatal quests and to kill nephews.
Murder by throwing hot stones in the mouth.
Murder by hot iron in mouth.
Killing tiger by throwing hot hatchet into mouth.
Murder by thrusting spear (tongs) into mouth.
Murder by throwing hot fruit into victim’s mouth.
Murder by feeding with bread full of pins.
Murder by throwing poisoned bread into mouth.
Murder by putting clod into person’s windpipe.
Animal killed by forcing ball (of hide, wax, etc.) into throat.
Murder by feeding with honey-covered sharpened cross-pieces of wood.
Ungrateful river passenger kills carrier from within.
Jackal, swallowed by elephant so it can drink water in his belly, eats elephant’s liver and kills him.
Ungrateful rat defecates upon head of (or kills) octopus that rescues him from sea.
Man transforms self to gadfly to enter giant’s stomach and kill him.
Man kills giant bear by crawling inside and cutting his way out.
Animal tricked into seizing hollow log.
Man reaches through and pulls animal’s heart out.
Murder by wrapping snake around man.
Crab carried by crane, clings round his neck and cuts off his head with pincers.
Murder by crushing in false embrace.
Murder by burning in hot oil.
Gradual murder by piecemeal destruction of separable soul.
Killing by throwing hot salt into eyes.
Murder by putting mouth of pot over victim’s head.
Woman’s father and brothers kill her husband in sleep for having married against their wishes.
Heroes dislike to kill sleeping people.
Man murdered at his wife’s side.
Woman marries king feigning that she can heal him, and murders him in sleep.
Afterward she takes the kingdom together with his counsellor.
Hero attacks and kills at night hero who wanted to go to sleep before their fighting.
Tent torn down over man, and he is then killed.
Rafter supporting giant’s house cut half through, so that it can be drawn down from the outside, and the giant killed.
Thorns planted so that birds are killed when they light on field.
Post-hole murder: people invite boy to enter post-hole and then try to crush him with log.
Flesh of certain animal alleged to be only cure for disease: animal to be killed.
Blood of certain animal said to be sweet.
Disease to be cured by heart of monkey.
Wolf tells sick lion that fox does not esteem him. Fox overhears it. Later fox tells lion that his only cure lies in his wrapping himself in the wolf’s skin.
Flesh (vital organs) of certain person alleged to be only cure for disease.
