A letter is changed on the way to its destination so as to falsify the message. See references to all the cross-references given below.
Forged letter: god of death replaced by another.
Hero substitutes for princess as gift to monster.
Servant impersonates dead master and makes a false testament.
Rascal in dead man’s place in bed makes dead man’s will.
Younger and preferred brother substituted by mother for elder to deceive father.
Death feigned in order to be carried.
Hero sewed up in animal hide so as to be carried to height by bird.
Death feigned to learn how soldiers are resuscitated.
False tidings of one’s own death in order to be able to leave without notice.
False tidings of another’s death in order to secure his bride.
Death feigned to establish reputation of false relic.
Death feigned in order to enter land of dead.
Trickster shams death and eats grave offerings.
Trickster shams death to get food.
Trickster feigns death and eats the ripe fruit from the tree.
Trickster shams death and eats grave offerings.
Deception: climbing silk thread tossed upward in air.
Sham cure by pretended extracting of object from patient’s body.
Reeds make ships appear like island.
Wound masked by other wound in order not to be recognized.
Banners of army appear like flock of many-colored birds.
Clods thrown up by hoofs of horses appear like flock of birds.
By stabbing bag of blood (or otherwise) trickster makes dupe think that he is bleeding.
Absent person seems to be present.
Objects (animals) attacked under the illusion that they are men.
Two soldiers slay each other thinking they are slaying a common enemy.
Slayers magically made to believe stone their enemy.
Comrade slain under the illusion that he is an enemy.
Invisible man eats bread and boy and girl quarrel.
Each thinks other had eaten bread.
Deception: mirror-reflection convinces dupe he is trickster’s captive.
Images set up to resemble watchmen.
Hero wears so many different costumes that he is believed to represent a host.
Lighted sponge in mouth of dead causes illusory breathing.
Following luminous tree in the desert.
Enemies magically caused to lose sight of each other while hunting.
Contract is to be fulfilled at dawn. Wolf makes fire as mock sunrise.
Mock sunrise: person causes cock to crow (simulates cock crow).
Mock sunrise: dupe made to believe that flaunted bare buttocks are the rising sun.
Mock sunrise causes supernaturals (thieves) to drop burdens and flee.
Travelers mistake brushwood at a distance for a ship.
Illusory shapes of animals made to appear on hilltops.
Tuatha Dé Danann cause island to appear to be “hog’s back”.
Wood-spirits imitate falling of trees, etc.
Fairies cause sound to appear to come from various directions.
Man told that he can be cured only with blood of his own child. He is made to believe that the child is killed. When he learns that the child is still alive, the excess of joy cures him.
(The Old Man of the Mountain.) Potion is given to dupes who are led into what they believe is Paradise. They are then forced to rob and kill to regain admittance through death.
Injurious food (drink) has delusive sweet taste.
Palace appears to be floating on water—actually glass.
Other deceptions by disguise or illusion.
Trickster hides in bag in order to be carried.
His father imitates and is beaten.
Trickster hides in box in order to be carried.
Trickster hides in basket and is carried.
Girl hides lover under clothing upon which she sits.
False proof: cloak dipped into water used as evidence of stormy weather.
An impostor takes the wife’s place without the husband’s knowledge and banishes (kills, transforms) the wife.
Circumstances of substitution of false bride.
False bride takes true bride’s place on the way to the wedding.
False bride takes true bride’s place when child is born.
False bride takes true bride’s place at fountain.
The true bride, left by her husband for a short time at a fountain, is supplanted by a moor or gypsy, who transforms her.
False bride finishes true bride’s task and supplants her.
The true bride must perform a certain task to win her husband and, being exhausted, commits the task to a slave.
Old woman substituted for bride in bridegroom’s bed.
Man palms off elder daughter as younger on wedding night.
Compels true bride to exchange places.
Ghost-ogress pushes bride into hole in tree and takes her place.
False bride steals true bride’s garments in bath.
False bride makes child cry and demand mother’s clothes and ornaments.
Prince substitutes peasant girl for the king’s daughter he has got for his father but with whom he himself has fallen in love.
Impostor kills fairy, hides body and dresses in fairy’s clothes.
Treacherous disposal of true bride by false.
True bride pushed into water by false.
True bride lives in fish’s belly.
True bride sits spinning at the bottom of river.
True bride’s children thrown away at birth (by false bride).
Substitution of false bride revealed by animal.
Substitution of false bride revealed by true bride in her animal form.
True bride takes house near husband.
False bride fails when husband tests her.
Uses slipper test, jumping test, or the like.
In order to wear the shoes with which the husband is testing the identity of his bride, the false bride cuts her feet.
False bride fails when magician tests her.
True bride reincarnated as reed reveals truth.
True bride reinstated by acting as mysterious housekeeper.
Snake adopts true bride thrown into well.
Man in woman’s clothing poses as bride for beggar.
Various deceptions practiced to mask bride as virgin.
Abductor pretends to have been sent to fetch princess by lover.
Takes the place of the true bridegroom.
Monk becomes husband to girl at night, so that his friend may have dowry.
Through power of saint, man is caused to assume lover’s form and sleep with princess.
Lover plots death of saint, but is accidentally slain in his place.
Handsome man substituted for ugly as bridegroom: wins bride.
Robber marries girl under pretence of being a fine gentleman.
After marriage he takes the bride to look at his land. He puts on soiled clothes.
An uncle gives the boy a coin and food to hold while he woos for him. He tells the girl’s father that the boy has a piece of money in hand and plenty to eat.
Penniless wooer: helpful animal reports master wealthy and thus wins girl for him.

“House of my father with one hundred fifty lights and goat pen.” When the servant in bed so remarks the master marries his daughter to him. Arrived at the hut, he explains that the lights are the stars whose beams enter through the cracks in the roof. One goat is tied to the tree.
Man wins girl’s love by pretending to wealth and nobility.
Deception is discovered and impostor is banished.
Forged credentials used to win girl.
“All of these are mine,” says wooer as he strokes his whiskers.
The girl thinks he is indicating the fields and live stock past which they are riding.
Slave poses as treasurer’s son and carries letter purporting to ask for hand of merchant’s daughter in marriage.
Borrows wedding garments one by one; later returns them one by one and reveals monster form.
Ugly fish borrows skin of handsome fish for courtship and marriage.
Ogre imposes on widow by assuming form of dead husband.
Son of the king and of the smith exchanged.
Two mothers exchange their children, a boy and a girl.
Queen changes her own ugly twins for slave’s pretty son.
Later recognizes the better character of the twins, and changes back again.
Woman substitutes child for her own and sells it.
Nurse exchanges children so that the preferred child will be assured of wealth.
Man is made to believe that his married daughter has borne a child.
In reality it is a foundling. When the supposed mother dies her father is about to forfeit dowry, when the child’s real parents claim him.
Barren woman pretends to bear child.
Woman pretends to be mother of child chosen to be king.
Midwife takes child and substitutes it for king’s stillborn child.
Queen passes off girl-child as boy by having pandits say raja must not see his son for twelve years.
Barren wife makes child by magic and claims it as her own.
False daughter: accepted as one’s resurrected child.
Impostors abandon (or kill) their companion and usurp his place.
Impostors throw hero overboard into sea.
Impostor tries to push foster brother into the water and then cuts rope so that he drifts alone out on the sea in boat without oars.
Impostors abandon hero in lower world.
Usually let rope drop on which he is to be raised.
Impostor leaves hero alone on island.
Impostor abandons hero on high hill.
Pulls down rope on which he is to be lowered.
Impostors claim reward (prize) earned by hero.
Hero or heroine swears not to tell of imposture.
Impostor forces hero (heroine) to change places with him (her).
Impostor (magician, demon) takes the place of the king.
The ladies of the harem recognize the false king, and the true king is reinstated.
Impostors exposed by girl at her wedding.
Impostor claims to be father of princess’s child.
Rascal pretends to be dead man’s heir and receives money.
An impostor dresses in the skin of his victim.
Disguised flayer tightens skin to look beautiful.
Impostors tricked into carrying hero in box.
Woman makes them think they will have her as reward.
Impostor demands box in name of king.
Person pretends sickness can be cured only with death (humiliation) of another.
Mother-in-law’s head is shaven, face blackened and she is led around city on ass-back as only cure for malady of daughter-in-law.
Boastful elephant killer: killed at one blow.
When the sham hero goes to war his horse runs away with him. To save himself he grasps a cross from a graveyard and waves it from side to side, putting the enemy to flight.
Runaway cavalry hero tears out limbs of dead trees.
Sham-warrior intimidates soldiers with his boasting.
Sham-warrior boasts and is employed at palace.
Tiger intimidated by boasting of the sham-warrior.
Ordinary man assumes high sounding name and challenges enemy chief to single combat.
Latter is frightened into believing him to be of exceptional prowess and desists from attacking the city.
Brahmin takes shape of a prince.
Servant takes prince’s horse and clothes and passes self off as prince.
Poor boy said by helpful cat to be dispossessed prince.
Poor boy said by helpful animal to be dispossessed prince (wealthy man) who has lost clothes while swimming (in shipwreck).
A poor boy posing as a prince in the king’s court always says that he has better things at home.
Brothers pose as princes, deeming their parentage not worthy of their merit.
Impostor claims to be earl’s son in exile.
Adventurer poses as son of dead king.
Wooing emissary poses as king and suitor, but is refused.
Impostor appears with letter authorizing that he be set on the throne.
Thieves set up poor weaver as prince and thus get possession of tribute and gifts.
Coward boasts that he has frightened bear away.
His wife has killed it and he has fled.
Helpful cat borrows measure for his master’s money.
The master thus gains a reputation for wealth.
Drunken man by pretending to want to buy an elephant makes king think him rich.
Sham physician cures people by threatening them with death.
Man undertakes to cure fat abbot of stomach ailment.
Starves him until he admits he can eat anything.
Patients frightened from hospital by harsh treatment.
Sham physician pretends to diagnose entirely from urinalysis.
Really from observation and inference from trifles.
Pepper as universal remedy of sham doctor: accidentally works.
Sham physician predicts the sex of the unborn child.
“From one side it looks like a boy, from the other a girl.” The woman bears twins and the husband pays the doctor.
Sham physician: using the flea powder.
Catch the flea, open its mouth, and place the powder inside.
Sham physician: making the girl grow up.
A king wants his daughter to grow up quickly. The physician says that he must send away for the medicine; meantime she must be shut up. After several years they show her to the king.
The sham physician and the devil in partnership.
The devil is to enter the girl and the physician will collect reward for driving the devil out.
Cheat: demon kills people so his pupil can resuscitate them and get reward.
Sham physician refuses to take his own medicine: unmasked.
Sham physician gives relative a medical degree.
Ignorant youth buys a medical degree.
Ignorant doctor draws his prescriptions by lot.
Sham physician hands out prescriptions haphazard.
Sham wise man gives a purgative and helps find a lost horse.
Sham wise man claims to find stolen goods by incantation.
He has really forced thieves to show them to him.
Sham wise man hides something and is rewarded for finding it.
Sham wise man sees jewel hidden and is rewarded for finding it.
Sham wise man declares who committed the theft: robbers.
Sham wise man does not know where his own house is.
Sham wise man stays alone feigning study.
Sham wise man (girl’s confederate) interprets pretended dream for girl.
Insists she be allowed to marry man of her own choice.
Sham wise man pretends knowledge from dream: really overheard conversation.
Sham wise man burns house where he pretends to keep his marvelous books, and is free from being called again.
Sham wise man accidentally predicts weather correctly.
Boy, posing as magician, agitates purported all-knowing pig’s head in front of his enemies, identifying them as dishonest men.
Pretends to read a document brought him as a letter.
Peasant as priest preaches on the troubles of laymen.
Sham parson repeats same expression over and over or says a few words of Latin.
He has sawed the pulpit almost through. He predicts a miracle. The pulpit falls down.
Sham priest dupes man into believing he can discover treasure.
Mohammed puts seed in his ears and when doves trained to feed there come, he tells people that they bring messages from God.
False magician exposed by clever girl.
Sham magician promises to induce love by magic.
Dupe is frightened (to death, robbed, or otherwise discomfited) by magician or confederate.
Master posing as magician plays tricks on his servant.
Sham magician belches fire to frighten dupes.
Trickster impersonates necromancer to seduce latter’s wife.
Sham magician makes wife believe that he (she) can be transported by demons.
Alchemist steals money from corpse and claims he has made the silver.
Juggler promises to fly from one house to another.
Keeps crowd waiting until dusk and then makes his escape.
Bought game (fish) used to prove prowess in hunting (fishing).
Boasts falsely of voyage and receives canoes which he appropriates.
Warrior buries oversized armor so as to convince posterity of soldiers’ gigantic size.
Impostors: servant enters dead body of master and takes his place.
Man behind statue (tree) speaks and pretends to be God (spirit).
Husband answers behind the statue when wife wants to know how to fool him.
He says to feed him well.
Trickster hides in hollow tree and eats food he has persuaded his wife to bring to feed a bird.
Man behind the tree threatens his debtor.
The latter thinks God is calling and repays the debt.
Boy behind the tree tells woman about the bad food he gets.
She thinks God is speaking and gives him good food.
Maid behind statue of Virgin advises the mistress to give the servants better food.
Husband behind saint’s statue advises wife to spin.
Wife behind tree advises husband against having his wife work.
Husband as God behind the tree forces his wife to confess adultery.
Man as God behind the tree forces the girl to admit having an illegitimate child.
Or prophesies himself as father so as to marry the girl.
Girl behind the tree advises the unwilling suitor.
Believing it to be the advice of angels, he marries her.
Wife behind tree advises the husband about his marital duties.
The man behind the crucifix says “Good Evening” to the drunk man, who thinks Christ is speaking to him.
Hidden man behind image gives unwelcome answer to suppliant: image blamed.
Sexton behind crucifix tells old maid she will have no husband; she tells Christ Child that he knows nothing about it, she is praying to his mother.
Sexton behind statue tells old maid praying for a husband to raise her foot to her neck.
Trickster concealed in sacred tree advises that he is to marry the princess.
Trickster in tree advises that tree and fruit belong to him.
Others think God speaks and leave.
Impostor acting as God in tree suspected and tree burned.
Alleged idol promises teacher certain payment for his book when finished.
Dupe overhears and pays him bargain price for what he is later to receive.
Man hidden behind idol in temple tells robbers they will have good booty but should leave half of it in the temple.
Oracular images occupied by spirits or priests who give the answers.
Statue made to raise its arm.
Woman wishing to go on pilgrimage (to meet lover) makes believe that statue of saint has raised its arm in answer to her prayer.
Priest makes congregation believe the painting of the Virgin weeps real tears.
Jackal inside carcass of bullock makes people think his voice is God’s.
Living man at the grave pretends to be dead man speaking.
Sham miracle: may the grass grow up! Tricksters who have done no mowing say to their master when he angers them, “May the grass grow up again!” He finds it is full height.
Sham miracle: wallet (bee-hive) changes to wasps.
Tricksters put a wasp nest in the wallet (bee-hive). When the master claims it they give it to him with the curse, “May it turn to wasps!” It does.
Sham miracle: rupees turn to ashes.

Cheat tells man rupees carried by horse in sack will turn to ashes if man’s tired wife rides on its back. Man promises to pay him back if that should happen. Ashes fall from under saddle when woman does and cheat collects.
Sham miracle: may the food turn raw.
Lazy wife takes uncooked food to husband in field.
Two friars take arm from corpse and allege it is a miracle-producing relic.
One of the tricksters questions its powers in public. Feigns being struck dead.
Deception by playing deaf and dumb.
Trickster feigns deafness and gets hospitality from miser.
In disguise obtains alms three times from the same person.
Trickster poses as helper and eats women’s stored provisions.
Girls keep up appearances to deceive suitors as to their desirability.
The girls have been warned against speaking, but forget and are found out.
The girl who ate so little.
When the suitor sees her baking he finds that she can eat.
Girl claims to have overeaten on a nightingale’s thigh.
The girl with the ugly name.
Her mother gives her a new one but the girl does not recognize it and her mother must call her by her old name.
Ugly women complain of falling flowers.
King hearing them supposes them delicate and beautiful.
Rearing the large-headed and large-eyed bird.
When the one rearing the owl learns its age he kills it.
Devil disguised as candidate for confirmation.
Devil disguised as man goes to church.
Brother (sister) secures blessing due to another.
Impostor: one sister borrows another’s clothes and gets religious blessing in her place.
Hare (jackal) makes horns of wax and poses as horned animal.
Devil tries to pass for Jesus.
Forbids man to cut wood on Sunday.
Wise man sent by king to rival to give him interested advice.
Man pretends friendship but attacks king to avenge violation of his wife.
Wolves sign false truce with sheep.
After the dogs have been dismissed the wolves devour the sheep.
Wolf poses as “grandmother” and kills child.
Wolf poses as mother and kills child.
Ogre father poses as mother and kills child.
Bogey imitates mother and kills child.
Hyena poses as father and kills child.
Leopard poses as brother and kills child.
Tiger-ogress pretends to be girls’ mother: explains tail as boil.
False friend causes man to eject his wife.
Enemy invited for marriage with relative attacked.
Enemy invited to meeting and attacked.
Women pretend to weep over warrior’s wounds while attempting to inflame them.
King has wounded ally attended by leeches, but bribes them to introduce beetles, awns of barley, etc. into the wounds.
Child adopted by rich man in order to get rid of him.
In payment of a debt, a woman permits a man to kiss her; he bites her cheek so that she has a permanent mark.
Man pretends to kiss relative: bites him instead.
Man embraces other to see if he carries gold in his girdle.
Unsuccessful suitor pretends friendship with woman’s husband.
Kills him while on a hunt.
Badgers treacherously slain in violation of pledge given by prince.
Crow accepts owl’s hospitality then burns owls to death.
Fox confesses to cock, then eats him.
Dog alternately bites and caresses hares.
Dog at his master’s table is friendly to guest.
On the street he barks at him.
Magpie leads other magpies into his master’s net.
Promises them that the master will teach them to speak.
Trickster makes basket for his partner tiger to carry meat, but does not sever bamboo from roots.
Same reward promised to many helpers.
King’s daughter secretly pledged to many to win their aid.
Supernatural personages seen in dreams advise opposing kings how each can overcome the other.
Helper steals object obtained at end of quest.
Jackal persuades deer to steal from farmer, then informs farmer who catches deer.
Double dealing physician hired to poison his master who has sent him to poison enemy.
Crow gets to owls pretending crows have cast him out.
Having learned secret retreats of owls, he returns to crows and leads them to victory over owls.
When wolf pretends to slander tiger fox agrees; later tells tiger he was trying to test wolf’s malice.
Adulteress pretends shame before male statue (mirror, male fish).
Adulteress pretends to faint when her husband strikes her with a rose.
She has allowed her lover to abuse her.
Adulteress feigns great disdain of men; will look at none but husband (and lover).
Women adorn their heads, though they are immoral below.
Girl who is frightened by love becomes insatiable.
Oversensitive bride pleads a headache (or other excuse).
Groom retaliates with similar plea when she changes her mind.
Doctor prescribes sexual intimacy for widow’s ills.
She claims to prefer death. Change of heart on daughters’ plea. Daughters adopt treatment as a preventive.
Wanted: a husband to manage estate.
Widow who claims to abhor intimacy rejects a eunuch with business qualifications.
Man consoles daughter whose husband is dying by telling her he has picked another husband for her. She feels insulted. No sooner does her husband die than she asks her father for details.
Trickster claims to have found a bag of gold. Confederate claims and receives it upon correct identification. Spectator is thus deceived into trusting the trickster with a large sum of money.
Boy pretends to take long trip in order to pay debt of a penny.
Thus he gets man’s confidence and robs him.
Fox confesses sins but is immediately ready to steal again.
The wolf in the company of saints.
Promises to give up slaying animals.
Hypocritical stepmother weeps as she tells departing husband she will take good care of stepchildren though they beat her (she beats them instead).
Hypocrite refuses gifts orally but stretches out his hands.
False ascetic in partnership with tiger shares his prey.
Treacherous plan of hypocritical animal detected and prevented.
Wolf offers to act as shepherd: plan detected.
Wolf proposes abolition of dog guards for sheep: plan detected.
Fox feigns to be playing with sheep: dog drives him off.
Dog caresses sick sheep: shepherd knows that he hopes for sheep’s death.
Wolf tries to entice goat down from high place: plan detected.
Famished wolf asks sheep to bring him water: plan detected.
Wolf offers to act as midwife for sow: plan detected.
Cat offers to act as doctor for cock and hen: plan detected.
Crocodile tells dog to drink in river without fear: plan detected.
Cat hangs on wall pretending to be dead: mice detect plan.
Fox’s plan detected by crickets: cricket wings in his excrement.
Jackal as nurse for leopard cubs eats their food.
Thief tries to feed watchdog and stop his mouth: dog detects plan.
“Would that Death take me in his stead.” When Death comes she points to her husband.
Peasant has kind words for daws, but drives them from his seeds.
Illness feigned in order to learn secret.
Illness feigned in order to get better food.
False guardian betrays refuge of fleeing lovers.
Love falsely pledged for wooer’s benefit.
Man announces finding lost jewel, but so softly that no one hears.
Hypocrite will not share in stolen chicken—only takes some gravy.
Hypocrite breaks vow to give coin in charity.
Thief robs blind miser of his hoard and gives a tenth away in charity in form of a banquet to the poor.
Miser goes to mass before committing usury.
King sends regrets for death of man he has ordered executed.
Falsely accused minister reinstates himself by his cleverness.
Falsely accused hero sent on dangerous mission.
Jewel presented to king brings false accusation of theft.
Man’s mistress accuses his wife of having leprosy.
A woman makes vain overtures to a man and then accuses him of attempting to force her.
Telling a story to allay a woman’s amorous desires.
Woman makes vain overtures to stepson and falsely accuses him of murder.
She tries to poison him but her own son accidentally takes the beverage and apparently dies. Plot is revealed when doctor states that he had substituted sleeping potion for the poison.
Spurned woman accuses man of theft.
Friar refuses to keep promise after enjoying woman and is accused of rape.
Adulteress tricks husband into killing allegedly importunate lover.
Mother falsely accuses son of incest with her.
Tokens are stolen from the woman, or her secret markings are seen by treachery.
Fingers as false token of wife’s unfaithfulness.
She has substituted a maid and the gallant has cut off the maid’s finger.
Man puts donkey’s foal under princess’s bed-cover and accuses her of lying with it.
Page is duped into hiding under woman’s bed (behind curtain).
Maidservant’s confederate feigns coming out of woman’s bedroom.
False abortion placed in innocent woman’s bed.
Man taking refuge in woman’s house causes her false accusation.
Villain brings (threatens to bring) naked servant to woman’s house.
Threat of false accusation of indiscretion forces woman to yield.
Other means of incriminating innocent woman.
Handkerchief left in woman’s room to cause accusation.
Giving madman food causes woman to be falsely accused.
Princess disguised as man is accused of illicit relations with queen.
Girl disguised as man accused of infidelity.
Rich woman, when her advances are repulsed by an ascetic (really a girl in man’s clothes) accuses her of adulterous assault.
A woman is accused of having given birth to animals. Her children are put out of the way and animals substituted.
Jealous queens tell child-bearing queen to put her head in the hole at the bottom of grain-bin, so that she fails to see what she delivers.
Malicious story that man is son of an animal.
Slander: woman has given birth to objects.
Prophecy of ogre-child so that pregnant woman will be killed.
Innocent woman accused of killing her new-born children.
Innocent woman accused of eating her new-born children.
Bones of puppies as false evidence of wife’s having eaten her new-born child.
Queen falsely accused of having poisoned husband.
Ignorant doctors cannot diagnose king’s illness. Queen burned at stake.
Girl falsely accused of murdering her lover.
Investigation reveals poisonous breath of toad as cause of death.
Incognito queen falsely accused of having killed child left in her care.
Man accused of having starved woman to death and taken treasure.
Person wounds self and accuses another of attempting murder.
Murderer makes outcry so that innocent person is accused of murder.
Warrior falsely accused of having killed his sleeping adversary.
Not supposed to have been able to do it if latter was awake.
The letter announcing the birth of her children changed on the way to the king, so that the queen is falsely accused.
Husband’s letter ordering the calumniated wife to be treated well is altered into an order of execution.
Man slandered as having deflowered princess.
Brother accused of paternity of mystically impregnated sister.
King’s faithful servant falsely accused of familiarity with queen.
Innocent woman accused of using witchcraft.
Slander: woman said to be possessed of demons.
Girl reported possessed of demon: suitors frightened away.
King’s advisor falsely accused of treason.
King’s man falsely accused of being in the secret service of another king.
Desiring woman they quarrel over, man accuses group of men of having abducted his wife.
False queen puts horseflesh in bed of one with child so as to identify her as horse-eating thief.
Jealous monk falsely accuses novice of laziness.
Sick crew accused of being magicians so that nobody wants to have anything to do with them.
Stepsisters scatter sugar in girl’s litter so that flies congregate; would-be bridegroom disgusted and tells bearers to abandon her in jungle.
Family is accused of stinginess by recipients of their hospitality.
Trickster makes two friends each suspicious of the other’s intentions.
Cat brings suspicion between eagle and sow.
Eagle lives in the top of the branches, cat in the middle, and sow at bottom; all are happy.
Envious jackal makes lion suspicious of his friend, the bull.
Woman destroys men’s friendship by pretending to whisper to one.
Trickster fills supposed treasure box with trash.
Joint owners each accuse other of theft.
Treasure-animal introduced into family’s flock in order to stir up dissension and enmity.
False message of love carried to hero and maiden by troublemaker.
Servant lays skin of dead dog in the bed of his mistress and master.
The complaint about bad breath: trouble for the king’s favorite.

A steward advises the courtier to hold his head away when serving the king, since the king objects to his bad breath. He then tells the king that the courtier holds his head back to avoid the king’s bad breath.
Officers praised in reverse from their real merit: trouble for them and their master.
The priest’s guest and the eaten chickens.

The servant who has eaten the chickens tells the guest to flee because the priest is going to cut off his ears, and he tells the priest that the guest has stolen two chickens The priest runs after him.
Comes riding a wolf and asks for hospitality. Wolf kills sheep.
Jealous courtiers shake king lion’s confidence in his councillor, the virtuous jackal, by accusing the jackal of stealing the lion’s food.
Two persons separately informed about each other’s death.
(The thrice-killed corpse.) Dupes are accused of murder when the corpse is left with them. The trickster is paid to keep silent.
Live man thought to be returning corpse pleads with trickster to save him.
Corpse is set up so that dupe addresses it and when it does not respond knocks it over. He is accused of murder.
Dead dog set up so that woman knocks it over.
Legs of a corpse cause accusation of murder.
Trickster wounds self and accuses others.
Animal nurse wounds self so as to throw blame for eaten young on other animal.
Evidence of crime left so that dupe is blamed.
Blood smeared on innocent person brings accusation of murder.
Bloody knife left in innocent person’s bed brings accusation of murder.
Slanderers kill a woman and put her body near Buddha’s cell.
Innocent man compelled to write treasonable letter.
It brings about his death sentence.
Sham blind man throws suspicion on real blind.
He admits his deception so that his companion, who is really blind, is punished.
The cat steals a sausage from the table but the dog receives the blows from the mistress.
Rats cause cats to be killed.
The rats unite and all go to houses together, increasing or decreasing their ravages with the increase or decrease in the number of cats. Thus the cats are suspected of the damage and are killed.
Grandmother causes grandchildren to be whipped: puts dirt and hairs into cooking pot by stealth and sand in the water they draw.
Treacherous sister attempts to poison brother.
Treacherous sister as mistress of robber (giant) plots against brother.
Treacherous queen has her brother killed.

(Vidua.) A woman mourns night and day by her husband’s grave. A knight guarding a hanged man is about to lose his life because of the corpse he has stolen from the gallows. The matron offers him her love and substitutes her husband’s corpse on the gallows so that the knight can escape.
Faithless wife and paramour throw hero overboard.
Love-mad queen pushes her husband into well, as fakir lover directs.
Faithless wife plots with paramour against husband’s life.
Faithless wife has husband and children killed so that she can be with paramour.
Faithless wife poisons husband to be with paramour.
Paramour fearing a like fate refuses to go to her.
Paramour demands that wife bring him her husband’s head.
Wife plots to kill her husband, but her paramour answers that he could never touch murderess.
Faithless wife deceives husband while she searches for lover.
Queen in love with own brother kills her husband.
Betrayal of husband’s secret by his wife.
Secret of vulnerability disclosed by hero’s wife.
Noah’s secret betrayed by his wife.
The devil persuades his wife to intoxicate him and then find out what he is doing (building the ark).
Husband at great sacrifice has brought his wife back to life. She immediately deserts him and plots with a paramour against his life.
Faithless wife betrays husband to her father.
Faithless queen aids lover to dispossess king.
Faithless wife incites sons to make war upon father.
Faithless wife tricks husband into setting lover free.
Treacherous queen tricks king into bestowing kingdom upon her son.
Young queen murders her old husband in order to get a new one.
Queen kills her husband as revenge of his killing of her father and brother.
Queen deceives her husband as revenge for his killing of her lover and brother (Helgi.
Treacherous queen lures her husband into chest and betrays him to hostile king.
He is hung up between two fires, but his second wife cuts the strings so that he falls down and kills his enemy and takes his kingdom back.
Wife betrays husband in revenge for his once having taken a second wife.
Daughter has aged father cremated with dead husband to honor the latter.
Treacherous daughter-in-law plots against husband’s mother.
Treacherous son: leads revolt against his father to whom he owes all.
Treacherous nephew kills good uncle for his money.
Jealous rivals prevail on person to break tabu (prohibition).
Wife’s paramour or rival in love.
Treacherous lover betrays woman’s love and deserts her.
Treacherous king spies so that he may levy fines.
Persons darks by race, habitual occupation, or complexion, or even marvelously colored, are frequently traitors in folk-tales.
Boniface VIII, when cardinal, impersonates angel and dupes Clement V into abdicating.
Villain disguised as ascetic or nun.
Man leaves his sweetheart in charge of friend.
He tries to force his attentions upon her and then claims it was a test of fidelity.
Man takes his friend’s mistress when the friend is away.
Restricted to a single cake during Lent, the peasants make one as large as a cart wheel.
Oath literally obeyed: to tell no Christian.
Woman thus sworn to secrecy talks to her unchristened child.
Saint, when forced to return to his monastery after swearing not to “come with his face before him,” comes walking backwards.
Various false explanations are given to prepare the hearer.
Saint has tribute remitted for a day and a night, i.e. forever, because there is but one day and one night in time.
One day and one night: object borrowed for a day and a night retained.
King induced by saint to remit tribute till Luan.
Water-monster allows saint to place cauldron over its head until Luan.
The peasant has hidden the fox in a basket and promised not to tell. When the hunters come, he says, “The fox just went over the hill,” but points to the basket.
Thieves dig field and drain tank when miser says gold is hidden there.
One foot in Ireland, one in Scotland.
Man carries sods of two countries with him that his whereabouts will be so defined.
Warrior proposes to fight in single combat.
Fights with aid of sons and grandsons. They belong to him.
Saint hides fugitive from king underground.

When king demand fugitive, saint (who never lies) replies, “Verily, I know not where he is, if he is not under thee even where thou art.” The king is satisfied and departs. Later suspects trick and arrests fugitive.
Corpse set up to frighten people.
Man who killed mother uses her corpse to get presents.
Dummy set up as corpse to frighten people.

A drunken man is employed, by the woman who has accidently slain three hunchback brothers, to throw one into the river. He does so. Then she puts another out and finally the third. The man thinks they keep coming to life. Finally he sees the woman’s hunchback husband and drowns him.
In the war between the wild and the domestic animals, the cat raises her tail; the wild animals think that it is a gun and flee.
Fox’s tail drops and frightens animals.
In war between birds and quadrupeds the fox’s lifted tail is to be the signal for the attack. Gnats sting the fox under the tail. He drops it and the quadrupeds flee.
He-goat bleats and frightens animals assembled for fight.
Old woman and tiger flee in terror from each other.
A cat shrieks and the frightened bear falls out of the tree and hurts himself.
Ferocious animal frightened by ass braying.
Devil frightened by threatening to bring mother-in-law.
Wolf-captor scared by fiddle-playing of captive ram, who escapes.
Parson is tricked into giving up his room.
Is told there is a snake in it.
Tiger frightened away from man’s tree refuge by man’s stick and rope.
Wife, to drive away parasite priest, tells him husband has gone to get drunk and will kill him with rice mortar on his return.
Tiger frightened at sound of clashing knives: thinks it is leak in house of which he is afraid.
Fire is attached to birds who fly in and set fire to a besieged city.
Fire tied to foxes’ tails: destroys enemy’s cities and fields.
Bees thrown into redoubt drive out enemies.
Bees carried in drum attack and defeat attacking army.
Ashes transformed into bees, wasps, scorpions and snakes drive invading army away for hero.
Mice and hogs let loose put elephant cavalry to flight.
Elephant drunk with toddy sent to attack enemy.
Horses frightened by instruments of war are backed into enemy’s ranks.
Birds frighten enemy’s horses so that they throw their riders down.
Wild horses with bags containing stones tied to their tails, driven into enemy’s camp to cause stampede.
Horse with basket of powdered peppers sent into hostile camp: enemy overcome.
Hot pepper mixed with flour supplying enemy camp.
Thinking they have been poisoned, they beat a retreat.
Wild fawn sent by saint into hostile army, so that all follow it and leader (enemy of saint) is slain.
Strategy to get into enemy city: huge rat makes a burrow.
Women spread shawls on enemy’s path and entangle them.
Fresh hides spread so that enemy slips and falls.
Treacherous priests prolong mass to let enemy destroy city.
Women throw ashes in eyes of attacking soldiers, so that they are defeated.
Man blinded by throwing dust in his eyes: he is robbed.
Owner admitted into his own castle, captured in his absence, in guise of a monk.
He has given news to conqueror of his purported death.
Disguise as musician to enter enemy’s camp.
Disguise as pilgrim to enter enemy’s camp (castle).
Disguise as old man to enter enemies’ camp.
Rabbi feigns death to be carried out of the besieged city and to approach enemy.
Weapons disguised permit entry to enemies’ camp.
Woman disguises as man to enter enemy’s camp.
Disguise in killed enemy’s clothes to enter enemy’s castle.
Disguise as woman to enter enemy’s camp (castle).
Disguise as beggar (pauper) to enter enemy’s camp (castle) or to spy.
Disguise as merchant to enter enemy’s castle.
Disguise as leper to enter enemy’s camp.
Disguise as carpenter (tradesman) to enter enemy’s camp.
Disguise as juggler to enter enemy’s camp.
Disguise as churl (bachlach) to enter enemy’s hall.
Capture by hiding warriors in baskets on back of oxen driven into enemy’s camp on pretence that food is being brought.
Man disguised as animal sent among enemy that first blood be spilled by other side.
Woman saves herself from soldiers by receiving them joyfully rather than fearfully.
Capture of castle by feigning death.
Spies’ false report of enemies’ weakness brings on premature attack.
Enemy’s ships fired by use of fireship.
Enemies defeated by setting forest afire.
Enemy induced to give up siege.
Enemy induced to give up siege by pretending to have plenty of food.
Enemy induced to surrender city by show of wealth on part of besiegers, who shoot golden apples over walls.
Enemy soldiers persuaded by show of great wealth and generosity of king to desert to his side.
City is falsely promised to enemy.
When they enter they are attacked and defeated.
Trickster admits defeat: enemy and friends invited to fort for ceremony and then attacked.
Besieger scatters beads in protecting hedge: besieged destroy hedge to find beads.
Enemy deceived into overestimating opponents: retreat.
Sound of artillery is simulated to overawe enemy.
Persons run wagon back and forth over a corduroy bridge to simulate sound of artillery.
Sounds of mock battle scare away attacking force.
Sounds of battle in playhouse scare away attacking soldiers.
Sham doctor prescribes medicine for king’s army; they fall ill; invading army, seeing multitudes being carried away in litters, flee, thinking there is a plague.
Enemy induced to give up siege by making it look as if the besieged have got reinforcement.
Marauder pretends beggary that king will underestimate his power.
Division of warriors hidden in pit on battlefield.
Largest part of fleet does not emerge until late in battle.
Treacherous king participates in battle only when he sees who is likely to win.
Treacherous ruler of city under siege sends sons to deliver city to enemy.
Postponing of payment asked in order to get time to gather reinforcements.
Besiegers drowned by diversion of river.
Military strategy: city won by turning river from its course through city.
Enemy soldiers march through empty bed into city.
Shammed discussing of peace while getting reinforcements.
Cauldron containing lighted torch brought into enemy’s camp ostensibly to be used for serving food: torch uncovered as signal for attack.
Fairy mist mistaken for smoke of enemy’s burning ships.
Hero causes confusion in enemy camp in dead of night: army men fall upon one another, convinced the enemy has infiltrated their camp.
Poisoned food sent to enemy camp.
Enemy leaders invited to banquet and poisoned.
Brambles heaped in ford to halt enemies.
Deceiving the higher powers (God, the saints, the gods, fate).
Heaven entered by trick: permission to pick up cap.
Trickster throws a cap or leather apron inside the gate.
Heaven entered by trick: demanding back the charity gift.
The trickster demands of Peter an article which he has given in charity. He then sits on it as his own property within the gates.
Heaven entered by trick: “wishing sack” thrown in.
Trickster wishes himself in the sack.
Heaven entered by trick: sitting on Peter’s chair.
Heaven entered by trick: slipping in along with holy person.
Heaven entered by trick: angel tricked by drink into telling woman how to enter.
Gods tricked into help in escaping one’s fate.

Ingeniously worded boon asked of God combines riches, issue, and restoration of eyesight: “Oh God! I want to see from above the seventh story of my mansion my great-grandsons playing in the streets and eating their cakes from golden vessels.”
Dog sent ahead so as to avoid seeing husband transformed.
Enemies reconciled by gifts which the one’s son tells are sent from the other.
The returned box on the ears.
At table each gives his neighbor a box on the ears. The soldier is to give it to the king, but he returns it to the courtier from whom he has received it.
Entering a garden by swimming down a stream that flows into it.
Temporary advantage gained by pretending to yield in a combat.
Person allowed to win first game so that he will play for higher stakes.
Warrior consents to flee for the sake of future victory.
Ammunition saved till enemy has used his.
Hero sleeps during the first part of battle and emerges only later.
Ruler diverts attention from misgovernment by beginning a war.
One animal injures another by deception.
Bird plucks another bird’s feathers out.
Dwarf-deer pastes other animal’s eyes shut and pretends that hunters are coming.
Tying cat to balky horse’s tail to make him move.
Man tricked to be one’s sworn brother in order to secure his help against his mother.
Demon enters person and refuses to leave until wishes have been fulfilled.
Attempt to kill by throwing knife.
“Thirteen” as name of victorious youngest son.
Abused son of younger co-wife becomes hero.
Seal of humiliation put by youngest brother-in-law on the back of his rivals.
Youngest wife’s son restores eyesight to blinded six wives of raja and reinstates his mother.
Only the youngest brother helps his sister perform dangerous task.
Younger brother given birthright of elder.
Youngest daughter agrees to marry a monster; later the sisters are jealous.
Only the youngest of group of imprisoned women refuses to eat her newborn child.
Youngest animal in group overcomes adversary.
Usually, but not always, the unpromising hero is also the youngest son.
Usually, but not always, the youngest daughter.
Unpromising hero given great powers by deity.
Fugitive bull-calf returns when grown and defeats his father.
Future hero found in boat (basket, bushes).
Future heroine found in hollow tree (calfshed, house “without door but only window and skylight”).
Future hero found on top of a tree.
Future hero found in wolf den.
Heroes sons of wife not favorite of king.
Heroine daughter of wife not favorite of king.
Hero of story neglected grandson of raja.
Loathly man father of supernaturally born boy.
Heroine endures hardships with menial husband.
Loved by a courtesan, he proves later to be a great man.
Famous poet does not speak until he is fourteen (four, seven) years old.
Unpromising son leaves his home and goes into the world.
Unpromising hero must live in hut.
The stupid monk recovers the stolen flocks.

A nobleman steals the abbot’s flocks, saying that the monks have no use for them since they eat no meat. The most learned of the monks tries to recover them, but without success. The most stupid is then sent. Asked to dinner, he eats till he can hold no more. He tells the nobleman that he ate as much as possible since he could take back with him only what he had in his stomach. The nobleman pleased with the reply returns the flocks.
Simpleton’s naive answer to robbers makes them think he knows their secret.
They share their loot with him.
Hero stupid at games but fleet of foot.
Poor girl chosen as wife in preference to rich.
Poor suitor makes good husband; rich suitor cruel.
Ignorant steward straightens his master’s accounts.
The educated stewards have always cheated. The ignorant puts his belongings in one box, his master’s in another. Both master and steward gain.
Farmer surpasses astronomer and doctor in predicting weather and choosing food.
Ape tries to flee with favorite child; neglected child saves himself.
The favorite child is killed through the mother’s overanxiety.
Tardy bird alone succeeds at bird convocation.
If you hasten you will not get there.
In spite of the saint’s advice the teamster hastens and breaks his wagon.
Daughter succeeds on quest where son fails.
Scorning stops when it turns out that the scorned has saved the king by fighting alone against four.
Disagreeable and disliked child surpasses the likeable one.
Unpromising hero kills those who scorn him.
Marriage of poor boy and rich girl.
Fool wins beautiful woman as wife.
Mercenary soldier (exile) accepted lover of princess.
Lowly successful hero invites king and humbles him.
Lowly successful soldier invites general and humbles him.
Objects from which choice is to be made are hidden in caskets (or the like). The worst looking casket proves to be the best choice.
The worst horse, armor, or the like proves best.
Saint, offered any gift from God, chooses (virginity and) wisdom.
Solomon, offered any gift from God, chooses wisdom.
Hero prefers fame to long life.
Modest choice proves good (simple unique privilege).
Girl offered reward of five villages chooses rather to be only one on certain night to be allowed to have light in her house and to keep all animals who enter as hers. All kinds of livestock come.
Poor girl chosen rather than the rich.
Modest choice best: wife chosen from crowd of women—only one poorly dressed.
Choice of ugliest girl as bride.
Accustomed rags preferred to new garments.
A Brahmin returns home to find a palace instead of a cottage; he recognizes his wife only after she throws off her jewels and ornaments to stand before him in her old rags.
Former poverty chosen over new riches.
Weaver laments loss of water vessel. Offered many new, but prefers old and modest life.
Modest request: present from the journey.

Asked what her father shall bring her as a present, the heroine chooses a modest gift. It is usually a flower but sometimes does not turn out to be such a simple gift after all (golden cloak, golden apple).
Present from the journey: what you first see.
Small gift with blessing preferred to large gift with parent’s curse.
Modest choice for parting gift—money or counsels.
Modest parting gift best—meat or bones.
Bones thrown to pursuing dogs delay them and allow escape; not so with meat.
Modest choice for parting gift: when offered money man takes magic stick.
Modest choice of parting gift: magic iron measure chosen.
Beggar with small bag surpasses the one with the large.
Latter refuses all but large donations; gets none.
Prosperity forever or for a day? King asks prince whether he has secret of prosperity forever or a day.
Prince says “forever” and is captured. Later his wife, asked same question, says “for a day” and is honored.
Gives everyone the same measure of wit, so that the smaller are more clever than the large.
Poorly-armed hero overcomes well-armed by strategy.
Little innocent girl is able to drive giant out of land.
Little strong man defeats giant in race.
Bird flies into large animal’s ear and kills him.
Mouse runs into buffalo’s ear and overcomes him.
Mouse torments bull who cannot catch him.
Fox burns tree in which eagle has nest.
Lark causes elephant to fall over precipice.
Elephant killed by mouse who runs up open end of trunk to head and there smears poison over his brain.
Insects worry large animal to despair or death.
Eagle at last goes to the sky and lays eggs in Zeus’s lap. The dungbeetle causes Zeus to shake his apron and break the eggs.
Fish pricks monster with fins and defeats him.
Falcon attacks eagle repeatedly and defeats him.
Hedgehog defeats tiger by jumping into tiger’s mouth and tormenting him.
Small animals dupe larger into trap.
Offended rats gnaw saddle girths of king’s horses so that he is defeated in battle.
Little fishes escape from the net.
Mice escape into their holes; weasels cannot follow them.
Hummingbird can see fowler’s net; eagle is caught in spite of his boasts of good eyesight.
Mildness triumphs over violence: queen advises husband to use kindness to enemies.
This wins them over where war failed.
Saint uses kind words to pagan priest who has just smitten a Christian.
Sun by warmth causes traveler to remove coat, while wind by violent blowing causes him to pull it closer around him.
Rain also tries unsuccessfully like wind.
Sun cursed by man for its burning rays, wind for its hot breath, but moon is blessed for its soft, cool, and beautiful light.
Priest who gives mild penances succeeds where others fail.
Goldsmith gives money to one who addressed him as friend (the goldsmith had no friends because he has cheated everybody.)
Reed pricks and drives away dog that urinates on it.
Mouse stronger than wall, wind, mountain.
Mosquitoes sting King Pharaoh and show they are stronger than the man who cannot escape them.
Bride asks suitors what they have to offer her. Poor youth who has nothing but love to offer gets her.
Slow flying swan lasts longer than speedy crow in flying.
Frog, tortoise, fish each tell of how long they expect to live.
Frog alone does not expect to live to a hundred and ten years and alone escapes fisherman’s net.
Proud king humbled: realizes that pomp, possessions, power are all of short duration.
King, defeated in battle, obliged to flee without money.
Boasting king insulted by crow dropping filth on him.
Defeated king must be peddler or beggar.
Queen forced to become a courtesan.
(King in the bath.) While the king is in the bath (or hunting) an angel in his form takes his place. The king is repulsed on all sides until he repents of his haughtiness.
Rich man made poor to punish pride.
He boasts that God has no power to make him poor. While he is at church, his property burns and he returns home poor.
Woman casts ring into sea boasting that it is as impossible for her to become poor as for the ring to be found.
Proud inscriptions sole remains of powerful king.
King vainly forbids tide to rise.
King vainly attempts to measure the height of the sky and the depth of the sea.
God punishes David for his pride in the number of his subjects.
An angel is sent to kill his people. Desists only when David repents.
King commanded to wear enemy’s shoes on his shoulders as sign of submission.
Proud king humbled when imprisoned by enemies.
God finds that his statue sells at low price.
He prices it in a statue shop and finds that his price is lower than other gods.
King shown he is less powerful than God.
In spite of all his plans, his servant recovers the lost (exchanged) treasure.
Both served up at same meal.
Man sets self up as a god.
Attempt to fly to heaven punished.
Attempt to climb to heaven punished.
Peter acts as God for a day: tires of bargain.
Man who has never known unhappiness or want is swallowed up by earth with all his household.
Dream (prophecy) of future greatness causes banishment (imprisonment).
Poor man aspires to high office: made a cook.
Arrogant mistress repaid in kind by her lover.
Haughty mistress makes extravagant demands of lover: repaid.
Scorned lover poses as rich man and cheats his scornful mistress.
