Miracles of healing performed before image of Virgin Mary.
Virgin Mary restores severed hand to Saint John Damascene.
He had cut it off to repress lust.
Virgin Mary saves life of man who at devil’s instigation has castrated himself.
She will not, however, restore his severed members.
Virgin Mary restores life to drowned man who always had saluted her.
Virgin Mary designates favorite for election for office.
Virgin restores office to an ignorant man because of his faith.
Virgin pardons man who repented for cheating in election.
Virgin Mary supplies mead for unprepared hostess of the king.
Portrait of the Virgin appears to devotee.
Virgin Mary rescues man attacked by the devil.
Virgin Mary brings man a pact he signed with the devil and frees the man from devil’s power.
Virgin miraculously prevents nun (monk) from deserting cloister.
Image of Virgin tries in vain to keep nun from leaving convent.
Devotee of Virgin is comforted in the hour of death.
Miracles performed under protection of Virgin Mary.
Boy under protection of Virgin Mary pulled from well alive after a week.
Virgin Mary saves devotee from death in waves.
Virgin Mary destroys Moorish army besieging Constantinople.
Virgin Mary saves devotee’s son from shipwreck.
Image of Virgin Mary works miracles.
Virgin Mary appears to erring man.
Virgin Mary appears to erring monk and exalts him to prayer.
His prayers weave her a garment.
Virgin Mary appears and pardons monk who has been too overworked to pray to her.
Virgin Mary aids repentant slayer of priest.
Priest is resurrected in order to forgive murderer and then is returned to tomb.
Virgin Mary appears to devout nun with infant Jesus.
Devotee of Virgin Mary given present by her.
Stella Maris: Virgin Mary as protectress of sailors.
During a flood the Virgin descends into the streets to save her image from the flood waters.
Belief in the life to come.
Doctrine of immortality taught by druids.
Man converted to belief in future life on deathbed.
Feels sure nevertheless that nothing will come of it.
Dying man refuses to believe in life to come.
Given choice between life and heaven, person chooses latter.
Proclamation of dogma of Immaculate Conception stops plague.
Man miraculously dies for opposing dogma of Immaculate Conception.
Attempt to disprove the dogma by false miracle. Sham dead man is to rise if the dogma is not true. He is found to be actually dead.
Hermit wants to prove truth of these words of the Gospel and asks for the hand of the princess. Performs the difficult task imposed upon him.
Insane man burns heretic in his bed: restored to his senses as reward.
Baptismal water vanishes before Aryan bishop.
Hero renounces heaven because dead companions (heathen) are not there.
Author of book against heretic honored by Virgin Mary and angels.
Man sets fire to his house and perishes in it rather than accept Christianity.
Conversion from one religion to another.
Three (two) Irishmen who believed in Christianity before the coming of St. Patrick.
Conversion to Christianity by miracle of seeing blood flow from Jesus’ image.
Conversion to Christianity through appearance of the cross and angels.
Conversion to Christianity because the heathen gods prove to be less powerful.
Conversion because saint’s staff miraculously goes through neophytes’ foot.
Conversion to Christianity on pain of death.
Miraculous beautification upon conversion to Christianity.
Conversion to Christianity out of gratitude.
Ruler has captive baptize his sister and then marry her. Grateful for past kindnesses.
Saladin asks to be made a Christian knight.
Swans (transformed children) do not suffer in harsh weather after conversion to Christianity.
Conversion to Christianity because of admiration for Christian virtue.
Conversion to Christianity through show of forgiveness and gentleness.
Pagan sybil draws picture of Madonna and Child in sand.
Jews protesting against marriage of Jewess and Christian are struck dumb.
Temple about to be taken over by pagans saved by appearance of a Sign of the Cross (image of the Virgin).
Dove flies out of man’s mouth.
Impious anchorite has agreed to forsake his religion in return for the possession of a maid. When he repents the dove reenters his mouth.
Idols found on their faces after saint’s arrival.
Duel (debate) to prove which religion is better.
Wise heretic is vanquished in debate with a Christian.
Brahmin wins a discussion on religion.
Magician overpowered in contest with a saint.
Contest of St. Peter with Simon Magus, a magician.
Prayer-contest to prove which religion is better.
Contest of miraculous powers between a Yogi and a Musselman.
Pagan disputant with Christian stricken dumb.
Pagan disputant with Christian bested by the words put in his mouth by God.
Life of heroic age preferable to Christian living.
Buddhists become slaves of Taoists because they cannot produce rain.
Saint dispels pagan devils from ancient shrines.
Pagan shrines and idols, or magic books destroyed by fire from heaven.
Heathen idols sink into earth up to their necks through power of saint.
Saint’s bachall pointed at idol defaces it.
Christian and Jewish traditions about each other.
Christian child killed to furnish blood for Jewish rite.
Jewish child thrown into oven by father for taking eucharist.
Jewish child resurrected (saved by power of Virgin Mary) after being burned to ashes for eating consecrated bread in Christian church.
A Christianized Jew becomes a priest.
During Mass, he stabs the consecrated host, blood flows (cf.
Heathen beats his god because of misfortune.
Doctor ridicules belief in Devil, Heaven, and Hell.
Prolonged prostration in worship causes death.
Hindu drinks water by mistake from Mohammedan’s vessel: his fortune turns to evil.
Romans won’t include Jesus in their pantheon because of his poverty which they hate.
Charity rewarded above prayer or hearing of masses.
Queen gives away a sleeve of her dress: miraculously restored.
Saint exchanges coat with beggar: gold sleeves miraculously appear.
Man who has given all in charity has foot amputated: restored miraculously.
Stones turn to gold for charitable money-lender.
Hence money borrowed for wedding is never refused by lenders.
Treasure given away by saint miraculously restored.
Man earns as much as he gave away for charity in his former life.
Food given away by saint miraculously restored.
Charitable king blows nose after having given to beggar.
Huge ruby appears in his kerchief.
Jesus appears to St. Martin when he gives his cloak to beggar.
Charity miraculously repaid: flame settles on forehead.
Miraculous manifestations during act of charity.
Bread stolen by St. Nicholas for purpose of feeding poor is miraculously restored.
The more bread (flour) the monks give to the poor the more God places in their bins.
Son’s acts of charity save his father’s soul.
Saint shares punishment of sinful man whose cloak he shared in life.
Children envious of money given by deceased father to bishop.
In vision they take their father’s body up and find a quittance saying that he has received more than a hundredfold reward.
Man convicted of cheating at his bookkeeping is excused when it is learned that he has given the money to the poor.
Shipman refuses alms: ship turned to stone.
Uncharitable knight drives bargain even in giving alms: devoured by serpents.
His alms of corn turn to serpents.
Conqueror restores kingship to king for charity.
Pious man charitable to man who has formerly refused him charity.
Mendicant refuses to accept alms from barren woman.
Saint repeatedly bestows father’s goods upon the poor.
Merit for charity lost by asking work in return.
First-born son and one of every ten born thereafter given to Church.
Obedient and industrious nun the worthiest in the convent.
Truthful monk refuses to cheat even for his order.
Monk lives where people speak ill of him to avoid danger of flattery.
Man captured by robbers is so confident that God will protect him that he is saved.
Kingship renounced to become an ascetic.
Since salvation is predestined, asceticism deemed useless.
Husband abandons wife to become ascetic.
Ascetic faster increases his sufferings by placing food and drink before himself.
Saint refuses pearls as alms and asks for food.
Cleric stands with hands extended in shape of cross.
Saint always extends one hand toward heaven while performing such acts as eating or reaping.
Ascetic cleric prays to become diseased.
Saint never wears woolen clothing, but skins of wolves and other beasts.
Ascetic cleric sleeps (prays) with wet sheet (mantle) about him.
Saint stands for seven years without sleep.
Ascetic cleric avoids listening to music.
Saint confines himself in narrow pen during Lent.
Saint stands (asleep) while bird builds nest and hatches brood in his hand.
Ascetic cleric lives for seven years on whale’s back.
Ascetic cleric renounces world (to become a herder).
Monk refuses chance of having temptation removed since he considers it strengthening to have it ever present to test him.
Evil ascetic misuses magic powers obtained through religious meditation.
Boy takes twelve years to wash off ascetic’s dirt.
Cleric surrenders life that body may consecrate land.
Monk seduces girl; then kills her; becomes infidel.
Nun hidden by abbess from pursuing knight betrays her own hiding place to him.
Nun tempted into sinning with man who tells her God can’t see things that happen in the dark.
Priest uses cook-book instead of breviary.
Priest is bribed into betraying the confessional.
Clerical vows because of disappointment in love.
Man becomes hermit when he realizes selfishness of his beloved’s love.
Former monk refuses to take pay for his work, considering it as a religious act.
Monk who has left order punished (dies in torment).
Monk who has left his order forgiven and miraculously reinstated.
Man who is disappointed with his religious order renounces his vow.
Saint leaves his order because he is fond of music.
Anchorite tempted by money to return to worldly life.
God speaks in vision to devotee.
Only man without sin can see God.
Vision of angels defending road to heaven against devils.
Girl sees vision of her mother in hell.
She chooses to live the poor life of her father which leads to heaven.
Visions of Land of the Saints.
Man sees his own soul being judged.
A clerk sees his good and evil deeds being weighed. He asks them to throw his faith in Christ (the Virgin) into the scale.
Man whose only good deed was unintentional sees this deed outweigh all his evil in the scales of judgment.
Vision of the earth in the devil’s snares.
Chairs of gold, silver, crystal (glass) assigned to saints according to merit.
Wife sees moon enter mouth of husband; husband sees star enter mouth of wife: famous child (saint) will be born.
Saint sees vision of flames covering Ireland quenched except for sparks; then great light appears, dispelling darkness.
Flames are those of the faith brought by St. Patrick; they become less until restored by St.
When shower falls, small stone becomes larger, large stone wastes away.
Vision of present and future state of Irish church.
Vision in which swineherd sees yew tree upon a rock, with an oratory in front of it and angels ascending from it.
Vision interpreted by druid as symbolizing founding of Cashel and the royal line of Munster.
Vision in which chieftain sees pair of gray seals that sucked at his two breasts.
They are two of his allies who are being overpowered by invaders.
Vision in which king sees whelp reared by him gather dogs of Ireland and Britain against him but suffer death in battle at last.
The whelp is one of king’s two foster sons.
Vision in which saint foresees allegorically the ramifications of king’s family Irish myth: Cross.
Vision in which king sees his four sons changed into lion, greyhound, beagle, cur, which fight with alternating success, until lion subdues the other three.
Sinner reformed after visit to heaven and hell.
The only king ever saved in spite of himself.
Sinner who thinks of God saved; devotee who thinks of worldly things goes to hell.
Worship of particular deity brings reward of birth in Brahma-world.
Pilgrimage to follow roads Christ walked.
Intervention of Providence saves person’s life.
Man is prevented from taking passage on ship which later sinks.
Man hears voice telling him to leave danger spot in mine.
Good inclinations enter body at puberty.
Saint never drives fly or gnat from his face.
Philanthropist will give his spurs if someone will drive his horse for him.
He has given away his coat, etc. to beggars. One finally asks for his spurs.
Emperor thinks day lost when he gives no gifts.
King will not eat breakfast till gifts are given.
Man divides money into three parts: (1) for the poor, (2) for pilgrims, (3) for himself and family.
Man lets himself be sold as slave so as to practice generosity.
They attack again and are killed.
Ruler pardons emissary who has come to murder him.
Wronged knight conquers enemy and then pardons him.
Conqueror returns defeated man’s wife and family to him.
Ruler reproaches son for bringing him the head of his fallen enemy.
Man saved through intercession of enemy.
Man pays fine for enemy who is falsely accused.
Warrior gives steed to his enemy.
Man’s life spared through the intercession of the daughter he has wronged.
Champion grants requested boon of safe convoy to his enemies.
Chieftain spares enemies whom he takes unawares (unarmed).
Chieftain who takes king unawares, spares him on condition that chieftain be called “lover” by women of king’s tribe.
Hero in battle refuses to slay charioteers, women, or physicians.
Ruler generously settles quarrel between loser and finder of money.
Nobleman’s generosity enables impoverished lover to entertain his lady.
Impoverished nobleman offers wife to ruler.
Latter spares her honor and aids the couple.
General sends for king so that the latter may get credit for victory.
Prince donates all including a tooth.
When he has nothing left he is asked for a gift. He allows man to extract a tooth from his mouth.
Asks for the stolen plate and hides it so that it will not be found on the culprit.
Ruler rewards man who would curb him.
King rewards knight with large sum of money.
It is the first time that what he has given away seems too much.
Youngest brother shares wealth with older brothers who foolishly lost theirs.
Generous person refuses no man anything.
Generous king gives away his only eye.
Man (king) prefers death to loss of reputation for hospitality.
Man looks for strangers so as to bestow hospitality on them.
Woman shelters son’s murderer out of charity.
Murderer goes to victim’s son and asks to be killed.
The son aids him to escape.
Bishop exchanges places with prisoner so as to have him return to his mother.
Envious man sets out to kill one who is noted for his generosity.
He is won over by the generosity of his intended victim.
Would act as he should like an emperor to act toward him if he were a common man.
When he sees his house carried off by a flood, he fiddles the whole time.
Does not complain when beset by a series of misfortunes.
Minister always says, “It is for the best,” when anything happens.
Man weeps with gratitude to God because He did not make him hideous as toad.
Woman drinks poison that son may be king.
Woman sacrifices life for son’s honor.
Man leaps from vessel into jaws of sea-beast so as to save remaining passengers.
Saint threatens to take place of homicide in hell unless soul is released.
King Richard leads host to victory by leaping his horse overboard.
Warrior refuses to delay battle in return for promise of long, happy life.
Man constrained to flee with leader’s fiancée resists her blandishments.
Loyal friends refuse to fight against disgraced comrade.
Cowardly to leave battle while lord is alive.
Fakir rewarded by prince with a life of luxury in city chooses to return to his monkey friends in jungle.
Man picked to judge bull-fight because he is “no fairer to his friend than to his foe.”
Upright judge refuses a bribe: he is responsible to a higher tribunal called Conscience.
Oil well digger runs out of money, leaves the country, forgetting to tell his driller.
He returns fifty years later, finds the driller still drilling away.
Man keeps promise to return to be eaten by tiger: let go without harm.
Rabbi returns jewel found with bought ass.
He had not paid for it.
Prostrate soldier asks his enemy to stab him in the chest instead of the back in order to save his honor.
The captor frees him and the two become friends.
Each cites instances of his laziness.
Man lets legs burn in fire rather than move them.
Man is burned to death because he is too lazy to put out spark.
He is too lazy to stop rats from playing with lighted candle.
Man too lazy to open eyes to see where fire is burning.
Three lazy beggars burn alive rather than run away from burning castle.
Mother calls to daughter to tell her that she (daughter) is standing on a live coal.
The daughter asks which foot the coal is under.
Man will not lift knife to cut rope about to hang him.
Man will not move in bed when water drops in his eyes.
Man so lazy that he will not wipe his running nose.
This causes him to lose prospective bride.
Man floating in river too lazy to drink.
Man too lazy to pick up berries (dates).
Lazy servant gets others to perform his duties.
Servant to call his master at daybreak: looks into dark closet to see if it is yet light.
Servant to close door at night: leaves it open so that he will not have to open it next morning.
“If it is day, give me food; if it is night, let me sleep.”
The master has told the servant to go to work.
Boy to see whether it is raining: calls dog (cat) in and feels of his paws.
Boy to see whether there is fire in the house: feels of cat to see if she is warm.
The boy eats breakfast, dinner, and supper one immediately after the other; then lies down to sleep.
Lazy boy always says that it is raining.
The peasant and the boy sleep during the rain in the hay barn. When the peasant asks, the boy always says that it is still raining.
Lazy boy says he cannot walk.
Servant tells master to cover his face: no need to put out lamp.
Lazy wife in soiled dress thinks husband is bringing her a new dress from market.
Lazy wife must hold cat and is scratched.
Lazy wife throws bread out of window instead of putting it back into oven.
Lazy wife beaten by husband maintains that she has done nothing. That is why he is beating her.
Supposed dead husband comes back to life and gives his wife a beating, because there was no shirt even in the event of death.
“Who will not work, shall not eat.”
Lazy mother given shoes of cotton; son knows that she will not wear them out.
Lazy girl does not know where the spring is.
Lazy man asked direction only points with his foot.
Lazy dog wakes only for his meals.
Man in mud too lazy to take hand extended to help him up.
Lazy son-in-law: afraid of a dog.
Ruler is too lazy to stop quarrels.
Man with stolen fig in his mouth submits to having cheek lanced rather than open his mouth.
Man is so lazy that he starves rather than open his mouth for food to fall in when it falls from trees.
Working independently, the lazy fellow spoils the materials received
Lazy man asks if wood is split before he accepts it as a gift.
Lazy man is being taken to poorhouse or out of town or to cemetery to be buried alive.
The group take pity on him, offer him various articles to help him get started again. One offers a bushel of corn.
Lazy man misses seeing the sheriff’s funeral; he is facing the wrong way as the procession passes.
Man digs three potatoes in one day: one dug, one being dug, one about to be dug.
Man weeds garden from cushioned rocking chair, using fire tongs to reach weeds.
Woman becomes clean only after three washings and the use of three pounds of soap.
Rancher is not recognized by his wife and family after he has cleaned up in town at hotel.
Old woman reaches town before vain fop who stops to adjust clothes.
Plain people made rulers have vain display.
Wasp seeking fame stings courtiers: killed.
Wealthy man pretends enjoyment of good music.
Use of strange language to show one’s high education.
Jackal forces all animals who come to drink to praise him like a king.
Neglected wife given trifle boasts of it.
Hunter wants to be shown lion tracks, not lion himself.
Coward boasts when there is no danger.
Crow sits on sheep’s back; afraid to sit on dog’s.
Dogs tear up lion skin: fear living lion.
Coward gloats over robber slain by another person.
Monkey safe in tree insults gorilla as “broken face”.
Cowardly soldier turns back when he hears raven’s croak.
Queen mother shames cowardly son and companions.
Cowardly spider rushes at fly but hides when wasp appears.
Coward gives his purse to thief with lame excuse.
Cowardly bridegroom flees elephant and loses bride.
The man who only tasted wine.
Will not drink but gets drunk nevertheless by frequent tasting.
Greedy animal eats poisoned fruit in spite of warning.
Gluttonous wife eats all the meal while cooking it.
New son-in-law given choice of meals eats all.
Pupil eats cakes given as alms for his master.
Husband eats wife’s share of food as well as his own.
Monk obedient only as long as work is agreeable.
Always says that unpleasant work is beneath his dignity.
Hog tired of his daily food.
Goes to the judge and gets better food assigned to him, but the fox cheats him out of it.
In kingdom of lions laments that he always gets the worst bits of food.
Say that it makes their water unusable.
Monk dissatisfied with things as he has them is admonished to take what he receives from God.
Sparrow dissatisfied with pond water wants to go to sea.
Profligate wastes entire fortune before beginning his own adventures.
Prince penalizes cursing, although he himself curses.
Woman admires marvelous shot of hero which kills deer, but angers him when she begs mercy for the deer.
Look! look! she cries from the barrel.

A nobleman has arranged for a peasant girl to become his mistress. When he comes to take her away he cannot find her. Disappointed, he is about to depart when the girl, who has hidden in a barrel, calls out “Look!” She really wants to be found.
Harlot weeps when her impoverished lover leaves her to think that she has left him his coat.
Visiting friends take everything from house of dying man.
Visitors of sick stag eat up all his provisions so that he starves.
Hospitable man impoverished by greedy guests.
Wolves devour an ox without leaving a share for the rightful owner.
Snake and weasel stop fighting in order to catch mouse.
Father-in-law sued for breach of contract because he does not die in two years as he has predicted.
Hog with broken leg refuses to tell another where peas are to be found.
Old man before dying eats his money. In church, son wants to cut corpse open and get the money.
Thieves quarrel over booty: owner comes.
Greedy person (animal) gets hand (head) stuck in food jar.
Greedy man tries to stuff food into his nostrils as well as into his mouth.
Fox spoils his food rather than divide with ape.
Man had rather be burned alive than to share food with a guest.
Stingy dead woman raises her head to correct account of laundress, who is overcharging her daughter.
Stingy man forced to share his money when he lies and says he has none.
Stingy woman will not give soup to man until she spills it.
Then she says he may have the soup.
Stingy king will not hire soldiers: defeated.
Spider in stingy woman’s house grows thin.
Stingy horse refuses ass little feed, though he promises much for later time.
Stingy man cancels invitations to his guests.
Drummer drums for own wedding so as to save expense.
Stingy men love possessions so much that they wear out their feet to save shoes.
Farmer gets help up early in morning for a light breakfast: a glass of water and a lantern.
Stingy farmer encourages help by promise of hot lunch.
The servant discovers that the hot lunch is a mustard sandwich.
Master insists that maid whistle when she brings in the dessert.
He is afraid she will eat the raisins out of the cakes.
Master insists that servants whistle as they pick strawberries so that they cannot eat any.
The stingy man and his animals.
A stranger notices that man’s cows need feed, feeds them.
They die of the shock of being fed.
Man who insists on using everything that is useful.
Man finds a bunghole lying around loose, has cooper build a barrel around it.
Man saves sausage skins, sends them back for refilling.
Stingy man does not eat butter; only looks at it and enjoys the thought.
Wife of stingy man prays that her husband become sick so that she can get better food.
Wife keeps half of the money she plans to give for a shrine.
Miser’s heart found in his strong-box.
Miserly husband spies on wife to see that she does not eat too much.
Gets burned in the chimney and beaten in the bed where he hides.
Miserly husband spies on wife, lest she cook too much.
Miserly wife exposed to guests by her husband.
Man is so miserly that he never drinks wine until it becomes strong.
Friar so miserly that he stays in ditch three days before “lending” a hand to his rescuers.
Miser dreams that he spends some money.
Miser decides not to commit suicide.
Does not want the expense of a rope.
Miser is given rope to hang himself.
Miser annoys merchant so much over the price of a rope that the latter gives it to him provided he will hang himself as he plans to do.
Miser appoints himself as the sole heir of his own estate.
Miser decides to kill his pigs himself.
“You get no benefit from your wealth.” Proves his folly.
Miser dies because he will not buy a candle.
Dying miser tells son to extinguish candle just as soon as he dies.
Miser runs back home to put out lamp left burning.
Miser is kidnapped and held for ransom.
Wood dealer prays for raja’s death so that he can sell sandal wood for funeral pyre.
Miser tries to reduce sacrifice promised to god.
Miser prays to enter heaven with his clothes on: gold coins sewn into undergarments.
Man dismissed after years of service with a pittance.
Dismisses him and charges him for a rope which he had cut while saving the usurer from hanging.
Man ungrateful for rescue by animal.
Crane pulls bone from wolf’s throat: wolf refuses payment.
“That you were allowed to take your beak from my throat is payment enough.” (Cf.
Lion rescued from net by rat: eats rat.
Tiger has thorn pulled by man: attacks man.
Hunter beats dog which has grown old in his service.
Dog tries to bite man rescuing him from well.
Ungrateful fox hits with tail the man who carries him across stream.
Man kills whale which carried him home across sea.
Man who has been rescued from pit tries to kill his monkey rescuer for food.
Ungrateful ape plucks feathers from heron who has carried him across water.
Ungrateful wanderer pulls nut tree to pieces to get the nuts.
Wanderers in shade of plane tree blame it for not bearing fruit.

A traveler saves a monkey, a snake, a tiger, and a jeweler from a pit. The monkey gives him fruit; the tiger a necklace of a princess he has killed. The jeweler accuses the rescuer before the king. The serpent saves him by biting the prince and then showing the man the proper remedy.
Man rescued from drowning kills rescuer.
Whales rescue drowning king who planned to kill them.
Tiger returns rope to former captor: rewarded by having tail cut off.
Man kills his rescuer in order to collect reward.
Knight is ungrateful for rescue in battle.
Ungrateful Brahmin brings his wild goose rescuer to king as remedy against leprosy.
Benefactor falsely accused of theft by ungrateful youth.
Woman who saves suitor from death is later condemned to die by the ingrate.
Kind magistrate is victim of ingratitude.
Gives lawbreaker a light sentence. The latter seduces the magistrate’s wife.
Ruler persecutes his friends and is kind to his enemies.
Man beheads rescuer for leaving him so long in pain.
Man ungrateful for life saved because rescuer helped others also.
Ungrateful Jew steals horse of Christian who has lent it to him.
Man beats people bearing him gifts.
Workers (builder) killed when secret building or grave is finished.
Person compared to nettle, which stings the hand that protects it.
Man fails to feed his animal rescuer.
Man sets dogs onto bear after bear has carried him home to safety.
Man trades an egg for a needle, demands treat of a gill of rum, the traditional reward for traders.
The storekeeper gives him the rum; he asks for an egg in it. The storekeeper breaks an egg (the one he has just traded the needle for) into the rum. It has two yolks; the trader asks for two needles.
Man works his horses to death, then complains that borrowed horse overeats.
Wizard makes pupil think himself Emperor and exposes pupil’s ingratitude.
Hardhearted horse allows ass to be overburdened until it is crushed.
Horse must then assume the load.
Old bullock deserted and left to die.
Man helping another across stream drops him when he learns that he has lost his high position.
Man unable to weep for hardness of heart.
Hardhearted person refuses reprieve for father’s murderers.
Permission refused to drink from water tank.
Has no use for the manger but refuses to give it up to the horse.
Priest uses fortune dishonestly made to erect monuments to himself.
Three envoys debate as to which of them should be received with the greatest honor.
Son ashamed of his peasant father who brings him money. Father disinherits him.
Humble man after speaking to king disdains his own family.
Ass after associating with lion disdains his own family.
Two stubborn goats meet each other on a bridge.
Neither will step aside; both fall into water.
Woman’s stubbornness causes loss of chance to go on pilgrimage.
Man winks both at buyer and seller.
He tries to appear friendly to both.
Sister gives due honor and regard to brother only in times of his prosperity.
Sheep jealous of dog because he does nothing.
Do not consider that he guards the flock.
King kills architect after completion of great building, so that he may never again build one so great.
Architect kills pupil who has surpassed him in skill.
Architect commits suicide when he discovers that his pupil has surpassed him in skill.
Raven wants to be as white as a swan.
Jealous fox betrays wolf to peasant and then appropriates wolf’s cave and food.
Peasant kills him in a few days.
Raven jealous of partridge’s way of flying.
Jealousy of Venus in the love of Psyche and Cupid.
Ruler who is jealous of his subjects’ happiness prohibits their games.
He stops crying so that after a rest he can cry louder than ever.
Man demonstrates his violence of temper.
He overhears a man tell of his temper. In anger he enters and demands to know when he has ever lost his temper.
Prayer that overbearing knight’s illness be increased.
A little sickness has made him kind; more may make him kinder.
Man so angered that he refuses to pay his workmen.
Monk loses temper at cup and breaks it.
Violence of judge’s temper leads him to have men given death sentence unjustly.
Man extorts large price for betel leaf from addict.
Goose and turkey envious of peacock point out its ugly legs and voice.
The boy: “If I had one and then got two more, I should have three.”
“I am not alone!” Man travelling alone through the forest at night, is afraid of robbers.
Eager warriors go through tent wall.

Animals one by one join the procession. The funeral carriage breaks down or the procession drowns.
(Der Tod des Hühnchens.) The cock chokes and the hen seeks aid of objects and persons (stream, tree, pig, miller, baker, etc.).
The death of the little hen.
She is characteristically mourned by objects and animals; e.g., flea, door, broom, cart, ashes, tree, girl.
The death of the little hen described with unusual words.
Little ant finds a penny, buys new clothes with it, and sits in her doorway.

Various animals pass by and propose marriage. She asks what they do at night. Each one replies with its characteristic sound, and none pleases her but the quiet little mouse, whom she marries. She leaves him to tend the stew, and he falls in and drowns. She weeps and, on learning the reason, bird cuts off its beak, dove cuts off its tail, etc.
She begs off; he goes to kill rooster .... goose, rabbit, toad, tiger.
Mourning about the dead ass (Tulsi Das): from washerman to the queen.
Chains involving the eating of an object.
A woman makes a pancake, which flees. Various animals try in vain to stop it. Finally the fox eats it up.
While the mistress is away, the cat eats the porridge, the bowl, and the ladle.
A troll eats the watcher’s five horses and finally the watcher himself. The master goes to investigate.
Louse and crow make covenant of friendship: louse eats crow despite crow saying, “If I strike you once with my beak you will disappear; how then can you talk of eating me?”
Likewise louse eats loaf of bread, she-goat, cow, buffalo, five sepoys, wedding procession with one lakh of people, elephant, tank of water. A sepoy cuts louse in two with his sword and rescues all.

By his singing the wolf compels the old man to surrender his cattle, his children and grandchildren, and finally his wife. The old woman goes in the wolf’s service. She returns home bringing butter, etc.
Chains involving other events without interrelation of members.
The goat who would not go home.
One animal after another tries in vain to persuade the goat to go home. Finally a wolf (bee) bites him and drives him home.
The goat who would not leave the hazel bush.
There was a wee wee woman who had a wee wee cow, etc.
The crow on the tarred bridge.
His beak and tail alternately stick.
Where have you been, goose?—In the fields.
Titmouse, what are you eating?—A large turnip—etc.
Sparrow, where are you going? —To eat seed.
The hen lays an egg, the mouse breaks it.
Sorrowing over this mishap, all show extraordinary behavior; the master puts an end to it.
Mother ties bell on child; cat cuts it off.
Girl left in tree by sisters: asks monkey, ape, bear, and tiger to put her down or else bite her.
Small grain-measure runs away when her husband beats her: succession of suitors.
Series of things acquired by mouse.
“You cannot have this but you may have that instead,” etc. Clod—fish—cakes—kid—goat—drum—girl. Girl kills mouse accidentally.
The old woman and her pig.
Her pig will not jump over the stile so that she can go home. She appeals in vain for help until the cow gives her milk.
Woman has meat (liver) stolen by bird.
Crow must wash his bill in order to eat with other birds.
Asks water; water must first have horn from stag, who must first have milk from cow, etc.
Wind obeys and breaks the chain.

The cat bites off the mouse’s tail and will return it in exchange for milk. The mouse goes to the cow for milk, the farmer for hay, the butcher for meat, the baker for bread. Other persons mentioned are the locksmith and the miner.
Mouse bursts open when crossing a stream.
My dog picked up a string, but did not wish to give it to me unless I gave her bread.

Cupboard did not wish to give bread unless I gave it a key; smith, charcoal; charcoal-burner, calf’s legbone; butcher, milk; cow, grass; meadow, water; clouds, dove’s feather. Dove gave me a feather which I gave to clouds, etc.
Lending and repaying: progressively worse (or better) bargain.
Bird’s pea gets stuck in socket of mill-handle.
She goes to carpenter, king, queen, who refuse to help. She asks snake to bite queen, stick to beat snake, fire to burn stick, etc.
Gram (parched grain) sticks in post ; parrot goes to raja, etc., for help.
The wormwood does not want to rock the sparrow.
Boy dirties his shoe and asks the hay stack to wipe it clean.
Pulling the needle out of the seamstress’s hand.
The lazy servant and the grain.
The Esdras chain: stronger and strongest, wine, king, woman, truth.
At nightfall Abraham worships a star, then the moon, then the sun, and finally gives up idolatry.
Brahmin worships idol and sets sacrifices before it daily.

Rat devours offerings and he sets it up as his idol as a being more powerful than his idol. When cat devours rat, he worships it instead. His wife accidentally kills the cat, so he sets her up to worship. He happens to slap her and she loses consciousness. Thereafter he worships himself as most powerful after all.
A mouse throws a nut down and hits the cock on the head. He also steals the cock’s whiskers. The cock goes to get an old woman to cure him.
Toad asks magpie in tree to throw down a chestnut.

Magpie refuses, saying it might break its beak. Toad promises, if that happens, to get a horsehair to tie it up again. Magpie throws chestnut and breaks beak. Toad asks ass for hair, but ass first demands grass; mower demands sheep; shepherd, pup; mother dog, bread; baker, stumps. Toad cuts the stumps and gets the hair.
The cock strikes out the hen’s eye with a nut.

The cock blames the hazel bush for tearing its knickers, the hazel bush the goat for gnawing at it, the goat the shepherd-boy for not tending it, the boy his mistress for not baking him a bun, the mistress the pig for eating up the dough, the pig the wolf for killing its young.
Nut hits cock in head: he thinks world is coming to an end.
He sends the hen to tell the duck, the duck to tell the goose, etc.
Fly frightens snake; snake frightens rats; rats frighten monkey, etc.
Boy changes self to nut; fowl eats nut; bush cat eats fowl; dog eats cat; dog swallowed by python.
Man invites animals to come and work in his field.
Rooster kills beetle; cat kills rooster; dog kills cat; leopard kills dog; hyena kills leopard; buffalo kills hyena; elephant kills buffalo, and lion chases elephant so that both fall into trap.
The house the old man was to build.
The woman for whom he is to build the house has some beans for him. The goat eats these up.
For want of a nail the shoe was lost, for want of a shoe the horse was lost, for the want of a horse the rider was lost .... and all for the want of a horseshoe nail.
Series of trick exchanges: razor—pot—bride—drum by tricky fox.
“I killed my grandmother because she refused to cook a hare.
I killed a priest because he said my crime was bad. A friar absolved me to avoid being killed.” (First ed.
Fat mouse cannot get into hole.
“Carpenter, please pare off a little flesh from my ribs.” Refused.

A man catches a mango-bird eating mangoes and strikes it against the roots of a mango-tree. The bird cannot be made to say it suffers from the blow. In turn, he puts it in water, strikes it on the ground, a stile, a door-frame, singes its feathers, cuts it up, cooks it, and eats it. The bird always expresses indifference in a cumulative rhyme. At last the bird asks him to look out of the window, whereupon it flies out of his nose and the man dies.
There was once a woman; the woman had a son; the son had red breeches; etc.
Where is the warehouse?—The fire burned it down.
“Where is that grain?” — “The cock snatched it.”
The wolf who wanted to make bread.
The farmer explained to him how bread is made.
Birds fight and cause series of accidents to other animals and people.
Man sharpening his dao is bitten by a prawn.

He cuts down a big bamboo; a fruit falls from bamboo and strikes a bird on the nape of the neck; the bird scratches up an ant’s nest with his feet; the ant bites a wild boar in the eye; and the boar bears down upon a plantain tree where a bat dwells under a leaf; the bat seeks refuge in the ear of an elephant, and the elephant kicks down the house on an old woman. She rushes out and falls into a well.
Cumulative tale: bird who seeks carpenter to release young caught in closed tree.
Beetle bites calf, calf bites cow, cow hoofs carpenter, carpenter beats wife, hunters save carpenter’s cow, carpenter releases birds.
Lizard eats cricket, frog eats lizard, snake eats frog, eagle eats snake, man shoots eagle; animals escape except lizard.
Who is guilty of the accident.
Finally the king finds out that the sea is guilty.
Thief breaks foot climbing wall to rob.
Suit against owner for dangerous wall.
Hermit must get cat to kill rats in hunt, cow to give cat milk, etc.
Chain of killings: bulbul destroys flower and is killed by cat; cat shaken by dog; dog killed by boy; boy sentenced to death by king.
The little old lady who swallowed a fly.
She swallows a spider to eat up the fly, a bird to eat up the spider, a dog to eat the bird, a cow to eat the dog. “The little old lady swallowed a horse
Builds cart, yokes frogs to it, arms himself with piece of reed, and proclaims war with king.
The animals with queer names: as hen (henny-penny), cock (cocky-locky), goose (goosey-poosey).
Various ways of expressing this idea. When black sheep turn white, when a dry branch sprouts, etc.
If person says he has gone to Butterby Church, he has not gone to church.
“He struck him such a blow that he remembered the milk he drank on the sixth day after he was born.”
The old and the new keys.
Hero marries his first sweetheart according to the proverb that the old key is better than the new.
“Bridegroom like the sun and bride like the moon.”
Formulas signifying fruitlessness, e.g. like putting a withe about sand, like mocking a beggar.
When explanation of phenomenon is asked, three explanations are offered of which the last is always the true one.
Proverb: one man for worship, two men for cultivation of a field, three men for a journey.
Red as blood, white as snow.
Often from blood on snow as a suggestion, a wish is made for a child (wife) with skin like snow and cheeks like blood, etc.
Red as blood, white as snow, (and black as a raven).
Usually applied to the cheeks, skin, and hair of a girl’s lover.
Series: white cock, red cock, black cock.
These crow at dawn and scatter ghosts.
Formulistic numbers: a number plus one (101, 1001, etc.).
Formula: three days and three nights.
Three chairs in heaven for three saints.
Three things that lead to hell (heaven).
Three innocent children: Ananias, Zacharias, Misael.
Three sods that none may escape: “The sod of his birth, the sod of his death, the sod of his burying.”
Three whom Christ raised from the dead.
Three persons who spoke immediately after birth.
Three weak things that are the strongest.
Three reasons why men should condemn wealth.
Three bad stories of the saints of Ireland.
Four places that cleanse the soul.
Four categories of souls at Judgment.
Four things that prevent the holy life.
Four things to which the glory of the world is compared.
Sending four messengers with four winds.
Five sighs we should vent over our sins.
Seven year’s peace with no killing of men.
Seven as a number in religious and social records.
Seven joys of the Virgin Mary.
Seven masses necessary to free soul from hell.
Seven to whom alms should be given.
Seven fair rivers in Inis Eidheand (Eden) in the East of Africa.
King with seven wives and seven mares.
The seven wives pregnant for seven years, the seven mares seven years in foal.
Nine materials used in building Tower of Babel.
Eight miracles of Christ’s body in the sacrament.
Fifteen characteristics of a good (bad) woman.
Twenty-two rooms and twenty-two doors built by skillful carpenter.
Seven years, seven months, seven days.
Seven years as length of course in school.
Every third year as period of tribute.
After four days—another two days—another day.
Formula: as many children as holes in a sieve.
Three-fourths of men of Ireland die in one night.
I’ll huff and I’ll puff till I blow your house in.
Formula for other world: “Where no man goes and no crow flies.”
“A tree on island beyond the seven seas and the sixteen rivers.”
Names of giants (Fomorians) with sinister significance.
Death imprisoned by a soldier in a magic knapsack, bottle or nutshell.
While he is bound no one can die.
Death allegorically personified as an animal made up of several different animals.
Death (fate) assumes various forms to destroy men.
Salt in food given Death’s messengers renders them harmless.
Life personified: old woman carrying healing potions and salves.
Man takes case against wind for damages.
Wanting to have nothing to do with a court, the wind generously makes good the damages, and punishes the judge guilty of bribery.
Waves as tresses of sea-god’s wife.
Truth leaves city because there is no place left for her.
“Time” overpowered when weight is taken from his clock.
Twelve months as youths seated about fire.
Fury personified as demon which enters man’s heart and counsels evil.
Valor personified as bird which flutters over champion’s head.
Sin personified as the goddess Venus with her train of nymphs.
Poverty personified as diseased beggar woman.
Fortune personified as a matron in fine clothing.
Wine personified in person of the god Bacchus.
Depreciated, takes revenge by becoming colder; praised, makes reward, gives clothing.
Ladder as symbol of upward progress.
Ladder to heaven as symbol of saint.
Virginity, Wisdom, and Prophecy personified as three beautiful maidens.
Color of flag (sails) on ship as message of good or bad news.
Colors corresponding to the four world quarters.
Color symbolism of the cardinal points.
Symbolism of colors in mass vestments.
Bridegroom inadvertently buys for bride cloth suitable only for widows.
Red garment to show anger of king.
Martyrs called “red wheat”; saints, “Dei triticum” (God’s wheat).
Mill in which two men are slain said to grind “red wheat”.
White rose the symbol of death.
Brown hair as sign child is descended from goddess.
Ring broken as token of broken engagement.
Princess crushes lotus-flower to show that she will be submissive.
Gray hair the symbol of departed usefulness.
Various figures employed to show it is not good for one warrior alone to fight the battles of a host.
Arthur’s Round Table symbolic of round earth.
Message or orders given symbolic action.
Inverted shoes at doors to indicate banishment.
Message delivered by means of the fingers, etc.
Witch, aided by dragon (lion) is vanquished by maiden, aided by lamb (ram). Witch is devil; maiden, church of Christ.
Mill turned by the water of the grace of God as symbol of saint.
Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away as joint adventurers.
Of brothers (sometimes twins taken from body of slain mother) one is abandoned and becomes wild. Later he joins his brother.
Brothers deliberately seek dangers they have been warned against.
Seven mothers each with a child imprisoned. Six eat their children to keep from starving. Seventh does not. He rescues all the mothers and becomes hero.
Supernatural origin of hero: magic conception.
Hero with extraordinary animal companions (cock, goat, cow, horse).
Spot below right ear only vulnerable one.
Leprosy cured by holy water except on thumb.
Man can be injured only in armpits.
Only one thing will kill a certain man.
Person can be killed only by red-hot spits being thrust through soles of his feet.
Giant ogre can be killed only with iron club he carries (with own sword).
Only one person can overtake hero.
Sword which will break in only one peril: this known only to the maker of the sword.
Ogre vulnerable only when his face is turned away when he is struck.
Only one way to besiege certain city.
Object will fit only one thing (or person).
Only one ferule fits certain staff.
Vessel from which nothing can be drunk save through certain tube.
Only one person refuses to weep at hero’s death.
All trees except aspen refuse to make Christ’s cross.
All snakes but one placated by music.
In snake den prisoner fails to placate one snake and loses his life.
Only one person left from destruction of his community.
